title: செல்வம் நிலையாமை
theme: Wealth does not stay with anyone: the feasting rich end up begging and kings lose their wives to enemies. Because death is near and certain, wealth should be shared and spent on virtue now, and the hoarder who neither enjoys nor gives has in effect already lost it.
structure_note: The quatrains move from examples of reversal (1-3) to the urgency created by death (4-7), then to the folly of the rich who forget it (8) and the hoarder's loss (9-10).
source_issues: Shanmuganar's commentary throughout chapters 1-5 ends with a running number (61 for quatrain 1 to 110 for quatrain 50) and carries section headings numbered 8 to 12; the text matches the right quatrains, so the numbers seem to come from his edition.
Quatrain 6: the Tamil reads பிழைத்தெரிணஇக், apparently garbled; Mudaliar glosses ஒரீஇ, suggesting பிழைத்தொரீஇ. Mudaliar also glosses அகவா where the verse has இகவா.
Quatrain 10: the last word appears as கா஢ with a garbled character; Mudaliar's gloss கரி (witness) gives the reading.
Quatrain 10: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: Those who ate erewhile, course after course, food of six flavours, supplied by their complaisant spouse, now roam as paupers and beg a mess of pottage here and there; if so, let wealth be counted as a thing of nought!
reading: Those who once ate six-flavoured food served by a willing wife, waving away a second helping, may go begging for gruel somewhere; so wealth is not a thing to be counted as lasting.
nuance: The detail of refusing the second mouthful sets the excess of the past against the single bowl of gruel begged later; the argument rests on a picture, not on a general claim.

pope: When you own ample wealth acquired by blameless means, with many sharing eat the grain that steers have trodden out! In centre poised prosperity stands with no man, but revolves like the waggon's wheel.
reading: When blameless wealth comes, from that very day share its food with many, because wealth never stays level with anyone but turns like a cart wheel.
nuance: துகள்தீர் (blameless) qualifies the wealth to be shared: the verse assumes it was rightly gained. Mudaliar reads the food trodden out by beasts as a hint that others have a share in it.

pope: Those who rode resplendent forth on the neck of an elephant, beneath the state umbrella's shade, as the leaders of the host, when 'other deeds' destroy, shallchange and fall, while foes lead away their wives as captives.
reading: Even kings who rode in state on elephants under the royal umbrella, at the head of armies, fall and are changed when their deeds turn against them, and enemies take the wives they married.
nuance: Both commentators take ஏனை வினை as evil deeds that destroy; Pope keeps it as 'other deeds'. The verse itself names only 'the other deeds', so the cause of the fall is left in the vocabulary of karma rather than of war.

pope: The things of which you said, ‘they stand, they stand,' stand not; mark this, and perform what befits, yea! what befits, with all your power! Your days are gone, are gone! and death close pressing on is come, is come!
reading: Realise that the things you think will stand do not stand, and do what good you can at once, for your days are passing and Death is coming in anger.
nuance: Mudaliar notes that the first two doublings express abundance and the last two continuity: the form of the verse enacts days going and Death arriving.

pope: When you have gained and hold in hand any single thing, retain it not with the thought, ‘This will serve some other day!’ Those who have given betimes shall escape the desert road along which death, an unyielding foe, drags his captives away.
reading: Whatever comes into your hand, do not hold it back thinking it can be given later; those who gave first will escape the waste land through which impartial Death drags his captives.
nuance: கோடில் makes Death impartial: it is the one force that does not favour the rich, which is why only what was given away counts.

pope: Man's days pass not their assigned bound. None here on earth have ever escaped death's power, made off and got free. O hoarder of ample wealth, dispense it! On the morn the funeral drum will sound.
reading: The appointed span of days cannot be exceeded and no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped; you who hold great wealth, give it away, for tomorrow the funeral drum may sound.
nuance: Mudaliar glosses the 'appointed day' as the lifespan set by past deeds, and cites Kural 269 for the verb குதித்தல், the very verb the verse uses to deny that anyone escapes.

pope: Death every day takes that fount of light the sun as a measure, metes out your days, and so devours.Do deeds of virtue full of kindly grace. Though all are born, none are exempt from death.
reading: Using the sun as a measure, Death daily measures out and eats your days, so do much virtue and be compassionate; the closing line is read in more than one way.
nuance: The image makes each sunrise a scoop of grain taken from one's store of days. Pope reads the last line as 'none who are born escape death', which is a third reading beside the two commentators'.

pope: The ample wealth of men of mean understanding, who say, ' We're rich,' yet ponder not their path and end, appears, and perishes, and leaves no trace; like the flash, when the black thunder-cloud by night opens its mouth.
reading: The great wealth of the petty-minded, who say 'we are rich' and never think of where they must go, appears like lightning from a dark cloud at night and vanishes without a trace.
nuance: Both commentators take 'where they must go' as the next world, so the fault is not having wealth but forgetting the journey it cannot make.

pope: He eats not, sheds no light of splendour around, performs no deeds that merit lofty praise, soothes no sorrow that choice friends feel, spends nought, but hoards his wealth in vain : “Aha! he's lost it all,' shall men pronounce.
reading: One who neither eats, nor wins honour, nor does deeds of renown, nor relieves the distress of close kin, nor gives, but only guards his wealth in vain, will be thought of with pity as one who has lost it.
nuance: The miser is pronounced to have lost his wealth while he still holds it: possession without use is already loss.

pope: Those who stint in clothes and food, and mortify their bodies, yet do not deeds of deathless virtue, and bestow nothing, hoarding shall suffer loss:— Lord of the cloud-capped hills !--this the hoarding honey-bee attests. ---------
reading: Those who stint on clothing and food, wear down their bodies, do no lasting good and give nothing, will lose what they hoard, as the honey bee's store shows.
nuance: Mudaliar spells out the comparison: as someone else takes the honey the bees gathered, thieves and others take the hoard. The verse names only the bee as witness.

title: இளமை நிலையாமை
theme: Youth does not last: old age, the loss of friends and the decay of the beloved's body come to everyone, and death can take the young as well as the old. The wise therefore renounce early and do virtue while they have the means.
structure_note: Quatrains 11-18 picture the coming of old age, several through the desired woman who will herself grow old (14, 17); 19-20 turn to death's taking the young, and urge virtue without delay.
source_issues: Quatrain 16: Mudaliar's commentary begins with glosses on this quatrain and then continues with the closing of his note on quatrain 7 (the citation of Kural 37 and the sun-as-measure figure). Only the opening glosses belong here.
Quatrain 20: Shanmuganar's commentary is missing; the field holds only the heading of the next chapter.
Quatrain 14: Mudaliar glosses சென்றாள், a word not in the printed quatrain, which suggests a variant text.

pope: "Grey eld will come,’—the wise remembering this renounce the world even in tender age; but they who joy in youth, unstable, never free from fault, shall erewhile painfully rise up leaning on a staff.
reading: Knowing that grey hair will come, the wise renounced in childhood itself, while those who delighted in faulty, fleeting youth will later rise painfully leaning on a staff.
nuance: குழவியிடத்தே ('in infancy') pushes renunciation as early as language allows; the verse treats the foresight of age, not age itself, as the mark of wisdom.

pope: Served are the ties of friendship; minished are the pleasant ones; love's bonds are loosened too; then look within and say, what profit is there in this joyous life of thine ? The cry comes up as from a sinking ship!
reading: The cords of friendship are cut, those once close have drawn back, the bonds of love have come loose: look within and ask what profit there is in living on, for misery has come as on a sinking ship.
nuance: The verse is spoken to an ageing person, perhaps the speaker himself (உட்காணாய், 'look within'). Pope's 'joyous life' is his addition; the Tamil asks only about the gain of living.

pope: Speech falters, they lean on a staff, and walk tottering, their teeth fall out; yet, till the vessel (the body) is scorned by all, they linger in the house, still indulging fond desires; to these no way of safety opens out.
reading: Those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff, walk unsteadily and lose their teeth, yet stay in the house with their eyes on desire until the body is scorned, have no way to the path of safety.
nuance: Both commentators take the 'path of safety' as the way to release and இல்செறிந்து as clinging to household life, so the verse faults not old age but desire that outlives the body's capacity.

pope: To men that cherish weak desire for her that's doomed to droop and fail, supporting her palsied limbs with a staff, and then to fall and pass away, what anguish comes, when she grasps in her hands the staff her mother held!
reading: When a once-desired woman, bent, frail, head shaking and leaning on a staff, comes to hold the staff her mother held, she becomes a torment to men of unsteady mind who still desire her.
nuance: அணங்கு is read by Mudaliar as an enchanting goddess and by Shanmuganar and Pope as pain; the line is hard, and the readings below differ on whose mother is meant.

pope: My mother bare me, left me here, and went to seek her mother, who in the selfsame manner has gone in search; and thus in ceaseless round goes on the mother-quest. Such is the grace this world affords !
reading: My mother left me here and went in search of her mother, and that mother did the same; this world goes on, mother seeking mother, a pitiable thing.
nuance: Shanmuganar reads the 'seeking' as taking a new birth, so the chain is the cycle of births; Pope and Mudaliar keep it as each generation following the last into death. அளித்து is read as 'pitiable' by Mudaliar's gloss எளிமையுடைத்து; Pope renders it ironically as 'grace'.

pope: The lamb in the ruddy slaughter-house will crop the fragrant shoots that dangle from the garland in the slayer's hand; such transient gladness of the thoughtless, youthful hour is never found amid the wise.
reading: The fleeting joy of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling the tender leaves of the garland held before it in the slaughter ground, is not found among the wise.
nuance: The garland that feeds the lamb is the sign of its slaughter: youthful pleasure is enjoyed in the presence of what ends it.

pope: The sweet fruit from every tree that bears in the dewy grove must fall to earth. Thus youth decays. Desire not her whose eyes gleam bright as darts. Full soon she too will walk bent down, with a staff to aid her dim sight.
reading: Youth falls as fruit drops from every tree in a cool grove; do not desire this woman for her spear-like eyes, for she too will stoop and walk with a staff for eyes.
nuance: The wordplay turns வேல்கண்ணள் (spear-eyed) into கோல்கண்ணள் (staff-eyed): the same compound form names her beauty and her decline.

pope: ’How old are you ?' 'How last your teeth ?' and, ‘Do you eat two courses yet?' men ask with kindly courtesy. By such close questions urged, the wise will learn to judge the body as a thing of nought.
reading: Because others ask in turn, 'How old are you? How are your teeth? Do you still eat twice?', and so examine one's body, the wise do not count on the body's vigour.
nuance: The questions are polite and routine; the verse's point is that such solicitude already treats one as declining. Mudaliar records two readings of இருசிகை, a second mouthful or two meals a day.

pope: Say not, 'in after time we'll learn virtue, we're young;' but while wealth is yours conceal it not; do virtuous deeds. When evil tempests rage, not the ripe fruit alone, but the unripe fruit's fair promise also falls.
reading: Do not say 'we are young, we will learn good deeds later'; while wealth is in hand, do virtue without hiding it, for a harsh wind can drop good unripe fruit while the ripe stays on the tree.
nuance: Mudaliar notes the alternative reading of கனி ஒழிய as 'the ripe fruit remaining on the tree', which sharpens the point: death may take the young and leave the old.

pope: Relentless death is roaming round, and eyes his man! 'Tis true. Take up your wallet, scape betimes. He bears away the new-born babe, while the mother sorely laments. It is good to bear in mind his guile. --------
reading: Since merciless Death roams looking for his people, take provisions for the journey in good time; it is well to keep his stealth in mind, for he takes even the unborn child while its mother wails.
nuance: Mudaliar reads தோட்கோப்பு, a bundle carried on the shoulder, as the good deeds one needs for the next world; Pope renders it 'wallet'. The verse leaves the provisions as a figure.

title: யாக்கை நிலையாமை
theme: The body does not last: kings die like everyone, wedding drums turn into funeral drums, and the body is a bubble, a passing cloud or dew on grass that the life within leaves behind. Because of this, the body should be used for its proper fruit, virtue and service, while it lasts.
structure_note: Death's reach (21) and the sun as the measure of days (22) open the chapter; 23-26 dwell on funerals and the indifference of the corpse; 27-30 give images of the body's brevity, three of them with a call to act now.
source_issues: Quatrain 21: Pope's text runs on into his translation of quatrain 22 ('Time is fleeting, use it ...'), and quatrain 22 has no Pope translation aligned.
Quatrain 30: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
Quatrain 30: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: Even kings that rode on elephants beneath the state umbrella's shade, like the moon appearing over some bill, have had their names proclaimed on earth as dead ;— not any in this world have escaped. Time is fleeting,—use it As the measure of your days the shining orb each day unfailing rises; so before your joyous days have passed away, perform ye 'fitting deeds of grace'; for none abide on earth.
reading: Even kings who rode on elephants under umbrellas like the moon rising over a hill have been carried off and spoken of as dead; no one in this world has been left over.
nuance: Mudaliar takes தூற்றப்பட்டார் as 'were disparaged by many', while Pope has 'had their names proclaimed' and Shanmuganar 'spoken of lightly'; whether the dead kings are mocked or merely announced is left open by the verb.

reading: Because the bright sun, as the measure of one's days, rises without missing a day, do ஒப்புரவு before your days run out; no one stays on the earth beyond them.
nuance: ஒப்புரவு is the Kural's word for serving the community with one's means; Mudaliar cites Parimelazhagar's definition. He also says some read the last line in strained ways, without giving them. Pope's translation of this quatrain is attached to 21 in the source.

pope: The marriage drums that sounded out in the festive hall, there and that very day have served for him as funeral drums! Men of lofty minds will note that thus it haps, and will strive to gain the way to escape.
reading: The drums that sounded through the hall as wedding drums may sound that same day, in that same place, as funeral drums for the bridegroom; seeing this, the minds of the worthy hold fast to the way of escape.
nuance: The same instruments serve both rites; the verse makes the reversal one of meaning, not of sound. Shanmuganar names the way of escape as virtue.

pope: They march and then strike once! A little while they wait, then strike the drum a second time. Behold, how fine! The third stroke sounds. They veil it, take the fire, and go forth :—the dying bear the deed!
reading: The drummers beat once on arrival, wait a little and beat again, and at the third beat the corpse is covered and the fire taken up; the dying carry the dead.
nuance: நன்றேகாண் ('fine, see!') is sarcasm for Mudaliar and a question, 'is such a life good?', for Shanmuganar; either way the last line carries the point, that the bearers are already on the same road.

pope: To him, who, although he sees them bear the corpse to the burning ground, while friends in troops loudly lament, boldly asserts that wedded life is bliss on earth, the funeral drum speaks out, and mocks his vain utterance.
reading: To the one who sees kin wailing in crowds as a corpse is carried to the burning ground, yet marries and believes there is joy here, the funeral drum answers with its டொண் டொண் டொண்.
nuance: The poem sets the man's 'உண்டு உண்டு உண்டு' (there is, there is) against the drum's 'டொண் டொண் டொண்'; Mudaliar calls the drum's reply a poetic fancy. Pope's 'mocks his vain utterance' paraphrases that echo.

pope: When the 'soul', that, taking its stand in this skin clad frame, has fully wrought its works, and partaken of life's experiences, has gone forth, what matters it whether you attach ropes to the body and drag it away, or carefully bury it, or throw it aside in any place you light upon, or if many revile the departed ?
reading: Once the dancer who stayed in this skin bag and did its work has left, what does it matter whether the body is dragged off with a rope, buried with care, thrown anywhere or reviled by many?
nuance: The life is a performer and the body a costume; once it has gone, the treatment of the remains has no meaning. Mudaliar lists several readings of ஊட்டும், among them the life enjoying, or being made to enjoy, the fruit of its deeds.

pope: 'Like a bubble, that in pelting rain appears full oft, and disappears, is this our frame.' So sages have judged, steadfast in wisdom, and have decided to end this dubious strife. On this wide earth who equal these?
reading: Who on this wide earth equals those firm in understanding who see this body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts again and again, and resolve to end their wandering?
nuance: 'Again and again' (பல்காலும்) suggests repeated births as well as the bubble's quickness, and Mudaliar takes தடுமாற்றம் as the confusion of births. Shanmuganar reads it as worldly confusion.

pope: Those who've gained and held fast by this well-knit frame (a human body) should take the gain the body they have gained is intended to yield. Like a cloud that wanders over the hills, the body here appears, and abiding not, departs leaving no trace behind.
reading: Those who have a sturdy body should take the fruit that body can yield, for it appears like mist on a hill and departs there without staying.
nuance: The verse does not despise the body here; it treats it as a means whose use must be taken quickly. Shanmuganar names the fruit as virtue.

pope: Considering that all things are transient as the dew-drop on the tip of a blade of grass, now, now at once, do virtuous deeds! "Even now he stood, he sat, he fell—while his kindred cried aloud he died :' such is man's history!
reading: Knowing that the body lasts like water on the tip of a blade of grass, do virtuous deeds right now, for people say 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, and with his kin wailing he was gone'.
nuance: The four verbs compress a death into one breath of speech, the way it will be reported; Mudaliar supplies 'the body' as the subject of நிலையாமை.

pope: Unasked men come, appear in the home as kinsmen, and then silently go. As the bird silently deserts the tree where its nest yet remains, and goes far off, so these leave but their body to their friends. -----------
reading: Unasked they come and appear in the home as kin, and wordlessly they go, leaving the body to their own people as a bird flies far off leaving its nesting tree.
nuance: The double வாளாதே (silently) frames a life with two unannounced events, arrival and departure; family is a place of passage.

title: அறன் வலியுறுத்தல்
theme: An urging to virtue: human birth is rare and the body brief, so its fruit, virtue, must be gathered now. Those who live on the merit of past births without adding to it end at others' gates; those who have gathered it face death without grief, and even a small gift to the worthy grows vast.
structure_note: The chapter turns between the consequences of neglecting virtue (31-33), the body as a means to be used up for virtue (34-37), the growth of a small good (38), the passing of days (39) and, last, honour over a body kept alive by begging (40).
source_issues: Quatrains 31-38: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
Quatrain 31: the Tamil reads பறங்கடை, apparently for புறங்கடை (outer door), as Shanmuganar's வெளிக்கடைவாயில் and Pope's 'outer gate' suggest.
Quatrain 37: the Tamil has two apparent misprints, பொரும்பயனும் for பெரும்பயனும் and ஒப்புராவு for ஒப்புரவு.
Quatrain 40: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: ‘Yet those within are blest,' so saying, they look up, but obtain no entrance: their place is at the outer gate. There will they suffer much, who thro' lack of former penitence do no penance now. [In a former state penance won for them a human shape. As men they have now failed.]
reading: Those who, on the strength of earlier austerity, do no austerity now will look up at a house and say 'those inside are the ones who live', unable to enter, clinging to the outer door and grieving.
nuance: The quatrain implies merit is a stock that is used up: present comfort is paid for by past austerity, and without renewal the next state is the beggar's at the gate. Pope's main text reads the cause as a lack of former penance, but his bracketed note agrees with Shanmuganar that past penance won their present state.

pope: Say not, O silly soul, we will live desiring wealth and die forgetting virtue! We'll say that ceaselessly toiling thou shalt live long; but tell me, what wilt thou do when all thy happy days are over?
reading: Base heart, which says 'let us prosper, desiring wealth and forgetting virtue', even if you live on toiling without rest, your days are gone: tell me what you will do.
nuance: The address is to one's own heart (புலைநெஞ்சே), and the closing question is left unanswered; the speaker is arguing with himself.

pope: When the ‘fruit of deeds' is come, the fool sighs heavily, and all his soul dies out; but those who reflect and say, ,'Tis old desert,' will pass beyond the bound of life's perplexity, and escape (by devoting themselves to virtue).
reading: When the fruit of past deeds arrives, the fool sighs hotly and his mind breaks; those who think of what comes as old desert pass beyond the bounds of confusion and are freed.
nuance: Accepting suffering as the ripening of one's own past deeds is presented as the way out of the round itself, not only as consolation. Pope's 'by devoting themselves to virtue' is his addition.

pope: As the gain from the mortal frame now reached —and which is so hard to reach —with all thy might lay hold of virtue's lasting good. As the juice expressed from the sugar-cane 'twill afterwards be thine aid, when the body goes like refuse flung away.
reading: With the gain of having obtained this rare body, take its great fruit fully; like juice pressed from cane, it serves you afterwards, and the body goes like the crushed refuse.
nuance: The body is valued only as the cane is: for what can be pressed out of it. The juice, virtue, outlasts the body and is what helps 'afterwards'.

pope: Those who have pressed the sugar-cane, and early taken the juice, when the refuse heaped up burns, will suffer no grief: those who have toiled and gained the fruit won from embodied existence will feel no pangs when death shall come.
reading: As those who crushed their cane and took the jaggery early do not grieve when the refuse catches fire and burns, those who laboured to take the body's fruit feel no distress when Death comes.
nuance: சிறுகாலை (early) carries the argument: the jaggery was made in time. The burning of refuse quietly suggests cremation.

pope: ‘This day ?’ That day? What day? O question not the time! Bethink you death stands behind you ever waiting! Put from you every evil thing; and with all your powers embrace the virtue which sages teach.
reading: Without asking whether it is today, that day or some other day, think that Death stands right behind you; leave evil as far as you can and hold to the virtue the worthy practise.
nuance: ஒல்லும் வகையால் (as far as you can) sets a measure within reach, unlike the absolute demands of renunciation elsewhere in these chapters.

pope: When you examine closely the mighty gains to be acquired by birth in a human shape, if they seem manifold, perform not deeds which suit the body's frame alone, but deeds whose fruit is joy in the world to come!
reading: If the gains that come through human birth are many when examined, one should not live doing service only to the gathered-up body, but should act so as to enjoy them in the world above.
nuance: The verse applies ஒப்புரவு, normally service to the community, to the body itself, ironically: serving the body is a misplaced kind of duty.

pope: The banyan seed, though it be minute as one might see in dreams, grows to a mighty tree of amplest shade; so gifts from a virtuous hand, received by a worthy hand, though small, will hide the diminish'd heavens.
reading: As a banyan seed of the smallest size grows and casts a vast shade, so the fruit of virtue, though small, when it reaches the hands of the worthy, spreads so that the sky seems small.
nuance: The growth depends on the recipient: தக்கார் கைப்பட்டக்கால் (if it falls into worthy hands). Pope reads உறக்கும் துணைய as 'minute as one might see in dreams'; Shanmuganar renders the size differently, but both make the seed tiny.

pope: Daily they see the passing day added to the sum of the days gone by, as a day that is spent from out the store of their days, yet daily, as they see day dawn, they say joyously, 'This day will abide with us till the close of day?’
reading: Seeing day follow day, they do not grasp it, and rejoice each day that the day will pass well; they do not count each passing day as a day taken from their own lives.
nuance: The quatrain plays வைகல் (day; passing) through eight forms, so the sound of repetition becomes the experience it describes. Mudaliar reports another reading of வைகுதல் as 'staying', and supplies the unstated conclusion: the wise would act on virtue at once.

pope: Parting with honour's jewel I might still consent to live a suppliant's life of shame, if when maintained by such disgrace, this body could abide in strength and last for length of days. --------------
reading: I would put off the rare jewel of honour and live by the shame of begging, if a body fed by such disgrace would gain strength and last.
nuance: The conditional is counterfactual: the body will not last, so honour is never worth selling for it. Mudaliar notes the particle மன் signals exactly this unfulfilled 'I would'.

title: தூய்தன்மை
theme: The body is impure: beneath skin, perfume and garlands it is a vessel of flesh, fluids and filth, and in death it is food for vultures and a grinning skull. Desire for a woman's body rests on not seeing this, and the renunciant who has seen it is not moved by the conventional praise of eyes and teeth.
structure_note: Quatrains 41-43 strip off the body's coverings, 44-45 give the renunciant's own refusal in parallel verses on eyes and teeth, 46-48 list what the body is and what becomes of it, and 49-50 let the skulls of the dead speak.
source_issues: Quatrain 44: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text of quatrain 45 and his commentary on it, which is repeated under 45.
Quatrain 41: Mudaliar glosses துச்சிலை where the printed verse reads புக்கிலை, suggesting a variant text.
Quatrain 45: the Tamil has misprints, விடுவெனோ for விடுவேனோ and வேன3 for வேன்.
Quatrain 46: Mudaliar glosses எத்திறத்தான் (masculine) where the verse reads எத்திறத்தாள்.
Quatrain 50: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter, and its opening is garbled (கண்டார் அஞ் நகைத்து).

pope: ‘O gentle maiden, fair and good !' These paragons that thus rave, know they not 'the heavenly home invisible?’ Let a bit of skin be broken slight as an insect's wing, and you need the stick that drives a way the crows !
reading: The 'worthies' who cry 'O fair, lovely girl': do they not see the body's paltry dwelling? If skin the size of a fly's wing is torn from it, a stick is needed to drive away the crows.
nuance: Both commentators take புக்கில் as the body, a temporary lodging of the life; Pope renders it 'the heavenly home invisible'. Mudaliar notes that சான்றவர் (worthies) is used ironically for the petty-minded. The crows show how little stands between the admired body and carrion.

pope: If the body which, with a covering of skin above, possesses many apertures, owes its beauty only to that outward cloak that veils the false (the inner foulness), then is it fitting to say no word of lustful desire which hides the false from itself by the covering veil, but to regard that body as an undeveloped embryo.
reading: If the body, full of openings beneath its skin, is handsome only through an outer covering that hides its falsity, then without speaking desire one should look at it as a bag turned inside out.
nuance: The commentators agree on the bag turned inside out; Pope instead renders பைம்மறி as 'an undeveloped embryo'. The verse asks for a change of viewpoint, not a change in the body.

pope: Will impurity ever cease from the worthless body which the great have abandoned, knowing it to be reeking with odours from processes connected with nutrition, though aromatics be chewed, the head covered with garlands, and the body adornedwith false splendour?
reading: Will chewing fragrant spices, filling the head with flowers and putting on a false finery remove the foulness the great saw and abandoned, which is always strengthened by the work of eating?
nuance: Mudaliar takes மயல் as the impurities of a woman's body; Shanmuganar applies it to the body in general. The verse says only that the great saw it and gave it up.

pope: Shall I abandon (my ascetic purpose) because blind, low men worry me, saying (that woman's eye is like) the water-lily in the clear stream, or the warring carp, or a javelin? I will pursue my virtuous way as having seen (that) the eye's real nature (is), like (that of) the palm-tree fruit (which is) scooped out, after the water has been drained off!
reading: Shall I give way when blind and petty men trouble me by calling eyes water-lilies in clear water, darting carp or spears? I will go on my way having seen what an eye is: like a palm fruit scooped out once its water is drained.
nuance: The speaker is a renunciant guarding his resolve; the verse is personal resistance rather than general teaching. கண்ணில் (eyeless) turns the praisers' subject back on them.

pope: Though worthless men untaught should fret my soul and rave of teeth like jasmine buds and pearls, shall I forego my fixed resolve, who have seen in the burning ground those bones—the fallen teeth —strewn round for all to see ?
reading: Shall I give way when untaught petty men chatter that smiles are jasmine buds and pearls? I will go on my way having seen the teeth and bones fallen and scattered in the burning ground for all to see.
nuance: A companion to 44 with the same frame; the evidence here is not anatomy but the cremation ground, so impurity and impermanence meet.

pope: (The body) is entrails, and marrow, and blood, and bone, and connecting tendons, and skin, and here and there flesh interposed, and fat. In the midst of these, what sort of a being is she who wears the fresh garlands?
reading: Entrails, fat, blood, bone, linking sinews, skin, and flesh and grease set here and there: among these, which part is the woman with the fresh garland?
nuance: The question is a search for the person among the parts, and implies she is none of them; the verse uses the list, not argument, to dissolve the beloved.

pope: The fool will address the earthen pot (the body), from which defilement oozes, which from nine disgusting outlets scatters pollution, and in which slimy liquids move to and fro—and say, 'O thou of the rounded arms,' ‘O thou with armlets decked, ‘—because it is made bright to his eyes by a covering of black skin.
reading: The fool calls out 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' to a pot that seeps filth from nine openings and churns with slime, because its covering of dark skin dazzles his eyes.
nuance: The terms of address the fool uses are the stock epithets of love poetry, so the verse aims at a literary convention as well as at desire.

pope: They know not what the body is; with sandal paste and flowers they make it fine. Have they not seen, I pray, the vultures and their mates in flocks with busy beaks devour the body foul when the chariot-axle is snapt?
reading: Those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is: have they not seen vultures, male and female, crowd in and tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks?
nuance: Mudaliar reads the axle as the life and the cart as the body. The cart image recurs from 2, where wealth turned like a wheel.

pope: The skulls of the dead, at the sight of which the gazer fears, with deep cavernous eyes appear, and grinning say to those who still survive, 'Guard well! In virtue's path stand fast. This is the body's grace and worth.''
reading: The skulls of the dead lying about, with deep sunken eye-holes that frighten those who see them, seem to laugh loudly and tell the living 'guard yourselves and keep to the path: this is what the body comes to'.
nuance: The speech is a poetic fancy, as Mudaliar notes (தற்குறிப்பேற்றம்). He names the path as renunciation; Shanmuganar names it as virtue.

pope: The skulls of the dead, grinning so as to excite disgust, cure the vain lovers of life of their folly. Those who are cured of this folly, seeing (the skulls in the burning ground), say “such is this body,' and so value themselves as nothing. --------------
reading: The white skulls of the dead, grinning so as to frighten, cure the infatuated of their fault; those so cured, seeing that this is the body's nature, do not count themselves as anything of worth.
nuance: Mudaliar takes the infatuated as men besotted with women and 'themselves' as their bodies; Shanmuganar takes it as the proud, cured of arrogance. The verse's own words allow both.

title: துறவு
theme: Renunciation, argued from impermanence: the wise see that home, youth, wealth and pleasure do not last and that pleasure is mixed with pain, so they leave household life without delay, keep their vows under hardship, pity those who insult them, and master the senses to reach release.
structure_note: 54 and 60 share their second line and make nearly the same argument. 52 and 53 both name the best of people (தலையாயார்) as those who act on impermanence; 57 to 59 turn from the reasons for renouncing to the conduct of those who have renounced.
source_issues: 59: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
60: Mudaliar's commentary breaks off after 'மற்று,'. Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
51-60: Shanmuganar's notes carry the numbers 111-120, apparently from an edition that orders the chapters differently; the content matches these quatrains.

pope: As when a lamp enters darkness dies, so sin stands not before man's penitence. As, when in a lamp the oil wastes, darkness rushes in, so evil takes its stand where deeds of virtue cease.
reading: As darkness dies when a lamp comes in, sin cannot stand before a person's austerity; and as darkness rushes back when the lamp's oil runs out, evil settles in once good deeds are exhausted.
nuance: The second half limits the first: austerity protects only while the merit that feeds it lasts, so the lamp makes merit something burned up, not something owned.

pope: The chief of men reflect on change, disease, old age, and death, and do their needful work. Those who raving teach the endless round of sevenfold science, and the lore of stars, are maddest of the foolish throng.
reading: The best of people reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do the work that is truly theirs; none are more foolish than the madmen who prattle endlessly of சத்தம் and astrology.
nuance: The target is not learning as such but study that never ends, pursued in place of what death makes urgent. 'Their own work' (தங்கருமம்) echoes Kural 266, which Mudaliar quotes.

pope: The chief of men in quite thought discern how house, and youth, and beauty's grace, and high estate, and wealth, and strength, all pass away; and thus, to save themselves, prolonging not the time, renounce all these.
reading: Seeing that home, youth, beauty, high repute, wealth and strength all fail to last, the best of people, considering slowly, renounce them without delay so as to save themselves.
nuance: மெல்ல and நெடியார் pull two ways: the examination is unhurried, the renouncing is not. Mudaliar keeps both, glossing one as deliberate inquiry and the other as acting without delay.

pope: Though wretched men suffer afflictions many a day, yet one day's delight they eagerly desire. The men of calm and full wisdom, in pleasure's core see pain, and quit the pleasant household paths.
reading: Fools, after many days of suffering, still long for a single day's pleasure; the full and settled, discerning pleasure for what it is and seeing its pain, keep off the household way.
nuance: The verse names household life (மனையாறு) as what the wise leave, which makes it a direct answer to the Kural's defence of the householder.

pope: In vain is my youth spent. Even now disease and old age will come. O soul ! be bold; wrangle no more with me, but rise! Wilt thou not go where both thou and I may gain virtue's path?
reading: The speaker tells his own heart that youth has passed to no purpose and disease and old age are coming now, and asks it to stop going its own way and set out with him on the good path.
nuance: The heart is treated as a separate, wayward party to be persuaded, not commanded. Mudaliar takes the good path to be release through renunciation; Shanmuganar says only 'a good way'.

pope: Though your wife possess no excellence and bear no child, it is hard to get rid of the marriage bond. For this cause since he who weds puts sorrow on, in olden days the learned made marriage a synonym of dread.
reading: Even if a wife lacks good qualities and bears no children, the husband cannot put her away; because marriage brings this hardship, the learned gave it the name கடி.
nuance: The argument turns on a pun, since கடி means both marriage and 'shun'. The verse finds no fault in marriage to a good wife; it argues from the worst case that the bond, once made, can't be undone.

pope: When troubles arise, hard to resist, to cause them to break the vows which their lofty spirits have pledged, the men of power set griefs aside and firmly fix their souls in right. These are the blessed, guarding decorum's rule.
reading: When unbearable troubles come that would break the vows they took on with zeal, those who push the troubles aside and hold the vows firm are the blessed ones who guard good conduct.

pope: To bear with those that speak contemptuous words; yea, more, to say, 'Ah, will these sink in the other world to hell, the place of fire, as fruit of their contemptuous words;' and to grieve, is duty of the perfect man.
reading: Bearing contempt is not enough: the worthy also grieve for those who scorned them, fearing that the deed will drop them into the fiery hell.
nuance: The pity looks to the offender's future, not to one's own injury, so forbearance becomes a form of compassion. Parimelazhagar cites this quatrain when glossing Kural 157.

pope: He who undisturbed, in the ordered way of right, has power to guard and guide the desires and lusts that find entrance by the five sense-gates, called 'body, mouth, eye, nose, and ear' - unfailing shall gain 'release.'
reading: One who has the strength to guard and steer, without wavering, the craving that enters through the five gates named body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears will surely reach release.
nuance: The senses are called five mouths (ஐவாய) through which craving feeds; the verse asks for them to be steered, not destroyed.

pope: Though wretched men behold afflictions urge and press, renunciation is not in their thoughts; delight they eagerly desire. The great in every joy behold its pain, and seek it not. -----
reading: Fools, though they see suffering mount, have no thought of renouncing and long only for pleasure; the higher ones, whenever pleasure comes, look to the pain in it and do not cling to it.
nuance: It reworks 54 almost line for line, but where 54 has the wise leave household life, this has them refuse attachment as each pleasure arrives: a discipline inside experience rather than a change of state.

title: சினம் இன்மை
theme: Freedom from anger: the worthy let honour and insult pass alike, guard their tongues, bear harsh words from those beneath them and do not return harm, while their anger, when it comes, cools of itself. The base nurse and broadcast theirs.
structure_note: Most quatrains set the worthy (விழுமியோர், சான்றோர், மேன்மக்கள்) against the base (கீழ், நீசர், கயவர்): 64, 66, 68 and 70. 65, 66 and 69 ground restraint in power and lineage rather than weakness.
source_issues: 61: the Tamil prints மதித்திறப் பாரும் twice and மதித்தேறி where Mudaliar (மிதித்து) and Shanmuganar (மிதித்து நடப்பவரும், மிதித்து ஏறி) read மிதித்-; சுதமின்மை in the last line looks corrupt (Shanmuganar has சுடும் சினம்). Mudaliar's commentary breaks off after மிதித்து.
62, 64: Mudaliar's commentary breaks off mid-gloss.
63, 65, 66, 69, 70: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
67: neither Mudaliar's nor Shanmuganar's commentary is aligned.
68: Pope's translation is not aligned.
61-70: Shanmuganar's notes carry the numbers 121-130, from an edition that orders the chapters differently; the content matches these quatrains.

pope: Who pass esteeming us, let them pass on! And those who contemn and trample on us as they pass, let them too pass on! If even a fly (especially unclean) should climb, trampling on their head, it is well that the wise who know its worth, should feel no wrath.
reading: Let those who honour us pass, and let those who trample us pass too; since even a fly can climb onto one's head, those who understand this do well to be free of burning anger.
nuance: The fly deflates the insult: being stepped on is something even the smallest creature does, so it carries no weight. The printed second and third lines repeat மதித்- where both commentators read மிதித்- (trample), and the last line's wording looks corrupt.

pope: Although disgraces throng thickly, and may not be repulsed, will those whose minds are set upon finishing the work begun, renounce sweet life's unfailing worth in their impatience, whenever they see (evils)?
reading: Those whose minds can carry a task through will not throw away their precious life whenever they meet disgrace, even when it presses so hard they cannot move a step.
nuance: Placed in a chapter on not being angry, the quatrain can be read as treating death at humiliation as anger turned on oneself. That is an interpretation from its placement; the verse itself argues only from the unfinished task.

pope: If a man open his mouth and speak unguarded words, his words will ceaselessly burn his soul. The wise who ceaselessly hear, and ponder well and calmly, even in their wrath, will never give utterance to words of fire.
reading: Unguarded words from an open mouth burn the speaker without end, so the learned, who listen and reflect without end, never speak scorching words even when angry.
nuance: The repeated ஓவாதே sets the endless burning of careless speech against endless listening as its cure. The burn falls on the speaker, not the hearer.

pope: When men who are beneath them confront them, and speak unseemly words, the excellent wax not hot with anger. The base man will brood over it, chafe and rave for all the town to hear, and leap, and dash his head against a post.
reading: The excellent do not grow hot with anger when people beneath them confront them with unfit words; the base brood on it, rant for the town to hear, leap about and butt a pillar.
nuance: The comic last line makes anger self-injuring rather than wicked: the head that hits the pillar is the angry man's own.

pope: The young man's self-restraint is self-restraint. The gift of him who owns no stores of wealth is gift indeed. When wan has means and might to punish every fault, if he forbear, call him the patient man.
reading: Restraint in youth is true restraint, a gift from one without wealth is the true fruit of giving, and the patience of a strong person able to punish everything is true patience.
nuance: Each virtue counts only where its opposite would be easy: youth tempts, poverty excuses, power permits.

pope: As stones the base shower down their bitter words: the noble bear, in sight of all, and let them pass, by sense of noble worth constrained : like serpent's crest at once by touch of sacred ash subdued.
reading: The well-born bear the stone-like bitter words of the base in front of everyone and let them pass, held back by their own lineage as a cobra's hood is quelled at once by sacred ash.
nuance: The image grants that the noble have venom: their forbearance is power held in, not its absence.

pope: When men stand forth as our enemies, and would begin the conflict, to decline the strife is not, in the language of the wise, lack of power. Even when men have confronted and done us intolerable evils, it is good not to do them evil in return.
reading: The wise do not call it weakness to decline a fight with those who come at you as enemies; even when they confront you and do unbearable harm, it is good not to harm them in return.
nuance: The first half answers the charge of weakness before the second recommends restraint. With neither commentary aligned, this reading rests on the Tamil and Pope.

reading: The anger of the low keeps spreading however long it runs and never dies, while the anger of the worthy cools of itself, like the heat water takes on when boiled.
nuance: Water's heat is borrowed from the fire, so the simile can suggest that the worthy's anger comes from outside and leaves them as they were. That is my reading of the image, not the commentators'.

pope: Though men think not of good received, and do much ill to men of family whose fame has touched the sky, these still do good; nor are they wont provoked by faults, to render evil to the thankless ones.
reading: Even when people forget the help they received and do great harm, those born in families whose fame touches the sky only keep doing good, and do not seek to repay the fault with harm.

pope: Though a dog, in range, should lay hold of them, there are none in the world who, in return, would lay hold of it with their mouth; and thus, when low men speak, not what is fitting, but low words, will high-minded men, in reply, utter such words with their mouth. ----------
reading: No one bitten by a raging dog bites it back; so when the low speak low words, will the high answer in kind with their own mouths?
nuance: The analogy works by ranking the insulter with the dog: answering in kind would mean stooping to its level.

title: பொறையுடைமை
theme: Forbearance carried beyond insult into friendship and privation: avoid fools, bear inferiors, value a friend's harsh words, bear with or quietly leave an erring friend, starve rather than beg from the graceless, and refuse blameworthy pleasure, harm and falsehood even at the greatest cost.
structure_note: Several quatrains address a chieftain of the hills, forest or shore (71, 73, 76, 77, 79), which Mudaliar calls ஆடூஉ முன்னிலை. 71 to 73 concern speech, 75 to 77 friendship, and 78 to 80 holding firm under want.

pope: Lord of the pleasant land, where down the cool mountains the streams fall as garlands!— With a fool hold no converse. If you speak with him, in replying he will pervert your words. To slip away from him as best you can is well.
reading: Lord of the good cool hill country where streams fall like garlands: say nothing at all to a fool, who will twist what you say; slipping away as best you can is best.
nuance: Forbearance here takes the form of withdrawal rather than endurance: the wise don't stay to bear the fool's talk.

pope: When persons not our equals say unfitting things, to bear and to be still is worthy conduct. The world girt by foaming waters regards not a contrary course as praise-worthy, but as discreditable.
reading: When those not one's equals say unfit things, it is fitting to bear them in silence; the world does not count the opposite as praise but as disgrace.
nuance: Mudaliar takes the 'world' that judges to be the worthy, not people at large.

pope: Lord of the swelling sea's cool shore, where bright insects hum around every flower!—Are severe words from loving lips harder to bear, if men can only rightly estimate their result, than pleasant words that strangers courteously speak?
reading: Lord of the cool shore of the teeming sea, where bees hum over every flower: for one who finds people who know what is good for him, are harsh words from those who love worse than pleasant words that strangers speak with a smile?
nuance: The condition carries the weight: harsh words are worth more only if one finds friends who know what is good (ஆவது அறிவார்). Mudaliar reads பெறின் as stressing how rare such friends are.

pope: Those who know what should be known and rule themselves thereby; who fear what should be feared ; who use all their faculties to bless the world; and whose nature rejoices in all good gained: are for ever free from woes.
reading: Those who know what must be known, keep restraint, fear what must be feared, do what is due so that the world rejoices, and live content with what they get, are hardly ever in suffering.
nuance: Mudaliar glosses அடங்கி as 'being forbearing', which ties this broad portrait of contentment to the chapter's theme.

pope: When two with strict accord unite in friendship's bond, if one betray the other's confidence by unkind act, this latter should endure as best he may. And if he can't endure, he should not divulge it, but withdraw himself.
reading: When two have joined in friendship without any distinction and one of them shows conduct the other cannot make sense of, the other should bear it as far as he can, and if he can't, should withdraw without spreading it abroad.

pope: but never forsake him. Lord of the woodlands! Separation is hard even to beasts; therefore if friends do things that are unpleasant, think them pleasant. bid yourself cease (from wrath), and blame yourself alone; but forsake not those that have been joined to you in the intimacy of friendship.
reading: Lord of the forest land: even if friends do hurtful things, wish them to pass as if pleasant and blame only yourself, but do not abandon those joined to you closely, for parting is hard even for beasts.
nuance: Blaming oneself is left open: Mudaliar records two readings, one moral and one karmic.

pope: Is not the reason why the close friendship of the great is sought, that they will bear even with faults hard to endure? Lord of the good land of high mountains, with resounding waterfalls! — to good people are intimate friends rare?
reading: Is it not because the great bear with faults that are hard to bear that people seek their deep friendship? Lord of the good high hills with roaring falls, are close friends rare for those who do good?
nuance: The closing question can be taken two ways: Mudaliar reads it as 'friends are not rare for the good', Shanmuganar as 'the great are not hard to win for those who do good without fault'.

pope: Though sore wasted with hunger, let not men tell out their destitution to ungracious churls. Those indeed who lack resolution to deny themselves may tell their wants to those who are able and willing to save them from destitution.
reading: Even if wasted and starving, do not tell your need to people without courtesy; those who lack the resolve to give up their life tell it only to those able to cover it.
nuance: Both commentators take தம்மைத் துறக்கும் துணிவு as resolve to give up one's life, so the quatrain ranks starving in silence above asking even the right person; Pope reads it as resolve to deny oneself. மறைக்கும் can mean relieving the need or keeping it secret, and Mudaliar allows both.

pope: Although shameful things may present themselves. as things that yield pleasure, flee from that pleasure's side! Though thou couldst see pleasures that cease not soon, — Lord of the land of fountains high! — the guiltless way is best.
reading: Lord of the land of high waterfalls: even if disgrace comes along the way pleasure opened, and even if the pleasure looks as if it would never end, the way that brings no blame comes first.
nuance: The second concession is the stronger: not only brief pleasures but lasting ones are to be refused if they carry blame. The first two lines are knotted, and Mudaliar resolves இருந்தைக்க as addressed to the listener.

pope: Though ruin seize you plan not ruin to the just! Though body's flesh should waste, eat not from hands unfit! Though the whole earth o'er-arched by heaven accrue as gain, never speak word with falsehood mixed !
reading: Though ruined, do not plan the ruin of the worthy; though your flesh wastes, do not eat from the hands of those you must not eat from; though you would gain the whole sky-roofed earth, do not speak words mixed with falsehood.
nuance: Each refusal is set against the extreme loss that would excuse it, which is how the quatrain belongs to a chapter on forbearance.

title: பிறர்மனை நயவாமை
theme: Not desiring another man's wife, argued mostly from consequences: constant fear, small pleasure, the king's punishment, family disgrace, hell and a degraded rebirth. The last quatrains turn from the act to desire itself, a fire worse than any outer fire, which the strong suppress in silence.
structure_note: 81 to 87 weigh the act's costs against its pleasure; 88 to 90 move to desire as an inner burning that water, hills and outer fires do not match.
source_issues: 81, 82, 84: Mudaliar's commentary breaks off mid-gloss.
85, 87: the Tamil has OCR errors in the அளபெடை forms (மாணஇ for மரீஇ, பாணஇ for பரீஇ, பெண்மாணஇ for பெண்மரீஇ); Mudaliar's glosses give the correct forms.
88: the Tamil's line breaks and punctuation are misplaced around ஓஓ கொடிதே. Shanmuganar's field for 88 also contains the Tamil and commentary of 89.
89: Shanmuganar's commentary is not aligned (it sits at the end of 88's field).

pope: The fear it brings is great ; its pleasure is brief ; each day if it is divulged death threatens by the king's decree; and ever it is a deed that tends to the pains of hell; O shamefast men, desire not your neighbour's wife.
reading: The fear is great and the pleasure small; thought through, it risks death at the king's hands and is a deed that daily sharpens toward hell, so those with a sense of shame should not set their hopes on another man's wife.
nuance: The case is prudential from start to finish, weighing fear against pleasure, but the appeal at the end is to shame (நாணுடையார).

pope: Virtue, praise, friendship, greatness, all these four draw not anigh the men who covet their neighbour's wife. Hatred, disgrace and guilt, with fear, these four possessions abide with men who covet their neighbour's wife.
reading: Virtue, renown, friendship and greatness do not come to those who desire another man's wife; enmity, blame, sin and fear do.

pope: In entering in there's fear; in home returning fear; during enjoyment is fear; in guarding the secret is fear; it evermore brings fear: why shuns he not with dread the entrance of neighbour's house?
reading: Fear on entering, fear on returning, fear while enjoying, fear in keeping it hidden: it brings fear at every moment, so why does a man enter another's house without dread?
nuance: The repetition of அச்சம் enacts the condition it describes. The closing question turns on the same word: the one who lives in fear lacks the one fear that would have kept him out.

pope: If any one see, disgrace lights on the house; if any hand should seize, leg's maimed; in the doing of the shameful deed is dread; it yields as fruit vast hell's affliction : tell me, O profligate, what measure of delight is thine ?
reading: If seen, the family is disgraced; if caught, a leg is cut off; the unmanly act itself is fear; and it yields long suffering in hell: tell me, profligate, what pleasure did you find?
nuance: Mudaliar reads ஆணின்மை as the absence of the qualities that make a man, so the adulterer's daring is renamed unmanliness.

pope: Those who, in a former state, without any regard to right, becoming associates of the mean, enjoyed the embraces of beautiful women, and by violence approached their neighbour's wife, in this state will become eunuchs, and dancing shall earn their bread.
reading: Those who in a former birth, with no sense of right and in the company of the mean, went by force to other men's wives become eunuchs in this birth and live by dancing.
nuance: The punishment mirrors the offence: those who used male force are reborn without it. This is the chapter's one claim about a past birth; the Kural's chapter on another's wife makes none.

pope: While his loving wife dwells in his home, the tender one whom he espoused, — seeking (out an auspicious) day, and sounding the drum, for many folks to know,—and 'whom he guards as his own, what means a man's glance at another's wife?
reading: When a man has at home a tender, loving wife, married on a day fixed by asking, with drums beaten for many to know, why should he look at a stranger's wife?
nuance: The public wedding is the point: a bond announced to many and guarded (கடி) is set against one that has to be hidden.

pope: The enjoyment of the man of unstable heart, who under the influence of infatuation approaches his neighbour's wife and sets his affections upon her, while neighbours spread abroad his guilt, and kinsmen dread and mourn, is like (that of the person who takes pleasure in) licking a serpent's head.
reading: The pleasure of the unsteady-hearted man who, maddened, unites with another's wife while neighbours gossip and his own people tremble and grieve, is like licking a cobra's head.
nuance: The image holds pleasure and lethal danger in a single act, so no separate weighing of costs is needed.

pope: The disease of lust in men mighty (in wisdom) gains not ascendancy, is not revealed, does not remain fixed on many objects. O! it is a cruel conflict; but fearing to incur shame in the midst of their foes, they say nothing about it, and it is extinguished within them.
reading: In the strong, the sickness of desire does not spread, show itself or settle on many; fearing shame among those outside, they say nothing and it subsides within. Oh, how cruel it is!
nuance: The strong are not free of desire, only able to contain it, and the cry 'how cruel' can fall on that containment. Mudaliar reads it so: desire that can't come out and must be suffered inwardly is the cruellest.

pope: Arrow and fire and sun with glistening rays may rage and burn; but these burn the outer man alone. Lust rages and distracts and burns the mind, and is more to be feared than they.
reading: Arrow, fire and the sun's bright rays, however they blaze, burn only the outside; desire, blazing and troubling the mind, burns the mind itself, so it is to be feared more than they.

pope: From the ruddy fire that fiercely rises in the village you may scape by bathing in water. — Although you bathe in water, lust will burn; and though you climb the hill and hide you there, still lust will burn! -----------
reading: From a fierce red fire rising in the town one can escape by plunging into water; but desire burns even if one plunges into water, and burns even if one climbs a hill to hide.
nuance: Water and the hilltop are the two refuges from fire, and both fail because this fire travels with the one who flees.

title: ஈகை
theme: Giving: give gladly and daily within one's means, even when poor and even a grain's worth, to those who cannot repay, because death and age are near and wealth comes and goes by past merit, not by clutching. The fame of giving outlasts all else, and one who cannot give should at least not beg.
structure_note: The reasons offered shift through the chapter: the next world (91, 94, 95), impermanence (92), merit governing wealth (93), the good of the world (96, 97), the nature of a true gift (98, 99) and fame (100).
source_issues: 92: Shanmuganar's field also contains the Tamil of 93 (reading தாந் துய்ப்பினும் and இடுக்குற்று) and his commentary on it.
93: Shanmuganar's commentary is not aligned (it sits at the end of 92's field).

pope: Even in their adverse hour, up to the measure of their means, as in the prosperous times, with large rejoicing heart to give is their nature still. To such good men heaven's gate is never closed.
reading: Those whose nature is to give gladly, as much as they can, even when they have little, as if they had plenty, will not find the doors of that world shut against them.
nuance: Gladness is part of the qualification: the gift is measured against the giver's means and his spirit, not its size.

pope: Before (you) are death's day and age detestable ; behind is disease that humbles pride. Discursive thoughts indulge not. Cling not to earth. Eat, sharing food; hide not your powers while wealth is in your hand.
reading: Death's day and hateful old age stand right before you, and disease that destroys strength comes after; don't run about in vain, don't clutch, share before you eat, and hide nothing while wealth is in your hand.
nuance: The case for giving here is impermanence, not merit or fame: wealth is to be used while the hand still holds it. Mudaliar takes பரவன்மின் as 'don't roam after more wealth'; Pope has 'indulge not discursive thoughts'.

pope: Though dread of want they do not relieve the woes of men who as suppliants draw near! Yet although men enjoy and give, wealth grows in growing time: cling to it, and yet it flies when former deeds that brought wealth have lost their power.
reading: Whether one ignores the misery of those who come trembling or gives and enjoys, wealth gathers when its time to gather comes; and however tightly it is held, it leaves when the good deeds that sent it run out.
nuance: The argument removes the miser's motive: giving can't lose wealth that merit holds, and clutching can't keep wealth that merit has stopped holding. Mudaliar notes the variant இடுக்குற்று (clutching tight) for மிடுக்குற்று (with force).

pope: Daily having given somewhat, though but the fraction of a grain of rice, according to your ability, eat ye (your own food). Those who gave not in that world, men say on this earth girt by deep waters are those on whose hearth nothing is cooked.
reading: Give daily, before eating, from what you can, even a grain of rice's worth; the quatrain backs this with a saying about those who do not give and those whose hearth is never lit.

pope: Regarding the other world and this world, give to any suppliant, in fitting way, according to your ability. And if on account of poverty giving is not possible, yet refraining from begging is twice as meritorious as giving.
reading: With an eye to the next world and this one, give what you can in a fitting way; and if poverty makes giving impossible, not begging is worth twice as much as giving.
nuance: Mudaliar names the two rewards: heavenly joy in the next world and renown in this one. The last line keeps the poor inside the economy of giving: they give by not taking.

pope: Those who live desired of many are as a fertile palm entered in the altar's enclosure in midmost of the town. Those who, even when their house grows great, give not before they eat, are like the sterile palm in the burning ground.
reading: Those who live so that many desire them are like a fruit-bearing palm enclosed by a platform in the middle of town; those who do not give before eating, even when their household thrives, are like a barren male palm in the burning ground.
nuance: Both are palms; fruit and place separate them. The giver stands where everyone gathers, the miser among the dead.

pope: Even when the rain rains not in due season, if all the world should fail in virtuous actions that ought to be done, —Lord of the warring sea's cool shore, where acrid fume of fish in Punnai's perfume dies! - how scapes the world?
reading: Lord of the cool shore of the pounding sea, where the punnai's scent drives off the smell of fish: if the rain does not fall when it should, and the world does not do what it should, how will the world survive?
nuance: Both commentators take the 'world' that must act to be its good or wise people, so their giving is set beside rain as a second support of life.

pope: Denying to no out-stretched hand, to give to needy men as he hath power, is duty of a man.—Lord of the swelling sea's cool shore !—A gift to those that can return the gift is usury !
reading: Never refusing an outstretched hand and holding nothing back, to give to those who can't repay is a man's duty; lord of the cool shore, giving to those who will give back earns only the name of a profitable loan.
nuance: Mudaliar lists several ways to take தாம் வரையாது: excluding no gift, excluding no person, setting no rules, or keeping nothing back for oneself.

pope: Say not ‘ 'tis passing little,' nor ‘ ' tis nought I give;' on all confer thy boon of virtuous charity, Like the dish the mendicant presents from door to door, by frequent doles 'twill be filled full.
reading: Never say 'it is too little' or 'I have nothing'; always do the good of giving, to anyone, for like the ascetic's bowl filled at door after door, it fills slowly.
nuance: The bowl belongs to the one who receives, but it stands for what fills in the giver: Mudaliar says the fruit of virtue fills his life, Shanmuganar that good deeds accumulate.

pope: The sound of beaten drum a katham off they'll hear; the thunder's voice through a whole yojanai will reach men's ears; the three successive worlds will hear the word that says, ‘Men excellent their gifts have given.' ------------
reading: A drum struck with a stick is heard a காதம் away and rolling thunder a யோசனை, but the word 'they gave', linked with the worthy, is heard through all three stacked worlds.
nuance: Mudaliar records a third reading, 'they gave to the worthy'.

title: பழவினை
theme: Old deeds (பழவினை) find their doer and settle each person's share of joy and suffering. Wishing, effort, holiness and learning cannot move that share, so the chapter ends by asking why anyone should grieve over it.
structure_note: The quatrains alternate between images from nature that no one made or can alter (the calf finding its mother, the round vilam fruit, rain that cannot be summoned or stopped, the palm and the millet seed) and the human cases they explain: decline, begging, wrongdoing by those who know better. Three quatrains (106 to 108) take apparent injustices and assign them to former deeds; 110 draws the conclusion that grief is pointless.
source_issues: 101: Shanmuganar's field ends with the Tamil text and Shanmuganar's commentary for 102, and 102 has no Shanmuganar commentary of its own.
Shanmuganar's verse numbers in this chapter run 31 to 40 rather than 101 to 110, and 110's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: Although you send forth the tender calf amid many cows, it has unerring skill to seek out its own mother. Deeds of old days have even so the power to search him out to whom their fruit pertains.
reading: A young calf let loose among many cows can still find its own mother, and an old deed has the same skill in seeking out the one who did it.
nuance: The image makes the deed active: it searches, as the calf does, rather than waiting to be met. Neither the verse nor Mudaliar says the deed comes from a former birth; Shanmuganar adds that.

pope: Beauty and youth, and glittering wealth and reverence abide not in one stay. To him who, though he sees this, does no single virtuous act in this one stage of being, life's joy stands with the body and falls with it.
reading: Beauty, youth, fine wealth and the awe one commands do not stay; one who sees this and still does not one good thing has a life that merely takes a body, stands, and falls.
nuance: The failure condemned is not vice but the absence of even one good act; the body is wasted rather than misused. Mudaliar offers two senses of ஒருவழி ஒன்றேயும்: any single good deed, or one deed of the kind that leads to the highest state.

pope: Who would not see Prosperity? All seek her gifts; but as men's ways are, so each man's enjoyments are meted out. Who made the Vilam's apple round? Or who gave its dusky hue to the Kalam fruit ?
reading: Everyone wants prosperity, but each person's enjoyments are measured out according to their own course, just as no one rounded the vilam fruit or blackened the kalam berry.
nuance: The fruits are chosen because their shape and colour belong to them by nature. The verse says only அவரவர் ஆற்றால்; both commentators take that 'way' to be one's former deeds.

pope: Not even saints can drive away predestined ills; and all the fated gain must needs accrue. In time of drought who can bestow the rain ? Or who can check its rich abundance when it falls?
reading: Not even the உறுவர் can remove what is bound to befall, and what is bound to be gained is the same; no one can bring rain in a drought or check it when it pours.
nuance: Mudaliar records Shanmuganar's kind of reading of the second line as another view, under which the verse is a reversed parallel: rain withheld matches gains withheld, rain unstoppable matches pains unstoppable.

pope: Those who lose like stately palms, when their greatness is gone, become small asthe millet seed, hiding their glory within, —and so they pass their days. This is the fruit of deeds of former days: when you think of it, what other cause can there be?
reading: Men once as great as palm trees shrink to the size of a millet seed, hide their brightness within and live on diminished day after day; think about it, and what cause is there but the fruit of former deeds?
nuance: The verse turns a common sight, the fallen great, into an argument by elimination: no other cause can be thought of. Mudaliar specifies that the deeds are evil ones.

pope: Those that know the fruit of varied and profound learning die off, while the unlearned joyously live on. Would you know the cause ? — The unlearned posses within no 'sap of sapience'; — so death deems then refuse stalks, and takes them not!
reading: If you ask why those who know the fruit of deep learning die while the unlearned live on, it is because the unlearned have none of the sap called sense, so Death passes them over as husks.
nuance: The verse is a joke with an edge: a long life for the unlearned is recast as Death's contempt. It doesn't say the learned die because of their learning; it supplies a fanciful cause, which Mudaliar names as a figure of imputed cause (ஏதுத் தற்குறிப்பேற்றவணி).

pope: Lord of the sea's cool shore, where amid the wave swans sport, tearing to shreds the Adambu flowers ! When those whose hearts are sore with urgent need standbegging, and wander through the long street, in sight of all, this is the fruit of former deeds.
reading: When people with aching hearts stand at the gates of great houses, begging in sight of everyone, all of that is their former deeds, lord of the cool shore where swans tear the adambu flowers.
nuance: The address to the lord of the shore frames the quatrain as words spoken to a chieftain. Both commentators make the deeds evil ones from a former birth; the verse says only முன்னை வினை.

pope: They are not ignorant; but, though what man should know they know, yet they do deeds that bring guilt to their souls. — Lord of the wide sea's pleasant shore, where breezes breathe the lily's fragrance round ! — This comes from former deeds.
reading: When people who are far from ignorant, who know what ought to be known, still do blameworthy things, that comes from the deeds they have done, lord of the long cool shore where the breeze carries the honey-scent of the neythal.
nuance: The quatrain explains a moral puzzle, knowing the good and doing wrong, by pushing the cause back into earlier deeds. It explains the act; it does not excuse it, and pazhi still attaches.

pope: On the earth begirt by gathering waters no men desire in anywise evil things, but choice fruit of good things. Yet whether they desire, or abhor, it is hard to shun the touch of what fate assigns.
reading: No one on this sea-girt earth wants evil in the least, and all want good results; but wanted or not, what is bound to come is hard to keep from touching them.
nuance: Desire is shown to be idle in both directions: wanting good does not bring it, and not wanting evil does not prevent it.

pope: The early fates diminish not, nor do they increase, they come not in order changedhelp in troublous times is none; what haps will happen, there and then; and so, when all things fail, why grieve? -----------
reading: What was set in the early mark does not shrink or grow, does not come out of order, gives no support in hard times, and arrives where it is due; so why grieve when the time of ruin comes?
nuance: சிறுகாலைப் பட்ட பொறி is literally 'the mark set in the small time'; both commentators read it as what was fixed in the womb. The chapter ends not with fear but with an argument for calm, since a fixed sum cannot be changed by grieving.

title: மெய்ம்மை
theme: Things as they truly are (மெய்ம்மை): the hard facts of the world, as opposed to how people would like it to be. Natures do not change, kin come with fortune and leave with it, the rich are heard and the poor are not, and in the end only one's deeds go with one.
structure_note: Unlike the chapter title's usual sense of truthfulness, only 111 concerns keeping one's word. The rest is a run of observations about how the world works, several framed as facts no one can alter (112, 116) and one as four rhetorical questions (119). The chapter closes on death (120), echoing chapter 11.
source_issues: Shanmuganar's verse numbers in this chapter run 41 to 50, and 120's Shanmuganar field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: O maid with many armlets graced! To answer 'no' disgraces no man, when the boon asked exceeds his means. It is the world's course. But to delay and cheat the soul faint with desire is a sin like his who 'slays' a benefit conferred.
reading: Saying 'I have none' about something one cannot give is no disgrace and is the way of the world; but keeping someone waiting till their hope dies and then failing them is a worse fault than killing a kindness received.
nuance: The verse doesn't fault refusal; it faults the false promise that turns refusal into torment. Both commentators read கொன்றாரின் as a comparison, worse than ingratitude, where Pope says only 'like'.

pope: Men of worth, and men unworthy too, retain their natures ever unchanged. Whoever they be that eat it, sugar can never grow bitter; and margosa is bitter even when eaten by gods.
reading: The worthy and the unworthy never fall away from their own natures: jaggery is not bitter whoever eats it, and neem is bitter even if gods eat it.
nuance: The claim runs both ways: circumstances cannot spoil the good, and they cannot redeem the bad. The gods are named to say that even the highest eater does not change the taste.

pope: When a man moves prosperonsly on, devoted kinsfolk are countless as shining stars that move in the upper heaven. But when grievous affliction haps,—Lord of the dripping hills !—few claim close alliance with him.
reading: When a man prospers, kin who cling to him are more numerous than the stars that move in the sky; when unbearable trouble strikes, few say 'we are related to him', lord of the cool hills.
nuance: Mudaliar notes that கிளைஞர் means, by its root, those who cling like branches, which sharpens the irony of their leaving.

pope: Of the three things that endure upon this faultless earth, he who gains the midmost gains the two extremes also. He who gains not the midmost gains the cruel smart that the turtle feels when put into the pot to boil.
reading: Of the three that endure in this world, whoever gains the middle one gains both ends as well; whoever does not gains a suffering like being boiled in a furnace.
nuance: The verse doesn't name the three; both commentators identify them as virtue, wealth and pleasure, with wealth in the middle. For a work that elsewhere calls wealth unreliable, this is a strong statement of its worth. Pope's turtle in the pot is his own; Mudaliar has a smith's furnace.

pope: A young heifer fetches a good price when it is the calf of a good cow; so the words of rich men though unlearned, pass current. Poor men's words, like the plough when moisture is scanty, merely graze the surface and are of no avail.
reading: Even a young calf fetches a price if its mother is a good cow, and the words of the rich are accepted even if they are unlearned; the words of the poor glance off like a plough in barely moist soil.
nuance: The calf image says worth is borrowed from the source, not earned; the plough image says the poor man's words do not sink in. The verse reports this as how things are, not as how they should be.

pope: O wide-eyed one! though you cook the wild gourd pouring in salt, ghee, milk, curds, and spices, it never loses its bitterness. So those who never discipline themselves, though they may learn extensive works of true wisdom, never become disciplined.
reading: Those without restraint stay unrestrained even if they study true wisdom widely, as a wild bitter gourd stays bitter though cooked with salt, ghee, milk, curd and asafoetida.
nuance: Mudaliar takes அடங்காதார் as those who are by nature not given to restraint, so the point is that learning cannot change a nature, not that learning is useless.

pope: When men scorn you, before their faces scorn them too ! what has a man to do with them? — Lord of shore where beauteous Punnai-flowers perfume the glades that surround the swelling tide, — what fated comes to all!
reading: Scorn those who scorn you, before they do; what have you to do with them? What is bound to come comes to everyone, lord of the shore fragrant with punnai flowers.
nuance: The link between the advice and the last line is not stated. One reading is that since what is fated will come anyway, there is nothing to lose by answering scorn. Mudaliar takes அவரின் முன் either as at the very moment they scorn or to their faces rather than behind their backs, and calls the verse a way to silence groundless slanderers.
