pope: Though cows in form are diverse, the milk they yield is not diverse. The way of virtue, like that milk, is one in nature, though the schools that teach it here are like those cows, of many forms.
reading: Cows differ in colour, but the milk they give does not; virtue, like milk, is of one nature, while its ways here take many forms, like the cows.
nuance: Mudaliar takes the many ways as the many means of practising one virtue. Pope makes them the schools or sects that teach it, which turns the verse into a statement about religious diversity; the Tamil says only நெறி.

pope: Look well! of whom hath not the world found word to say ? And who have not by prudence prospered in life's way? Ah! who in life's mid course no bitter grief have known ? Ah! who to end of life have kept their wealth their own?
reading: Who in the world has escaped having a word said against them? Who has not lived by stratagem? Who has not met hardship midway? Who has kept their wealth to the end?
nuance: The four questions expect the answer 'no one', so the verse states the common lot without saying it. Mudaliar gives two senses of உபாயம்: the four political stratagems, or the ordinary means of livelihood.

pope: Save a man's deed: nought goes with him, search where you will. The body which men cherish so, and adorn, is itself profitless indeed when death shall seize and hurry off with it. ------
reading: Search where you will, nothing goes with a person but the deeds they have done; even the body they guarded and adorned is of no use when Death seizes it and runs.
nuance: வினை here is not only good deeds: what goes along can be a burden as well as a support.

title: தீவினையச்சம்
theme: Dread of evil deeds (தீவினையச்சம்): harm done to creatures returns in kind, and bad company is itself a source of evil, turning even the upright. The chapter ends by urging the heart to give up household attachment, since only good done profits the soul.
structure_note: Three quatrains give retribution in kind for harming creatures: eating flesh (121), caging birds (122), eating crabs (123). Five more (124 to 129) concern company and friendship; Mudaliar on 125 says the chapter's point there is to fear the friendship of the small. 130 closes with an address to the heart.
source_issues: 129: Mudaliar's commentary breaks off mid-word at நற்செய.
Shanmuganar's verse numbers in this chapter run 51 to 60, and 130's Shanmuganar field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: The burning ground is filled with the corpses of men that will not give themselves up to a self renouncing life, but oscillate amid sorrows; and the maws of perverted foolish men are a mere burning-ground for beasts and birds.
reading: The burning grounds are full of the corpses of people who linger in sorrow and do not turn to renunciation, and the bellies of senseless, petty-minded people are burning grounds for the beasts and birds they eat.
nuance: The two halves mirror each other: people end in the burning ground, and the eater's belly becomes a burning ground for animals. The image says that the meat-eater carries a cremation ground inside.

pope: Their legs in iron bound, as slaves to alien lords they will till the black and barren soil, who snared and kept in cages partridges and quails, that dwell in wilds where beetles hum amid the flowers.
reading: Those who catch partridges and quails that live in the humming forest and keep them in cages will go, with irons clanking on their legs, as slaves to strangers into the fields.
nuance: The punishment mirrors the crime: those who confined free birds are themselves confined and made to serve. Mudaliar reads கரும்பு ஆர் கழனி as sugarcane fields, and as an alternative as barren and fertile lands; Pope follows the barren reading. Shanmuganar places the punishment in the next birth; the verse doesn't say when.

pope: Like fire their palms shall glow, their fingers rotaway, who loved in other times on crabs to feed, and broke their joints, what time the guilt of ‘olden deeds' comes home, and leprosy's fierce pangs assail.
reading: When the old deed of loving to eat crabs and breaking their legs comes home, people get the painful skin disease, white like conch beads, their fingers rotting away and only the palms left.
nuance: Again the punishment copies the act: the crab's legs were broken, and the eater's fingers rot. Mudaliar and Shanmuganar read அக்கே போல் as like conch beads; Pope has palms that glow like fire.

pope: Even things (soft and soothing) like ghee, when joined with the fierce heat of fire, will blaze and burn, and cause bitter anguish : so even upright men are perverted and give themselves up to deeds of utter evil, when they attach themselves to those whose deeds are evil.
reading: Even ghee, when it meets fire, burns and causes painful wounds; so even upright people turn and do widely cruel deeds when they join those of harsh deeds.
nuance: Mudaliar notes the force of the image: ghee is what soothes burns, so the very thing that heals becomes what wounds. The verse makes company stronger than character.

pope: Great men's intimate regard will daily grow in order due like the crescent moon. Mean men's alliance like the full moon that rides the sky daily by degrees dwindles away of itself.
reading: The friendship of the great grows day by day in due order like the crescent moon, while the bond with the small wanes by itself day by day like the full moon moving across the sky.
nuance: The word தானே says the waning needs no cause: such a bond decays of itself.

pope: Thou didst attach thyself (to unworthy persons), saying, they are men of absolute integrity! If to thee who hast thus attached thyself, integrity in those thine intimates does not appear; hear, O thou who hast so attached thyself, it is as if one opened a casket, thinking it contained an odorous unguent, and saw a snake within.
reading: You attached yourself to someone, thinking him one of the worthy; if the worth is not in him, listen, it is like opening a casket expecting sandal paste and finding a snake inside.
nuance: The repeated சார்ந்தாய் ('you who attached yourself') is a reproach: the fault lies partly with the one who did not examine before attaching.

pope: What single man has power to search and clearly know the inmost self of other men? Lord of the land where weighty gems glisten on mountain slope, O hear ! — Men's minds are otherwise, and otherwise their deeds.
reading: Who is there with the power to examine another's mind and know it? Listen, lord of the land where heavy gems glitter on the slopes: people's minds are one thing and their deeds another.
nuance: The gap between mind and deed is offered as the reason minds cannot be known: behaviour is no evidence.

pope: Lord of the flowery hilly land where streams wash out and carry hither and thither (precious things) from the marshy land ! — The effusive friendship of those who do not attach themselves (to us) in heart, but perform certain friendly acts merely to strengthen their own position, and who form friendships guilefully, will issue in disappointment to the minds (of those who are intimate with them).
reading: The lavish friendship of those who do not join you at heart but act with an eye to their own gain, befriending you with guile, turns into a stain on the mind, lord of the flowering hills.
nuance: Whose mind is stained is left open. Mudaliar says the friendship itself becomes a fault, Shanmuganar that it grows tainted and perishes, and Pope that it brings disappointment to those deceived.

pope: If the glittering swords a man brandishes (be allowed to) fall into the hands of his foes, it will assuredly come about that he will thus destroy also his own power of action. So wealth (bestowed on the foolish) will go and burn up (merit accruing in) both worlds, and therefore the really good thing is to keep clear of the foolish.
reading: If a raised, gleaming sword falls into an enemy's hand it truly destroys one's strength; since ஆக்கம் among the unlearned burns one in both worlds, the good course is to get away from them.
nuance: Pope offers a third sense, wealth bestowed on the foolish. On every reading the sword image says that what should protect you turns against you once it is in the wrong hands.

pope: O mind! thou leavest not the bonds of home. How many cycles, pray, with thou live yearning still for children? Save the good he has done, however small its measure may be, there is no true result to any living soul.
reading: Heart, you won't let go of attachment to home, and you pine for the sake of children; for how many ages do you think you'll live? Apart from the good one has done, however small, there is no real gain for a living being.
nuance: Both commentators read மனைப்பாசம் as attachment to one's wife. The verse doesn't call family evil; it says family is not the gain the soul carries.

title: கல்வி
theme: Learning (கல்வி) is the only true beauty, a medicine for delusion and the best legacy, and it outranks birth. Because life is short, one must choose what to learn, keep learned company, and prefer the books of wisdom that free one from confusion to merely worldly study.
structure_note: The chapter moves from learning's worth (131, 132, 134), to learning against birth (133, 136), to how to learn given a short life (135, 140), to the company of the learned (137 to 139). Its last quatrain ranks books of wisdom above worldly books, turning learning toward release.
source_issues: 136: Mudaliar's commentary has a placeholder, '***', where a word (probably காணாய்) has been lost.
138: the Tamil text has a corrupted character in துரி஢ன் (probably தூரின்), and Shanmuganar's verse number reads 38.
139: Pope's translation is not aligned; Mudaliar's commentary starts mid-gloss at ஒழுகின், missing the first words' glosses; Shanmuganar's field ends with the Tamil text of 140.
140: Shanmuganar's commentary is not aligned.

pope: Beauty of locks, beauty of circling garments' folds, beauty of saffron tint: these are not beauty true. Integrity of soul that brings the conscience peace is learning's gift: that only is beauty true!
reading: The beauty of a man's hair, of a garment's curving border, of a saffron wash, is not beauty; the beauty of learning, with the fairness of heart that lets one say 'we are good', is beauty.
nuance: Mudaliar notes that some read the three adornments as a man's (hair), both sexes' (garment) and a woman's (saffron), and so take the verse to commend learning for women as well as men; he says others give the verse other meanings too.

pope: Since in this world it yields fruit; since given it grows not less ; since it makes men illustrious; since it perishes not as long as (its possessors) themselves exist; in any world we see not any medicine that, like learning, removes the delusions of sense.
reading: Learning yields fruit in this life, does not lessen when given, makes its owner shine, and does not perish while they live; in no world do we see a medicine like it for cutting away delusion.
nuance: The disagreement is whether learning lasts as long as its owner or outlasts them through fame. Mudaliar notes that learning is called a medicine without delusion being called a disease, an incomplete metaphor.

pope: The excellent regard the salt produced in brackish ground as choicer than the Nel from fertile soil. It is fitting to place in the first rank the learned wise, though (sprung) from the lowest origin.
reading: The worthy prize salt born in brackish ground above rice grown in fertile fields; so the learned, though of the lowest origin, are to be set in the highest place.
nuance: The image works because the place of origin is called low only by habit: salt from barren soil is worth more than grain from good soil. Mudaliar takes கடைநிலத்தோர் as those born in a low caste.

pope: It cannot be taken from its place of deposit; it does not perish anywhere by fire; if kings of surpassing grandeur are angry they cannot take it away; (and therefore) what any man should provide for his children as a legacy is learning. Other things are not (real wealth).
reading: It cannot be taken from where it is kept, it is not lost when given to a fit person, and kings angered by its eminence cannot seize it; so what a man should leave his children as their inheritance is learning and nothing else.
nuance: Each clause is a way ordinary wealth is lost: theft, giving, a king's anger. Both commentators read வாய்த்து ஈயின் as giving to a fit recipient; Pope reads வாய்த் தீயின் and has learning not perish by fire.

pope: Learning hath no bounds, the learners' days are few. If you think calmly diseases many wait around! With clear discrimination learn what is meet for you, like the swan that leaving the water drinks the milk.
reading: Learning has no shore, learners have few days, and, thought over calmly, many illnesses; so the wise learn with clear discernment what is fitting, like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water.
nuance: The argument for selection is arithmetic: boundless material, a short life, and illnesses that shorten it further. Mudaliar names the bird as the swan and notes the belief that it can separate milk from water.

pope: As none contemn the ferryman, by old caste rule to lowest rank assigned, but cross the stream by help he lends; so take thou teachings good and wise by help of him who is the learned man.
reading: No one despises the ferryman for being of the lowest of the old castes, but crosses the river with his help; so take what is good from a man who has learned books, whatever his birth.
nuance: The argument is from ordinary practice: people already accept help from the low-born when they need it, so they should accept teaching on the same terms. The verse speaks of using the learned man's help, not of honouring him.

pope: We shall see whether any greater bliss is found in the city inhabited by the dwellers in the ample heaven than is felt when men of natures formed by old imperishable lore, from rivalries exempt keen as tempered steel, meet together and laugh.
reading: If the city of those who live in the wide heaven is sweeter than when people of sound and ancient learning, free of rivalry and sharp of mind, gather and laugh together, then we'll go and see it.
nuance: The conditional is a polite refusal: Mudaliar reads it as saying that such joy is found on earth and not in heaven, so there is no wish to go.

pope: diminishes in sweetness. Lord of the cool shore of the resounding sea intimacy with learned people is like eating sugar cane from the (tender, juicy) tip; association with graceless. sapless men is like leaving the (tender) tip and eating it from the (hard, dry) root.
reading: Friendship with the learned is like eating sugarcane from the tip, sweeter as one goes; association with graceless, unfeeling people is like eating it from the root end, lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea.
nuance: The cane is the same in both cases; only the direction differs. So the verse is about how a bond develops over time, not how it begins.

reading: Even the unlearned, if they keep company with the learned, gain good sense day by day, as a new pot gives its water the scent of the bright, long-prized pathiri flowers placed in it.
nuance: Mudaliar explains the image: the new pot is the unlearned person, the flowers the learned, and the scent good sense. The water gains the fragrance without becoming flowers, so the change is real but borrowed.

pope: If men leaving works of wisdom, that contain well-weighed instruction, unstudied, devote themselves to the recitation of mere worldly literature, they will acquire a store of empty high-sounding words, but not that wisdom by means of which mental confusion (that treats unreal things as real) is removed. ------------
reading: Of all the many kinds of learning, studying worldly books while leaving the books of wisdom unread amounts only to clamour; there is no one who knows how to make confusion leave by that means.
nuance: Mudaliar names the worldly books as logic and grammar, and takes தடுமாற்றம் as the stumbling through births; Pope takes it as the mind's confusion that treats unreal things as real. The verse does not say worldly learning is false, only that it cannot do this.

title: குடிப்பிறப்பு
theme: Noble birth (குடிப்பிறப்பு) shows in conduct that holds through poverty: the well-born keep their principles, courtesy and generosity when they have nothing, while the low-born fail to do good even when they can. The chapter treats these qualities as belonging to birth.
structure_note: Most quatrains pair the well-born with an image of something that keeps its nature in distress: the hungry lion (141), the ruined mansion with a dry corner (147), the moon half-swallowed by the serpent (148), the dry river that yields water when dug (150). 142, 145, 146 and 149 make the contrast with others explicit.
source_issues: 141: Shanmuganar's field ends with the Tamil text and Shanmuganar's commentary for 142, and 142 has no Shanmuganar commentary of its own. Shanmuganar's verse numbers for 141 and 146 read 41 and 46.
142: the Tamil text is corrupted in இநவ்முன்றும் (probably இவைமூன்றும்) and வேற்ப (probably வெற்ப).
143: Pope's translation and Mudaliar's commentary are not aligned.
144 to 148: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
150: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: Though their clothes may be old and their body worn with want, men of noble birth diminish nothing of their due observances. Will the lion nibble the creeping grass although sorest need should assail him?
reading: Even when their clothes are in rags and their bodies wasted, the well-born do not fall from their principles; would a lion, however hard pressed, chew creeping grass?
nuance: The lion is chosen because grass is not merely beneath it but against its nature, so the verse makes principle a matter of what one is. Mudaliar records a variant reading, வரிமா, which would make the animal a tiger.

pope: Lord of the hills traversed by clouds that touch the heavens! true excellence, and dignity, and good conduct, — these three things belong to men of race that touches heaven, and not to others, even though they may have acquired great wealth.
reading: Fullness of character, gentleness and good conduct belong only to those born of a family that touches the sky; they do not come to others even when they gain great wealth, lord of the hills where clouds creep.
nuance: The point is aimed at wealth: money cannot buy these qualities. Mudaliar glosses சாயல் as mildness, restraint in mind, word and body, and notes that some take it as restraint from blame and sin.

reading: Rising from one's seat, going out to meet, seeing a guest off, and the like are what the well-born have taken as unfailing conduct; they are not to be thought of as one with the base.
nuance: Only Shanmuganar's commentary is aligned here, and the readings of விடுப்ப ஒழிதல் (as seeing off) and of whom the courtesies are for (elders who visit) are his.

pope: If men (of noble birth) do good things it is natural to them. As to evil things (to commit these is impossible to them); for this would be guilt which many would bruit abroad. What greater good then can accrue to men than high-birth, if it be their lot, to which the perception of all (these things) belongs!
reading: If the well-born do good, it is called their nature; if they do evil, it becomes blame spread by many; what then does a person gain from the all-knowing high birth that falls to them?
nuance: Pope reads the same question the other way, as praise: what greater good can come to anyone than high birth? So the two readings reach opposite conclusions. Mudaliar's commentary isn't aligned for this quatrain, so this can't be recorded as a contest between commentators.

pope: Dread of unlearned ignorance; dread of the work that base men do; dread of forgetful slip in words which one must not utter; dread of not giving to those that ask: those who are born of a race not so distinguished by conscientious fears are as trees.
reading: Fear of being unlearned, fear of base work, fear of a slip in speech, and fear of not giving to those who ask: those born of an undistinguished family who lack all these are like wood.
nuance: These fears are presented as marks of good birth, a moral sensitivity. The third fear is read two ways: Pope takes it as dread of a careless word, and Shanmuganar as the dismay of being unable to speak in an assembly of the good.

pope: Lord of the roaring salt-sea's cool shore, where gleam rare gems with pearls!Association with the good, pleasant speech, a liberal hand, and purity of mind, —all these are only found among the nobly born.
reading: Good company, sweet speech, giving, and goodness of mind are all found only among the well-born, lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea where great gems gleam with pearls.
nuance: The claim is exclusive: these qualities are found only among the well-born, not merely more often.

pope: Though its frame-work has perished, and thronging white ants infest it, in a spacious mansion some room will still afford shelter from the rain. Thus, although want annoys them, the nobly born even yet will do what should be done.
reading: A great house whose woodwork has decayed and which white ants have overrun still keeps one corner where the rain does not fall; so even when hardship presses, the well-born do what is theirs to do.
nuance: The image does not claim the house is intact, only that some shelter remains; the well-born, too, can do less but not nothing.

pope: Like the moon which affords light to the fair and spacious earth with one side, while the dragon holds the other, the nobly born do not become remiss in works of seemly benevolence, though poverty (inability) stand fronting them.
reading: Like the moon that lights the wide fair earth with one side while the serpent holds the other, the well-born do not slacken in serving others even when poverty stands squarely before them.
nuance: The serpent is the eclipse, as Shanmuganar notes. The last line shares its words, ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார், with Kural 218.

pope: Men of mean descent, even when all goes well with them, will not perform the good deeds that the well-born will do, even when things do not go well with them. Though the antelope should bear a pillion, it rushes not to war like the prancing charger.
reading: What the well-born do even when they cannot, the small will not do even when they can; an antelope may bear a saddle, but it cannot do battle like a leaping horse.
nuance: The saddle is outward equipment, so the verse says that giving the small the means does not give them the nature.

pope: The nobly born, even when destitute, are props in time of feebleness to the needy ones that draw nigh to them. So, when the wide river is dry, if you dig in its bed, forth with clear waters gush out. -------------
reading: Even when they have nothing at all, the well-born are a prop to those who come to them in need, as a wide river, when dried up, yields clear water at once if you dig its bed.
nuance: The river image implies that the means of giving is still there below the surface; the well-born have to be dug for, not asked from.

title: மேன்மக்கள்
theme: Portraits of the noble (மேன்மக்கள்): they cannot bear a stain, aim high whatever the outcome, stay within bounds in want, keep their speech clean under abuse and welcome those who come to ask. Wealth draws the base, but meeting the well-born is the real treasure.
structure_note: Most quatrains pair a natural image (moon, arrow, worn path, sugar-cane, treasure cave) with a trait of the noble. Mudaliar's note on 151 reads மேன்மக்கள் as the high-born, while the verses themselves mostly describe conduct.
source_issues: 151: Pope's text is garbled ('while the truly worthy endure it. not;'); the sense is that the worthy do not endure a stain.
152: Tamil has a corrupted character in நா஢மா, which Mudaliar's gloss shows is நரிமா.
157: Tamil reads கடிந்தெரிணஇ, apparently a corruption of கடிந்தொரீஇ, as Mudaliar's gloss 'கடிவ கடிந்து ஒரீஇ' shows.
159: Tamil reads விமுமியோர், a typo for விழுமியோர் (Mudaliar's gloss has விழுமியோர்).

pope: The moon that diffuses light through heaven's fair realms, and truly worthy men are alike: yet that endures a spot, while the truly worthy endure it. not; — perplexed and sad they pine away if but one stain appear.
reading: The noble resemble the moon that spreads its light across the sky, except that the moon carries its spot while the noble, if one stain falls on them, pine away and waste.
nuance: The comparison turns into a contrast: the moon is the lesser because it puts up with its blemish. Sensitivity to stain is made the mark of superiority.

pope: Whether success attend, or do not attend the work, the excellent will even ponder blameless ends.—Is the shaft that missed the lion worse than the arrow sent forth, that with its impulse pierced the jackal's heart?
reading: Whether the aim succeeds or not, the worthy plan only what carries no blame: is the arrow that missed a lion worse than the one that tore open a jackal's breast?
nuance: Two ideas sit together: the aim must be blameless, and it must be high. A noble failure outranks a mean success.

pope: The excellent though emaciated and poor, do not transgress the limits of virtue and commit evil. With wisdom for the pillar, with perseverance as the band, they bind (the mind); and as long as they live they do what it behoves them to do.
reading: Though poverty leaves them all sinew, the worthy do not cross the bounds into wrongdoing; binding the mind with understanding and resolve, they do what ought to be done as far as their means allow.
nuance: The last phrase sets a measure: duty is scaled to what one has, not abandoned. 185 ends with the same words, செய்வர் செயற்பாலவை.

pope: Lord of the land of goodly hills ! —If trodden for a few days a path is formed over even the craggy hill; so excellent persons, though they have seen (worthy) men only for one day, as they were travelling, will bind them to their soul, exhibiting all the marks of an ancient friendship.
reading: If the worthy see someone just once on the road, they bind that person to them as if in a friendship of long standing, just as a few days' treading makes a path even over rock.
nuance: The image cuts two ways: a path on rock needs repeated treading, yet the worthy form the bond at one meeting. Pope adds that those so bound are themselves worthy; the Tamil does not say so.

pope: Even when one speaks who has an ungrammatical knowledge of the letter, but not of the meaning who is of a low (empty) school, and is unlearned the good with kindly compassion will listen, though it is pain to them, being grieved that he should be put to shame in the presence of many.
reading: When an unlearned man who knows neither grammar nor meaning speaks in an empty gathering, the good listen out of kindly regard, though it pains them, to spare him shame before many.
nuance: Mudaliar glosses கண்ணோடி as தாட்சிண்யம், courteous indulgence. The good endure bad speech not for its sake but for the speaker's face.

pope: Although you bite the sugar-cane, crush it till its joints are broken, grind it, and express its juice, it still will be sweet. The highly born, even when men have passed by abusing them so as to wound, never lose their self-respect so as to utter from their mouth (words of abuse).
reading: Sugar-cane bitten, crushed at the joints and pounded for its juice is still sweet; so the well-born, even when abused so as to wound, do not lose themselves and speak in kind.
nuance: Shanmuganar reads the close as positive, that they keep speaking sweetly; the Tamil says only that they do not speak as people undone.

pope: They defraud not, drink not palm-wine, shun what is forbidden, never despise and speak contemptuously of their neighbours, nor even forgetfully do they utter anything untrue with their mouth : these men of faultless vision grieve not though they fall into distress.
reading: Those of faultless vision do not steal, do not drink, shun what is forbidden, do not scorn others, and never lie even by a slip; and if they decline in fortune, they do not grieve.
nuance: The list of abstentions ends in an inner state: equanimity in decline is presented as the fruit of clean conduct.

pope: Deaf to others' secrets, blind to his neighbour's wife, dumb to evil backbiting—if, knowing what is befitting, a man thus abides, it is not necessary to teach him any virtuous precepts.
reading: One who is deaf to others' secrets, blind to a neighbour's wife and dumb in evil backbiting, knowing what is fitting, needs no teaching of virtue at all.
nuance: Mudaliar reads 'if he stands so' as stressing how rare this is. Virtue here is a matter of restraint of the senses, not of instruction.

pope: They who are destitute of kindly courtesy, even after the lapse of many days, will contemn (those that visit them), saying, ‘they will ask something of us'. The excellent will treat them with distinction whenever they see them, saying, ‘if they ask something of us, it is well'.
reading: Those without good character scorn a frequent visitor, thinking he wants something from them; the excellent, thinking it good even if he asks, honour him every time they see him.

pope: The lowest sort of men say, there are men of property,’— cling to them steadily, follow them, and so flourish. Is it not as when a mine of treasure has been found, when men of good lineage have become our friends. --------------
reading: The base settle on the rich as their one hope and live by trailing after them; yet meeting people of good family is like coming upon a treasure cave.
nuance: The contrast is between attaching oneself to money and to lineage. The verse prizes good birth as company; it does not say what the treasure consists of.

title: பெரியாரைப் பிழையாமை
theme: Not wronging the great: their goodwill, once lost, cannot be restored, their anger reaches into any fortress, and their esteem is the only esteem worth having. Time with them is precious, and their bond grows where the bond of the small shrinks.
structure_note: 161, 164 and 168 address a chieftain of hill or shore country, a convention of address. 167 and 168 sit oddly under the chapter heading; neither commentator explains how they belong to it.
source_issues: 162: Tamil has a corrupted character in கா஢யாரை, read as அரியாரை.
163: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.

pope: Lord of the pleasant land whose hills resounding water-falls adorn ! — You may not even to faultless men do things that enkindle wrath; for when their wrath is once kindled, it is hard for any one to change their mood.
reading: Do not do what offends even the faultless, counting on them to forgive; once they turn away, no one can undo it.
nuance: The warning targets presumption: the very forbearance of the great is what tempts the offence. Pope reads the last line as the great one's mood being hard to change; both commentators read it as the resulting harm being impossible to remove.

pope: Although those whose (pretended) wisdom is without moral excellence have gained access to men to whom approach is difficult even by gifts of gold alas! they pass away (the precious moments) as mere waste time.
reading: People of loveless cleverness who have freely gained the company of the great, whom others cannot reach even by paying gold, alas, let the time pass without profit.
nuance: Mudaliar takes நயம் as delight or relish, so the fault is an inability to enjoy and draw on what the great offer, not ill will.

pope: Both disesteem and thorough esteem are in the class of things that depend on the estimation of the great. Those who have a discriminating knowledge of true science, lay no stress on either the abuse or the fulsome praise of man who comprehend not moral principles, and know not the rules of propriety.
reading: Disesteem and high esteem alike are for the superior to judge; those versed in refined learning take no account of the scorn or the extravagant praise of the base who know neither grace nor propriety.

pope: The serpent rich of hue, though it dwell in the mountain-cleft, from far is frighted by the thunderbolt's fierce wrath; so men escape not though hid in strongholds hard to reach, when those great in virtue are wroth.
reading: A brightly hooded snake living in a crevice still dreads the thunder's fury from afar; so those who have angered the great do not escape even inside a fortress hard to reach.
nuance: Pope reads them as those great in virtue, closer to Shanmuganar. On Mudaliar's reading the fortress is a defence against royal power; on the others, against a moral force no wall can stop.

pope: ‘You know not all our worth, for equals have we none:’ when self thus estimates itself, this is not ‘esteem’ ! When perfect men, proficients in virtue, regard any as dear, and esteem them as great, this is ‘esteem’ !
reading: Saying 'you do not know us; there is none like us' is not esteem; esteem is when the worthy who know virtue see one as rare and accept one as great.

pope: Lord of the great sea’scool margin !—Friendships formed with mean men dwindling die like shadows of the morn; friendship of men of old renown as shadows of the after-day will lengthen out and grow.
reading: The friendship of the small dwindles like the morning shadow, while the bond of those of long renown keeps lengthening like the shadow of the declining day.
nuance: Mudaliar offers two timings for the shadows (dawn against noon, or forenoon against afternoon); the point, shrinking against growing, is the same either way.

pope: Those who press their suit, fitness a part, enjoy the wealth of kings, and the charms of maidens fair; so all the cool (shady) trees that droop earthward with thick foliage, give room to those that thronging seek their shelter.
reading: Those who keep close enjoy the wealth of kings and the beauty of women, without needing to be worthy; just as cool trees heavy with leaf give shelter alike to all who come near.
nuance: The verse states a fact about proximity rather than merit. Under this chapter's heading it may counsel staying near the great, but neither commentator draws that out.

pope: Severance from even those who have no under standing [lit. no understanding that understands (so as) to understand] causes great and spreading sorrow. — Lord of the shore of the great, unfailing, swelling bay !—To be intimate with none is ten million times the best.
reading: Parting even from those who lack discernment brings great, lingering sorrow; so, lord of the long brimming backwaters, not mixing with anyone at all is ten million times better.
nuance: This is the renunciant's conclusion drawn from the pain of attachment, and it cuts against the next chapter's praise of good company. Mudaliar spells out the comparison: not joining is better than joining and then parting.

pope: Days gone by without learning, those passed without any intercourse with the great, those spent without giving what is fitting;— in the case of the excellent, if you tell them over, none such occur.
reading: Days passed without learning, without going to the great, without giving what one can: if you count them, none such are found among people of good character.

pope: The greatness of the great is [the quality of littleness (in their own sight), i. e.] humility; the (real) acquisition of those who have acquired (any). one (science) is modest self-restraint. If you rightly understand things, those possessors of wealth only are really wealthy who relieve the wants of those that approach them (as suppliants). ----------------
reading: The greatness of the great is humility; the fitting quality of one who owns any one excellence is restraint; and, rightly seen, the wealthy are wealthy only if they relieve the distress of those who come to them.
nuance: Mudaliar takes ஒன்றிற்கு as any one of learning, wealth or manliness, and records another reading, 'to the Supreme'. Pope narrows it to one science.

title: நல்லினம் சேர்தல்
theme: Joining good company: it washes out the faults of youth, raises the lowly as river water sanctifies sewage, protects the weak and hides meanness. Life's pain makes the company of the wise the thing to seek, and bad company ruins even the pure.
structure_note: 173 and 174 frame good company against the pain of birth; 175 to 178 give four images of the low raised by the high; 179 and 180 turn to the damage done by evil company.
source_issues: 171: the Shanmuganar field also contains the text of 172 and Shanmuganar's commentary on it; 172 is marked not aligned for Shanmuganar, so that commentary was not used.

pope: In youth unwise, though men consort with haughty ones and walk in lawless ways; yet, when they join with those that know the righteous path, their faults shall melt away as dew from off the grass when sunbeams scorch.
reading: Faults committed in thoughtless youth, keeping company with the unruly and going astray, vanish once one joins good people who know the right way, as dew lets go of the grass when the sun grows hot.
nuance: Mudaliar names these faults the faults of association (சகவாச தோஷங்கள்). Company is both the cause of the wrong and its cure.

pope: Know virtue's path ! Dread death! Beat others' words severe! Beware ye practise no deceit! Friendship detest with men of evil deeds! Daily get gain of words that fall from greatmen's lips!
reading: Know the path of virtue; dread Death; bear the harsh words of others; guard against deceit; shun friendship with evildoers; and always take in the words of the great.
nuance: Mudaliar reads போற்றுமின் வஞ்சம் as preventing deceit from arising in oneself, and allows வாய்ச்சொல் to mean the blessing of the great.

pope: Severance of close-joined friends and sore disease and death, all these combined hap to those that have assumed a human body: so the truly wise have felt that birth, from the very first, is bitterness. Ah! soul, cleave close to these!
reading: Since parting from those one is close to, grievous illness and ruin come together to all who take a body, O my heart, cling to those of great understanding who see that birth is bitter from its start.
nuance: The speaker addresses his own heart. The reason for seeking the wise is not their virtue but their insight into birth as suffering.

pope: Though when you ponder it, it is surpassing: bitterness, none hate (this mortal) birth, if in (this mortal) birth they ever perform friendly acts to men whose hearts are set on noble excellence, and gain their friendship.
reading: Though birth, when thought through, is extremely bitter, no one would resent it if within it they could keep lasting friendship with people whose hearts practise goodness.
nuance: Mudaliar notes that 'if they can get it' (பெறின்) marks how rare such friendship is. The verse redeems birth without denying its pain.

pope: When water from the town-sewers has joined the great river its very name is changed, and it becomes a 'sacred stream’. Ponder well! Even those who have no greatness of clan, if they ally themselves with good men of goodly fame, shall stand firm as a hill.
reading: Town drain water that joins a great river loses its name and becomes holy water; consider: even those without lineage stand like a hill by joining the good.

pope: Because it is in the bright-beamed moon the very hare in heaven's lofty fair expanse is worshipped. Though scant their worthiness, men obtain worth who share friendship with those firm as a hill.
reading: The hare in the bright moon is worshipped along with it in the sky; so those of slight worth gain worth by friendship with men as steady as a hill.
nuance: Mudaliar explains the hare as the moon's dark mark: no one removes the spot before worshipping the moon, so the flaw shares the honour.

pope: Commingled with milk water becomes milk; at least, it shows no more as water by its hue. Look close, the mean men's meanness shows not if they join themselves to greatness of the good and great.
reading: Water mixed with milk becomes milk and no longer shows its own colour; so, on inspection, the smallness of small people does not show when they join the greatness of the good.
nuance: The verse says the meanness is hidden, not removed. That is a weaker claim than 171, where faults vanish.

pope: Grass close around the stump in the field adjoining the house will not be destroyed by the ploughshare of the farmer ; [thus] though men are weak, if they get under safe protection, the wrath of their foes will not reach them.
reading: Grass growing against a stump in a large field is not moved by the farmer's plough; so the anger of enemies cannot reach the weak who have joined good company.

pope: As Nel that flourishes through the goodness of the soil, good men become illustrious by the excellence of their respective clanships. Goodness perishes when it comes near evil associates, as the tornado advances and destroys the excellence of the ship.
reading: As paddy thrives by the goodness of its soil, the worthy flourish by the goodness of their own group; and worth is ruined by joining evil company, as a gale wrecks a sound ship.
nuance: Pope's 'clanships' leans toward birth. Which reading one takes decides whether this verse agrees or collides with 195.

pope: Though themselves pure in mind, even good men incur contempt because of their associations. So in the woodland glade when a conflagration takes place (not the worthless brushWood only, but) the fragrant Sandal and Vengai too are consumed. --------------
reading: Though spotless in mind, people are scorned for the company they keep: when a cleared field is set on fire, the fragrant sandal and the vengai burn with the rest.
nuance: The verse concerns reputation and fate together: the pure are blamed, and the fire also destroys them.

title: பெருமை
theme: Greatness of character: it renounces when the season of giving and loving has passed, sees home and its supports as passing, and keeps giving even in decline. Its faults show more than others' crimes, it stays unshaken by slander, and it feeds others before itself.
structure_note: 181 to 183 speak of renunciation and impermanence; 184 to 190 describe the great in their giving, their visibility and their steadiness.
source_issues: 181: the Shanmuganar field also contains the text and commentary of 182 and 183 and the bare text of 184; 182 to 185 are marked not aligned for Shanmuganar, so that material was not used.
184: neither Mudaliar nor Shanmuganar is aligned; only the Tamil and Pope were available.
185: Shanmuganar's commentary is missing, not even misfiled.
186: the Shanmuganar field also contains the text and commentary of 187 and 188, which are marked not aligned for Shanmuganar; that material was not used.
190: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.

pope: To give is no longer ours; and youth is gone far off ; our once beloved ones think of us no more! To depart, having abandoned 'desire' that bids us love and hope for future joys, appears the thing that's meet.
reading: We can no longer give, youth has gone far off, and those who once loved us no longer think of us; it seems the right course is to give up the craving that says 'we will love and prosper' and to leave.
nuance: The reasons for renouncing here are practical and even rueful, not doctrinal. Mudaliar specifies the departure as going into renunciation, and the loved ones as women.

pope: Fools thinking 'we have found joy in the refuge of home,' and 'we are here in perfect repose, forgetful (of the instability of all things), go on their way. Those who have felt that 'refuge' is unstable, while it seems to stand fast, never fix their fond desire (on it).
reading: Fools think 'we found contentment by taking to home life; here we are complete', and go on heedless; those who see that such supports only seem to stand and do not last never grieve.
nuance: Mudaliar allows பரிவது to mean either grieving or desiring; Pope takes the second. The verse targets complacency in home life; whether it condemns home life itself depends on the reader.

pope: See that ye sow seed that in other world may germinate; free your lives from earth's bewilder-ment and meanness ; stand in your lot as wise men; the changing hue of things shall without cause fade, and many things be new.
reading: Without confusion sow the seed for the next life, and live wisely without being brought low; for standing just where it stands the body changes its colour without any cause, and many ills arise.
nuance: Mudaliar supplies the subject: it is the body whose youth and qualities change unbidden. Pope's version speaks more vaguely of 'the changing hue of things'.

pope: The well of springing water serves the town that draws and drinks, even in time when rains are scant; so great men in adverse hour dispense due gifts that others give not even in their best estate.
reading: They say a spring-fed well, even in a season of scant rain, serves the town that draws from it; the great keep their duty of giving even when they have declined, as others do not even when they have prospered.
nuance: Only the Tamil and Pope are available for this quatrain; neither commentary is aligned to it.

pope: The river pours forth a mighty stream and feeds the world; and when it is dried up, if men dig in its bed, streams gush out! So good men when rich, give to many; and, when ruined, give still at least to some, and do what should be done.
reading: Like a river that poured out abundant water to feed the world and, when dry, still yields water from springs dug in its bed, the generous who gave to many still give to a few when ruined, and do what ought to be done.

pope: Lord of the lofty hills! Any evil in men of moral greatness shows like a brand on a mighty bull; but although mean men do painful deeds, like the slaughter of that same mighty bull, none of these attracts attention.
reading: Lord of the high hills, a fault in the great shows like a brand on a great white bull, while the small may do things as cruel as killing that bull and not one of them is noticed.
nuance: This is an observation about visibility, not a defence of the small. The high standard applies because the great are watched.

pope: In proportion to the degree of one's intimacy with men essentially mean and without good qualities sorrow accrues; but even the hostility of those who do not desire forbidden things even in jest will confer dignity.
reading: Intimacy with the inherently mean brings grief for as long as it lasts, but even enmity with the wise, who would not want harmful things even in jest, brings dignity.

pope: With gentle fair ones use gentleness surpassing theirs; with foes display a wrath that death's self might dread; with persistent men show a persistency to match ; amongst men of good do good; let the law of life be thus laid down.
reading: Be gentler than the gentle good; toward foes, be a terror that Death itself would fear; toward the false, utterly false; toward the good, goodness itself: let these be one's bounds.
nuance: A policy of matching each person in kind. Pope reads சலவர் as the persistent, to be met with persistence; Mudaliar reads them as liars, to be met with lies. Mudaliar also notes that others construe the verse differently.

pope: These are the pure in heart who, though any vex, and with use of slanderous words would fain perplex them, with calm unruffled mind abide unwavering, like the bright flame within the lamp.
reading: Though someone hurries in and tries to confuse them with cruel slander, the pure in heart stay unshaken, with no division in their mind, like the bright flame inside a lamp.
nuance: The flame is steady because the lamp shields it; the image suggests an inner composure that slander cannot reach.

pope: The excellent will daily give to the needy in charity their first-served food; they themselves will eat what is served after: such good conduct removes the three faults, and from sorrow sets men free, through all the days, till comes the end. ---------------
reading: The worthy daily give in charity the food served first and eat what is served after; that eating removes the three faults and keeps them from sorrow as long as life lasts.
nuance: Shanmuganar names the three faults as desire, anger and delusion. Pope leaves them unnamed, and no Mudaliar gloss is aligned.

title: தாளாண்மை
theme: Energetic effort (தாளாண்மை): it makes a person, as a twig hardens into an elephant post, supports kin and an ageing father, and is what lineage really consists of. Manliness is persisting when things fail, and food won by one's own effort tastes better than a patron's feast.
structure_note: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned for 191 to 195, so for those quatrains only Shanmuganar and Pope are available.
source_issues: 191-195: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned for any of these quatrains.
199: Tamil has a corrupted character in உளையலா஢, which Mudaliar's gloss shows is அலரி.

pope: As for kindred that feed upon what relatives give them they will die off like green grain below a tank, which does not hold a sufficient supply (of water). Is failure possible to men of energy that are quick in movement as the eyes of those who perform the sword-dance ?
reading: Like the green crop below a tank that does not hold back its water, kin live by what their relative gives and rest easy; can failure come to the energetic, who move as quickly as the eyes of women in the sword dance?
nuance: Pope reads the first half in reverse: kin who live on handouts die off like crops under a tank that holds too little water. The Tamil supports Shanmuganar's 'rest' (துஞ்சுப) at least as well, so the verse probably praises the energetic as the one who feeds the family.

pope: What once stood by the wayside, a twig that bent to every touch, when its core is developed within, may become a stake to which they tie an elephant. Life too is thus, if man himself, unfailing make himself !
reading: A twig that swayed by the path, once its core has hardened, becomes a post to tether an elephant; life is like that too, if a person makes himself without slackening.
nuance: Shanmuganar reads தாழ்வின்றி as not letting oneself sink; Pope as 'unfailing'. Either way the self is something made over time.

pope: The huge tiger, when lacking flesh for food one day, may even seize a little frog and eat it. Think not 'By (all my) knowledge I only gain menial tasks;" to the skillful hand nobler employments shall even there abound.
reading: A mighty tiger that finds no meat one day will catch and eat even a small frog; so do not think your knowledge fits you only for lowly work: through skill, higher work will come in that very place.
nuance: Pope titles it 'Stoop to conquer'. Shanmuganar reads the advice as taking the humble job that is available, since better skilled work may follow.

pope: Manliness is working on, in no wise faltering, remaining stedfast though the matter succeed not. When all is successful,— Lord of the cool lovely shore, in whose groves the waves agitate the scented thorn, — will not even women live and flourish?
reading: Manliness is standing firm in the way one has undertaken even when the thing does not succeed; lord of the cool seashore groves, when things succeed by themselves, don't even women manage to live?
nuance: The taunt assumes that women cannot persist through failure. The point is that persistence, not success, is the measure of effort.

pope: When men speak of 'good caste' and 'bad caste' it is a mere form of speech, and has no real meaning. Not even by possessions, made splendid by ancient glories, but by self-denial, learning, and energy is Caste determined.
reading: 'Good caste' and 'bad caste' are only words with nothing behind them; not long-famous wealth but austerity, learning and effort are what make a lineage.
nuance: A strong claim from a Jain text that questions birth rank. Shanmuganar takes ஒண்பொருள் ஒன்றோ as asking whether fine wealth alone suffices; Pope reads it as 'not even by possessions'.

pope: The world is subject to the nod of the brilliant (diplomatists) who search out (and know) men's designs from outward indications (lit. from) their members, i.e. from eye, gesture, tone, expression etc.).
reading: The perceptive keep their plans to themselves until the work is done and do not voice their drive; the world lies under the sign of those bright ones who read others' drive from their features.
nuance: Mudaliar takes the first ஊக்கம் as one's own effort and the second as the stirring in others' minds, so the verse pairs concealment with insight. He also records a reading in which the world serves at their nod.

pope: If the banyan's trunk be eaten by the gnawing ant, its 'branch root' bears it up, like a buttress; even so, when decay appears in the sire, the son he has begotten shall hide it, and weakness is no more.
reading: When termites have eaten the banyan, its aerial roots stand as pillars and hold it up; so when weakness shows in a father, the son he begot covers it and it disappears.
nuance: Mudaliar notes that மதலை, the prop, also means a son, so the image and the claim share a word.

pope: The lion's pointed claw and mighty foot will wound the spotted face of an elephant; those who have power like his , — though bereft of all, they die in want within their home, — will they do deeds that bring disgrace?
reading: Those with the strength of a lion, whose sharp claws and mighty paws wound an elephant's spotted face, would sooner die in want and low estate at home than do anything that brings disgrace.
nuance: Mudaliar reads மானம் here as dishonour (அவமானம்) and maps the lion's claws onto keen intelligence and resourceful effort.

pope: Like the flowers on a rounded stalk, with hair like filaments that sweet cane bare, when the sweet fragrance they breathed is lost, what gain accrues from birth in a lofty noble house when energy that makes the name noteworthy, is wanting?
reading: As the cane flower on its thick stalk, with its mane of filaments, loses its honeyed scent, what is birth in a lofty family worth without the great manliness that engraves one's name?

pope: The base feed full of rice and savoury food, that men, great lords of the triple lands, with generous gladness give; but water won with willing strenuous toil by those who know, not savoury food by name even, will turn to nectar. -------------
reading: The base fill themselves on rice and fried dishes that the great Mutharaiyar give with delight; but for those who do not even know the names of such dishes, water won by their own eager effort becomes nectar.
nuance: Pope makes the Mutharaiyar 'lords of the triple lands', one of the readings Mudaliar reports. The verse brands even the guests of a generous patron as base for living on another's food.

title: சுற்றந்தழால்
theme: Holding one's own close: the sympathy of kin dissolves suffering, the worthy bear everyone who leans on them without sorting people into ours and others, and plain food from those who love is sweeter than a feast from those who don't. The bond is proved when it goes into the fire with you.
structure_note: 201 to 205 concern the comfort kin give and the duty of the worthy to bear all who come; 206, 207 and 210 make one point three times through food; 208 and 209 test the bond by adversity. The verses move between kin (கேளிர், கிளைஞர், தமர்) and intimates (நட்டார்), and Mudaliar glosses நட்டார் as kin.
source_issues: 207: Shanmuganar's commentary for 207, with the quatrain text, is printed at the end of the shanmuganar field for 206; 207's own field is not aligned.
208: Pope's translation is not aligned.
210: Pope's text carries a trailing separator line, and the shanmuganar field for 210 ends with the header of chapter 22.

pope: As a mother when she sees her son upon her lap forgets the languors, the pains, and the throes of birth; so trouble arising from weakness will die when a man sees his sympathizing kinsmen around him.
reading: As a mother forgets the cravings of pregnancy, the strain of carrying and the pain of birth when she sees her son on her lap, the trouble a person has suffered through weakness vanishes when he sees kin who ask after him.
nuance: The kin do nothing but come and ask how he is (உசாவுதல்). The comfort the verse describes lies in being asked after, not in material help.

pope: To yield ready protection alike to all, as a tree affords shade to those that seek its shelter when the heat grows fierce; and to live toiling so that many may enjoy the gain, resembling thus a fruit producing tree, is the duty of the manly man.
reading: The duty of a good man is to shelter all who come to him alike, as a shade tree does in fierce heat, and to toil himself so that many enjoy what he yields, as a fruiting tree does.
nuance: தான் வருந்தி makes the giver's own hardship part of the duty rather than a cost to avoid. Mudaliar takes பழுமரம் as the banyan and notes that others read it as a ripe fruiting tree, as Shanmuganar and Pope do.

pope: Lord of the land where mountains piled on mountains rise! the great demur not to support their kith and kin ;—there is no bough but will support the fruit it bears, though clustered thick great fruits and many cling thereon.
reading: Lord of the land of piled-up hills, the great never say 'we will not support' those who have come to depend on them; is there any branch that cannot bear its own fruit, however many and heavy they hang?
nuance: The image makes dependants the supporter's own fruit, so bearing them is part of his nature rather than an act of charity.

pope: Though mingled in a complete intimacy so that all the world knows of it, the friendship of the little will last but little time. Connection with the firm unyielding men endures till the great one's path, who never swerve, is reached.
reading: The friendship of small-natured people does not last beyond a few days, even when they mingle so fully that the world knows it; the bond with those who never falter holds as steadily as the ascetics who keep to their path to the goal.
nuance: Both commentators read the comparison as ascetics who never leave the discipline of renunciation, and Mudaliar names the goal as release (வீடு). Pope's translation makes the line say how long the bond lasts, which is less clear in the Tamil.

pope: ‘Such are they and so many;’ ‘these are ours; those strange :’ those worthy to be classed as chief of men say nothing like this ; so to speak is not their nature ; for they relieve the distress of ALL that troubled come to them!
reading: Those fit to be counted chief among men have no trace of the talk that sorts people as 'of this kind, so many, ours, others', and they draw near and relieve the distress of anyone who is perishing.
nuance: In a chapter on embracing kin, this verse removes the boundary of kinship: for the best people, anyone in distress counts as their own. Mudaliar glosses எமர் and பிறர் as those we want and those we don't.

pope: More sweet than rice, though white as tiger's claw with milk and sugar served on plate of gold, by loveless hands, is any tasteless mess, in any dish, when shared with kindred dear as life.
reading: Saltless millet gruel in any vessel, taken among kin as dear as life, is always sweeter than rice white as a tiger's claw, served with sugar and milk in a golden dish from the hands of those who are not one's own.
nuance: The contrast is total on every count, the vessel, the grain, the salt and the giver, and only the giver decides the taste.

pope: Most bitter (Margosa) is the bounteous meal of dainty food at early dawn in house of those who love us not. Hear thou! though not till evening given, the mess of herbs when eaten with our own is sweet.
reading: A hot fried feast given as hospitality at the proper hour in the house of those not close to one is bitter as neem; greens served at an untimely afternoon hour are sweet when they come from one's own people.
nuance: Even the hour is reversed: the stranger's meal is punctual and the kin's is late, and the kin's is still the sweeter.

reading: Those who pound at you every day like a hammer, eating off you, let go like tongs when the fire comes; those rightly called intimates enter the fire with you like the smith's poker.
nuance: The three smithy tools sort people by how they behave in the heat. Mudaliar offers two readings of முனியாது, 'without tiring' or 'showing affection', and of கொட்டி, 'striking' or 'pestering'. Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain.

pope: O maid adorned with fresh garlands of fragrant flowers! is there one thing that even in other world, friends may perform for friends, if till they die, their joys they share, but shun to share their griefs ?
reading: Maiden with the cool garland of fragrant flowers, if friends share their friends' joys until death but not their sorrows, is there anything they could do for them even in the next world?
nuance: The claim is negative: sharing only joys makes no bond at all. Mudaliar again glosses நட்டார் as kin, where Shanmuganar has friends. The verse is addressed to a woman, which Mudaliar notes.

pope: The savoury fried curry, (in colour) like a cat's eye, which one eats seated a part in the house of those who are without affection, will be bitter as margosa; but cold gruel (weak and insipid), like clear water, in the house of affectionate equals, is ambrosia that cleaves to the bones. --------------
reading: A hot fried dish the colour of a cat's eye, eaten sitting apart in the house of those without affection, is bitter as neem; watery cold gruel in the house of loving equals is ambrosia that joins with one's bones.
nuance: வேறிருந்து, sitting apart, names the slight: the food is served but the guest is kept separate.

title: நட்பாராய்தல்
theme: Test a friend before taking him: by learning, by family, by loyalty under injury, by constancy, and by whether he actually helps. The reason is given at the end: once a bond is formed, parting hurts even when the friend was a snake.
structure_note: 211 to 216 sort friends through images (sugarcane eaten from either end, elephant and dog, tree flowers and pond flowers, three kinds of palm). 217 to 219 weigh what a friend's love, help and understanding are worth. 220 gives the reason for all the testing.
source_issues: 213 and 220: the Tamil has corrupted characters (நண்பெரிணஇ for நண்பொரீஇ; மாணஇ, பெரிணஇ, பாணஇ, மாணஇஇ in 220 where Mudaliar's glosses have மரீஇ, பொரீஇ, பரீஇ).
219: Mudaliar's gloss reads 'கோறல் -சொல்லுதல்', probably a misprint for கொல்லுதல்.
220: Pope's translation has only a title; the text is a separator line. The shanmuganar field ends with the header of chapter 23.

pope: Intimacy with those who understand the real intention (of one's words), and who have acquired wisdom by learning, will at all times be like eating sweet cane from the tender shoots; but attachment to those who have no sweetness of disposition is like eating it in a direction opposite to the tender shoot (it grows harder and less sweet).
reading: Friendship with those who have learned with understanding is always like eating sugarcane from the tip down, sweeter as one goes; the bond with those who lack sweetness is like eating it from the root toward the tip.
nuance: The quatrain nearly repeats 138 in the chapter on learning, with a different refrain. Mudaliar explains that eating from the tip makes the cane grow sweeter as one goes, and from the root less sweet.

pope: Lord of the land of flowery hills, where wild-fowl golden in hue fly, scared by the rush of the waterfall. Regarding the mobility of their birth—these will not swerve:—To say thus is a good ground of confidence—(a good position to take up); but to say ‘their minds are known,' is not any (i. e. real ground).
reading: Lord of the flowering hills, where birds scatter as golden water pours down, one may befriend people on the good ground that, mindful of their family, they will not change midway; apart from that, a person's mind is not something that can be known.
nuance: The verse doesn't praise high birth for its own sake. It falls back on lineage because the mind can't be read. Mudaliar draws the rule: befriend those of high family.

pope: Forsaking friendship with those who resemble the elephant, embrace and hold fast intimacy with those who are like the dog; for the elephant will slay even its keeper though it has long known him ; but the dog will wag its tail when it has in its body the javelin (hurled at it by its angry master).
reading: Give up the friendship of those who are like elephants and hold close those who are like dogs: the elephant may kill even its keeper after knowing him for years, while the dog wags its tail with its master's spear in its body.
nuance: The test is loyalty under injury, not strength or rank: the elephant is the nobler animal and still loses.

pope: Though men dwell side by side for many days when their souls cleave not (are not congenial) for even a few days they retain not their friendship. But is it possible to let go attachment's well-knit ties, though those to whom one's soul is knit dwell many days afar?
reading: Those who are not joined in heart for even a few days do not become close, though they stay beside one for many days; and would anyone let go of the bond with those tied to their heart because they have been away for many days?
nuance: Nearness and distance are both set aside: the heart's tie alone makes and keeps a friend. Shanmuganar supplies 'the great' as the subject.

pope: The use and wont of friendship is that, what once it has loved it loves always,— like the flower on the tree-branch which having once unfolded afterwards closes not; but who will esteem, or make friends of those who are like flowers on the surface of the excavated tank, which unfold and afterwards close themselves?
reading: The true conduct of friendship is to go on loving what it first loved, like a tree's flower that opens and doesn't close again; no one esteems or befriends those who open first and close later, like the flowers of a dug pond.
nuance: Pond flowers such as the lotus close each evening, so the fault condemned is changeability, not coldness.

pope: The lowest sort of men in friendship are like the Arecanut tree. The middle sort are like the cocoa-nut tree. Attachments to the chief of men — who are old friends —is like the Palmyra tree of rare worth : what was given that first day was given once for all.
reading: In friendship the lowest are like the areca palm and the middle like the coconut; the bond of the highest, who keep old ties, is like the palmyra of untold worth: what was given on the first day stays given.
nuance: Mudaliar explains the trees: the areca yields only with constant tending, the coconut with occasional tending, and the palmyra gives richly after a single watering. On that reading the grades measure how much a friend has to be given before the friendship yields.

pope: If one receive you courteously, though what he gives is but rank herbs dressed in water in which rice had been washed, it is ambrosia. To eat from the hands of those who love us not, though it be white rice with rich spicy condiments, is nux vomica.
reading: Even dark greens cooked in rice-water are ambrosia if someone gives them with high regard; white rice with fine seasonings and relishes, taken from the hand of those not in accord with one, is the bitter strychnos fruit.

pope: Of what value is the friendship of those who being very near like the little claw on a dog's leg, afford not help as much as a fly's foot? Though you go far to seek it, lay hold of the friendship of those who are like the water channel that causes the crops in the field to flourish.
reading: What use is the friendship of those as close as the little toe on a dog's foot who give not even a fly's foot of help? Go even far to gain the bond of those who are like the channel that makes the field yield.
nuance: Nearness is set against usefulness, and the channel image implies that real help often comes from a distance.

pope: Better hate than friendship of the ignorant. Better death than disease which comes on yielding to no remedy. Sweeter is killing thin contempt that breaks the spirit. Better abuse than undeserved praise.
reading: Enmity is better than the friendship of those without clear understanding, death better than an incurable disease, killing kinder than contempt that wounds, and abuse better than praise of qualities one doesn't have.
nuance: Only the first of the four comparisons concerns friendship; the other three give it company. Mudaliar's gloss of கோறல் is printed as 'சொல்லுதல்' (speaking), probably an error for கொல்லுதல் (killing), which Shanmuganar and Pope have.

reading: Mix with many over many days, find who matches you, and take only those worth valuing; for it is painful to part after becoming close, even with a snake whose quick bite kills.
nuance: The argument rests on the cost of parting: because breaking a bond hurts even when the friend was deadly, the testing must come first.

title: நட்பிற் பிழை பொறுத்தல்
theme: Once a friend has been chosen, bear their faults: everything has its husk, the patience of one keeps two in friendship, and one who exposes or pries into a friend's faults is worse than the friend.
structure_note: 221 to 226 give images for bearing a chosen friend's wrongs (husk and foam, the dam the stream keeps breaking, fire, the hand that pokes the eye). 227 to 230 turn to exposing a friend's faults, and the chapter ends in a first-person curse on anyone who pries into them.
source_issues: 221 to 228: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
223: the shanmuganar field ends with the text of 224 and Shanmuganar's comment on it; 224's own shanmuganar field is not aligned.
224, 226 and 229: the Tamil has a corrupted character (கா஢யா, தமா஢னும்) where ரி is expected.
230: Pope's title and translation run together, and the text field is a separator line. The shanmuganar field ends with the header of chapter 24.

pope: When those to whom with strong desire we clung as good, prove otherwise, keep the sad secret bid, - cling to them still! The growing grain has husks; the water has its foam: flowers too have scentless outer sheath of leaves.
reading: Those one eagerly took as good should be kept close, with their faults held within, even if they prove otherwise; rice has its husk, water its foam, and flowers their rough outer petals.
nuance: அடக்கிக் கொளல் can mean holding the friend close or keeping the fault to oneself. Shanmuganar takes the second, and Pope's version has both.

pope: If though they dam it up, the fresh flood should burst its bonds, men do not feel aggrieved; but straightway imprison it again, for by the precious stream they live: so though their friends again and again do very disagreeable things, men bear with those whose friendship is dear.
reading: Those who live by water don't rage at the fresh flood when it breaks the dam each time they build it, but dam it again; in the same way people bear with those whose bond they sought, even when they do one hateful thing after another.
nuance: The friend is needed the way the farmer needs the stream, so here forbearance rests on dependence as much as on goodness.

pope: Lord of the lofty hilly land, where the bees hum through all the flowery Gongu-glade ! — Though friends should work us surpassing ills, the only thing that is meet is forbearance: patience of one is friendship of the twain.
reading: Lord of the high hills where bees hum over the bright kongu flowers, isn't it right to bear with one's friends even when they do great wrong? The patience of one is the friendship of two.
nuance: ஒருவர் பொறை இருவர் நட்பு is the maxim: a friendship survives if either party absorbs the injury, so it doesn't need both to be faultless.

pope: Lord of the shore where pearls of purest lustre are thrown up by circling waves, and where swift darting boats are borne through the surf !—when friends who we may not leave have alien hearts, it is as a scorching fire enkindled in the soul.
reading: Lord of the shore where folding waves cast up bright pearls and swift boats rock against the beach, if those one cannot let go lack good nature, they are a fire lit to burn one's heart.
nuance: The verse doesn't say to leave them. It names the pain of a bond one cannot leave. Pope's title, about being angry with those we love, is not in the Tamil. Neither commentary is aligned to this quatrain, though Shanmuganar's comment on it appears under 223.

pope: Though those, from whom you may not part, do grievous things, O maid who art as Lakshmi! you must still cherish your chosen friends—fire destroys men's wealth and happy homes, yet is it sought there and kindled every day.
reading: Those one ought not to part from must be cherished like gold even when they do harm, since the fire that once destroyed a good house along with its gold is still sought out and kindled at home every day.
nuance: Fire both destroys and is needed daily, so the friend is cherished because life needs them, not because the harm is forgotten. Pope takes பொன்னாக as an address to a maiden 'as Lakshmi'; Shanmuganar reads it as 'like gold'.

pope: When those from whom it is hard to part do evil things should men at once renounce them?—Lord of the lengthening hills that pierce the sky, whence rarest giftsdescend !—Do men cut off their hand because it pricked their eye?
reading: Lord of the sky-piercing hills of rare excellence, is it right to cast off those hard to part from, though they hurt you? Does anyone cut off their own hand because it poked their eye?
nuance: The image makes the friend part of one's own body, so cutting them off harms oneself again and undoes nothing.

pope: Lord of the cool shore of the shining sea! The perfect ones when they have contracted an intimacy with any, see no faults in them, even if they do things that cause pain. Those who, being without stable wisdom, take up and tell out men's evil deeds after contracting an intimacy with them, are themselves worse than they.
reading: Lord of the cool shore of shining waters, once the worthy have joined with someone they see no fault in them even when hurt; those without firm understanding who bring out another's wrongs after joining with him are themselves lower than he is.
nuance: The verse ranks exposing a friend's wrong as worse than the wrong itself.

pope: Lord of the land of resounding waterfalls ! Though what those alien to us have done may be surpassingly evil, what is there to be pained at, when you regard it? Things done by affectionate friends, will be excellent when so regarded by the mind.
reading: Lord of the land of roaring falls, what is there to grieve over, on reflection, when strangers do great wrong? And what those bound by love have done becomes good when held within the heart.
nuance: The same harm is treated by who did it: from a stranger it is to be shrugged off, from one who loves it is to be turned into something good within.

pope: If we perceive those we have accepted as our own to be not really ours, we must pay even more respect to them than to our own, and keep concealed in our own mind the fact that they are not really ours.
reading: If you find that those you took as your own are not, honour them even more than your own and keep the knowledge that they are not yours shut within you.
nuance: Pope's title says to love them the more; the verse says மதித்து, to value or honour.

reading: If, after taking someone as my friend, I go about searching out his faults and his other qualities, may I go where the man who did not guard his friend's secret goes, while the world encircled by the roaring sea laughs.
nuance: A curse spoken in the first person. Mudaliar names the destination as hell. Examining a friend belongs before the friendship (chapter 22); after it, examining is treated as betrayal.

title: கூடா நட்பு
theme: Friendships that don't fit: with those who stay only for their own ends, whose bond is shallow, who are of another nature, or who lack discernment. Such friendship fades, pains, and drags down even the discerning, while the company of the wise is like heaven.
source_issues: 233: the Tamil has a corrupted character (நுண்ணு஡ல் for நுண்ணூல்).
240: Pope's text ends with a separator line, and the shanmuganar field ends with a section header labelled இன்ப இயல் for chapter 25, though chapter 25 is listed under பொருட்பால்.

pope: Lord of the pleasant well-watered mountain land, where boiling waterfalls pour down from the dark hills! (Poor men) linger beneath the old roof that affords no shelter, baling out the water, and making mud embankments, and enduring the down-pour; (even so unreal friends stick by you) till their purpose has been attained.
reading: Lord of the well-watered hills where waterfalls pour from dark peaks, like people who stay under an old leaking roof, making mud dams and bailing out and catching the water, some stay by you only until their own business is done.
nuance: The simile is of discomfort put up with for one's own sake: they stay as one stays under a bad roof, because they need it for now. Shanmuganar adds that they pretend to share one's troubles.

pope: Lord of the land of pure (white, forming) waterfalls! The friendship of the virtuous is of exceeding excellence, and yields glorious results — like (seasonable) rain; but the friendship of the vicious, even in the time of its exuberance, is as when the rain fails in the time of drought.
reading: Lord of the land of white waterfalls, the friendship of the excellent is of surpassing worth and fruitful like rain; that of the worthless, even at its height, is like rain that has failed.

pope: Enjoyment of the society of men of refinement resembles the heavenly world in the pleasure it affords. Closest contact with those destitute of fine perception of the value of learned pursuits —men who gain no wisdom from you, nor you from them—is one of the hells.
reading: Enjoying the company of people of fine understanding is as desirable as the heavenly world; being joined to profitless people without understanding of subtle learning is one of the hells.

pope: Lord of the land where wide groves of Sandal cover the hilly slopes! Friendship with those who feel not its real obligation, like fire in the straw (suddenly) appears, seeming as though it would increase, but never advancing dies out.
reading: Lord of the hills whose slopes are lined with long sandal groves, the bond with those who have no real tie seems to grow, then, like fire in straw, dies without lasting even a moment.
nuance: Mudaliar glosses பந்தம் as the bond of love; Shanmuganar as true attachment.

pope: The promising to do what cannot be done, and the putting off and leaving undone through delay things that could be done, will forthwith bring experience of sorrow even to those who have condemned truthfully the pleasant experiences of life (ascetics and saints).
reading: Saying 'we will do it' of what cannot be done, and putting off what can be done, bring suffering at once even to those who have truly scorned the enjoyment of pleasure.
nuance: 'Even to ascetics' means these faults hurt whatever one's indifference to pleasure. The verse doesn't mention friends; only its place in this chapter suggests these are marks of an unfit friend.

pope: The Ambal (water-lily) does not equalthe expanding Kuvalai though born and growing together with it in the same pool : though they attain to intimacy with those of generous instincts, the deeds of men in whom these instincts are lacking will be diverse.
