reading: Though born in the same pool and growing up together, the water-lily never equals the spreading kuvalai; so though they gain the friendship of the large-natured, the deeds of those who lack that nature remain different.
nuance: Pope's title speaks of a lotus; the Tamil compares the ஆம்பல் with the குவளை, the blue water-lily.

pope: Lord of the hilly land where the immature little monkey, with its finger like a bean-pod, will flip its father when it meets him, and poke him and snatch fruit from him! Afflictive indeed is friendship with the uncongenial.
reading: Lord of the hills where the unripe little monkey, with fingers like dry bean-pods, pokes and prises at the father who meets it to snatch his food, the friendship of those not of one mind with you is painful.
nuance: The image is of closeness without regard: the young monkey takes from the one nearest to it.

pope: If I hasten not to put forth my hand and offer my precious life to my friend when in distress, may I depart whither he goes who has violated the sanctity of his friend's wedded wife, while the far-famed world laughs!
reading: If, when my friend is in distress, I do not hurry to put my precious life in his hands, may I go where the man who violated his friend's guarded wife goes, while the world of lasting words laughs.
nuance: The chapter on unfit friendship includes this vow of what a fit friend owes. Mudaliar names the destination as hell and gives three readings of நெடுமொழி வையம்.

pope: Lord of the land of goodly hills where honey flows! To forsake the friendship of those who know the right, and cultivate that of shallow pretenders to knowledge, is like emptying out cow's ghee from a vessel and pouring into it margosa oil.
reading: Lord of the good hills where honey flows, leaving the friendship of those who know what is good to befriend the petty-minded is like emptying cow's ghee from a vessel and filling it with neem oil.

pope: The absence of generosity in those whose exterior is pleasing, is like the mingling of water with the milk provided for food: when men of understanding take to bad company it is like the disporting of a Cobra with a female viper. -------------
reading: One fitted for good form who lacks generosity toward his town is like milk fit to drink mixed with water; the discerning taking up with bad company is like a cobra mating with a female viper.
nuance: Mudaliar records the belief that a cobra mating with a viper dies, so the image predicts ruin.

title: அறிவுடைமை
theme: Understanding shown in conduct: restraint toward fallen foes and in poverty, judging people by mind and conduct rather than birthplace or kind, steadiness in friendship, and knowing that a person raises or lowers himself. It ends with the picture of a life that completes work, pleasure and virtue.
structure_note: The quatrains range from conduct toward enemies and superiors (241, 249) and in poverty (242), through birth and environment (243 to 245) and friendship (244, 246, 247), to the self as the cause of one's standing (248) and a whole life well finished (250).
source_issues: 246: the Tamil has 'ம்ருஉச்செய்' where Mudaliar's gloss has மரூஉ.
247: the Tamil has a corrupted character (புணா஢ன் for புணரின்).
249 and 250: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
250: Pope's text ends with a separator line, and the shanmuganar field ends with the header of chapter 26.

pope: Worthy men, when they behold where foes are foiled, themselves too feel sore abashed, and do not hasten on to crush them. Behold, the strong invulnerable dragon draws not near the moon (to swallow it) when it is in its tender crescent days!
reading: When the worthy see their enemies humbled, they themselves feel shame and do not advance on them; see, the snake whose strength nothing can trouble does not seize the moon while it is a young crescent.
nuance: The shame belongs to the victor, not the defeated. Shanmuganar names the snake as Rahu, the eclipse serpent.

pope: Lord of the cool shore of the spreading sea ! To men in poverty a modest self-restraint is the chiefest ornament. If a man live in unbending pride, and in a manner unbefitting his position, his fellow-townsmen will revile his race.
reading: Lord of the cool shore of the vast sea, for the poor, restraint is the ornament; if one lives without humility and beyond measure, the town one lives in will speak ill of one's family.
nuance: The cost of a poor man's lack of restraint falls on his lineage, not only on himself.

pope: Whatever soil you sow it in, the Strychnos nut grows not into a cocoa-palm. Some of the Southern land have entered Paradise! It is man's way of life that decides his future state. Full many from the Northern land are denizens of hell.
reading: In whatever soil it is sown, a strychnos seed will not become a coconut; since even those of the south enter heaven, one's next world comes from oneself, and in the north too there are very many idle wasters.
nuance: Pope calls the northerners 'denizens of hell'; கொன்னாளர் means those who spend their days to no purpose, which is milder.

pope: Though ripened amid margosa leaves the fruit of the plantain loses no atom of its sweet flavour. Even so the friendship of men of noble mood, although their race be evil, can hardly work ill to the mind.
reading: Though ripened among neem leaves, the plantain keeps its sweet taste unchanged; so, though their company is bad, the friendship of those of good nature rarely turns to a bad mind.
nuance: Pope reads இனம் as 'race'; both commentators read it as the company one keeps.

pope: Though close by the sea, sweet waters oft-times spring up there; on the hill-side the waters often gush out all brine! Thus men are not as their race. — Lord of the dashing sea's cool shore! Men are as their minds.
reading: Lord of the cool shore of the dashing sea, since sweet water rises even beside the sea and brackish water even on the hills, people are not as their kind but as their minds.

pope: Lord of the cool sea-shore, where flourishes the thick-stemmed laurel ! Men whose minds are good (constant), and who adhere to whomsoever they have formed an intimacy with, will not sometimes avoid men, and at other times be intimate. It is good not to have fits of alternating warmth and indifference.
reading: Lord of the cool shore where thick-trunked punnai trees grow, do people of steady mind, who stay with whomever they have formed a good bond, leave and then rejoin? It is good not to mix with people indiscriminately.
nuance: Pope takes விராய் as alternating warmth and coldness; both commentators take it as mixing with people without examination.

pope: Join the men who throughly feel true wisdom's inner sense, and forthwith joy joins you. Join yourself to men devoid of the accurate preception of knowledge, and then parting from them is parting from pain.
reading: Join those whose understanding grasps things as they should be grasped, and joy joins you; if you join those without discernment, the pain parts only when you part from them.
nuance: The verse is built on repeated words (உணர உணரும், புணரப் புணரும், தெரியத் தெரியும், பிரியப் பிரியும்), a figure Mudaliar names.

pope: He that establishes a man in good, and he that disturbs that good position and casts him down, and he that more and more exalts a man and establishes him, and he that makes a man head (among men) is (the MAN) HIMSELF.
reading: The one who sets a person in a good state, the one who unsettles and casts him down, the one who raises him ever higher, and the one who makes him the head of others, is that person himself.
nuance: Mudaliar names the cause as one's understanding or lack of it; the verse itself names none. It also names no fate, which sits uneasily with chapter 11 on old deeds, unless those deeds are counted as one's own doing too.

pope: Lord of the cool shore of the sounding sea, where from old time the billows roar!— In the course of their affairs when even great men follow after the unlearned, this is not folly but wisdom.
reading: Lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea, when even the great follow behind the unlearned for the sake of a task, that is not folly but understanding.
nuance: The verse allows status to be set aside for a purpose (கரும வரிசையால்); it doesn't say the great should follow the unlearned in general.

pope: If a man has wrought all fitting works, enjoyed all seemly pleasures, done deeds of charity to worthy men: if he shall have accomplished all these three unchecked, in this one state, of him men will say: ‘that is a ship that has gained the haren' -------------
reading: If one does one's work, enjoys one's pleasures, and does virtuous giving to the worthy, and all three are completed without hindrance in a single life, people call it a ship that has reached the port.
nuance: A full worldly life is praised here, in a work that mostly urges renunciation, through the image of a trading voyage brought home. Pope reads ஒருநிலையே as 'in this one state'; Shanmuganar as 'all together'.

title: அறிவின்மை
theme: Want of understanding (அறிவின்மை) is the real poverty. The unlearned and the base cannot take in good counsel, show themselves for what they are among the learned, and set up petty assemblies of their own, while the learned keep silent before those who would not absorb what they say.
structure_note: The chapter opens by making understanding the true wealth (251) and explaining, as a fancy, why the learned are poor (252). It then shows the unlearned among the learned (253-254), the learned holding back their speech (255-256), and the base who cannot receive good words (257-260), with a run of similes: the pig's trough, charcoal washed in milk, the fly on dung.
source_issues: Quatrain 256: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of quatrain 257 and his commentary on it; 257's own Pope and Shanmuganar fields are not aligned, and Pope's translation of 257 was not found.
Quatrain 260: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: The want of refined knowledge is poverty, its possession is very great and abundant wealth. When one considers, will not a sexless creature, more woman than man, adorn herself with the jewels that her eye desires ?
reading: Lack of fine understanding is poverty and having it is great wealth; when one thinks about it, a eunuch who longs to be a woman will still put on the jewels that catch every eye.
nuance: The simile is left unexplained in the verse. Shanmuganar draws the conclusion that the wealth of the senseless is like the eunuch's jewels: an adornment on something that lacks the essential thing. Pope's heading puts it as 'mere externals are nothing'.

pope: Men of vast and varied lore are seen in low estate, and suffer want. Would you know the reason? The anciently renowned ‘Lady of the tongue' abides with them). ‘The Lady of the flowers' is jealous, and draws not near !
reading: If you would know why men of wide learning lose standing and suffer want: the ancient Lady of the Tongue lives with them, so the Lady of the Flower keeps away in a sulk.
nuance: A playful explanation (Mudaliar names the figure தற்குறிப்பேற்றம், an imputed cause), not a theology of fortune. Mudaliar offers two reasons for the quarrel: Lakshmi and Sarasvati are mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, or two women do not share one man in peace.

pope: He who, when his father urgently bade him learn, did not take it as a serious matter, but contemned it; when, before many men, some one gently presents a written palm-leaf, will in anger fetch a stick to beat him as guilty of an insult.
reading: One who scorned his father's urging to learn, not taking it as worth heeding, will grab a stick in anger when someone quietly holds out a written leaf to him before many people.
nuance: The anger is the unlearned man's shame turned outward: he cannot read the leaf in public. Mudaliar records other readings of the last line, one in which he laughs in contempt, one in which he makes a noise to slip away.

pope: When a man who has grown up without learning enters the society of the wise, if he sit still, it is as if a dog sat there; and if he rise to speak, it is as though a dog barked.
reading: When a man who grew up without learning enters among the wise, if he sits quietly it is as if a dog sat there, and if he speaks it is as if a dog barked.
nuance: Silence does not save him: Mudaliar allows மெல்ல இருப்பினும் to mean 'even if he sits with restraint', which makes the verse deny the unlearned any good way to be present.

pope: All the baser sort consorting with scholars of a heterodox and low school, will utter illiterate rubbish; but men replete with learning, though urgently asked, utter not the results of their learning, knowing that (the asker) would fail to apply their minds to the import of what was said.
reading: The low all go among the poets of petty, senseless assemblies and say things they never learned; but the worthy, even when asked, do not speak of what they have learned, knowing it would not be taken in.
nuance: Pope calls the assembly 'heterodox'; neither commentator says so. Mudaliar has it as an assembly not joined to understanding, and Shanmuganar's poets are false poets.

pope: Men of learned tongues are silent, fearing some slip; others (ignorant men) will speak out; on the Palmyra tree the dried-up leaves make a loud rustling noise ; but evermore the green leaf gives forth no sound !
reading: The learned and eloquent hold back, afraid of a lapse, while others talk freely: on the palmyra the dry leaves rattle, but the green leaf never makes a sound.
nuance: Mudaliar notes the images answer the statements in reverse order (green leaf to the learned, dry leaves to the rest). Silence here signals life and fullness, noise dryness.

reading: Telling the way of virtue to people who do not know the good is like pressing sweet mango juice into a pig's trough; like a stake driven on a rock, it splits at the head and does not go into their ears.
nuance: Two similes for two failures: the teaching is wasted (the trough) and it cannot penetrate (the stake on rock). Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain, and Shanmuganar's commentary appears under 256.

pope: Though you wash it with milk for many days and dry it, charcoal on no hypothesis becomes white ! So into the undisciplined body wisdom enters not, though you teach it, driving it in with a stick.
reading: Charcoal washed in milk and dried for many days never turns white, and understanding will not enter a body that has not earned it, though you drive it in with a stick.
nuance: நோலா உடம்பு is the hinge. Both commentators take it as a body without merit from good deeds (Mudaliar: from a former birth, so without innate understanding); Pope reads 'undisciplined body', which moves the cause from past births to present discipline.

pope: To those whose minds are full of foul things, — like the fly which goes not to feed on the flower that pours forth sweetness and breathes perfume, but fixes its eager desire on ordure,—What clear comprehension can there be of the lucid words full of honied sweetness that issue from the mouths of the worthy?
reading: Like the fly that will not settle on a flower pouring honey and fragrance but craves filth, those whose minds are set on low things get nothing from the clear, honeyed words of the worthy.
nuance: The fault is in desire, not capacity: the fly passes the flower by preference. Mudaliar notes that 'low things' is a polite way of naming filth.

pope: The base man does not apprehend the faultless words of accurate instruction which the learned utter. These pain his mind. He therefore looks in the face of some other one like himself (for encouragement), and convenes a wretched assembly of his own: i.e. He finds one like-minded, and the two set up a sect. -------------
reading: Because his heart kicks away the faultless, subtle teaching of the learned, the base man looks into the face of another like himself and sets up a petty assembly of his own.
nuance: The rejection breeds a rival: two of a kind confirm each other. Pope reads it as founding a sect; Mudaliar's கோட்டி is the talk given there, Shanmuganar's a platform speech.

title: நன்றியில் செல்வம்
theme: Wealth that does no good (நன்றியில் செல்வம்): the riches of the base and ungiving are of no use to anyone near them, and the poor turn away to givers however far. The chapter also faces the scandal that wealth goes to the senseless while the good are poor, and explains it by former deeds.
structure_note: Three nature similes show that the base man's wealth draws no one (261-263). Then the chapter turns to the injustice of fortune (264-268), answered by former deeds (265) and met with a curse on Lakshmi (266), and ends on the folly of the rich man's giving (269) and a set of reversals that redefine learned, unlearned, rich and poor (270).
source_issues: Quatrain 261: Shanmuganar's field also holds the texts and commentary of 262 and 263, and the text of 264 without commentary; Shanmuganar's commentary on 264 and 265 is missing.
Quatrain 263: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
Quatrain 266: the verse reads நாறாக் தகடேபோல், apparently for நாறாத் தகடேபோல்; Mudaliar glosses நாறா.
Quatrain 270: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: The bat approaches not the Heronia, with its dry stem, though it be night at hand and bear abundant fruit; so although mean people are very close at hand, their wealth is not a thing that can be counted upon.
reading: Bats do not go to the wood-apple tree with its cracked trunk, though it stands near and bears much fruit; so the wealth of men without worth, however close they live, is not something anyone thinks of counting on.
nuance: Nearness is the point: what is close but unapproachable is as good as far. Mudaliar specifies who does not count on it: the poor.

pope: Men reach not out their band to the Kalli (Cactus), though it bears delicate round buds by the handful, because these are not flowers they can weave into a garland to crown themselves withal; so wise people from no friendships with the base however great their wealth may be.
reading: No one reaches for the cactus, though its small buds look lovely enough to gather by the handful, because they are not flowers to wear; so the wise do not seek out the base, however rich.
nuance: The cactus buds are attractive but unusable; wealth is the attraction, character the use. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 261.

pope: Though men live on the curved shore of the sea with its multitudinous waves, they go and drink at the well, with its perennial fountain of fresh water from the rock; so even if those (who are neighbours) are very wealthy, the desire (of the poor) is towards the liberal, though these may be far to seek.
reading: Though they live on the shore of the wave-filled sea, people go and drink at a well with a strong, sweet spring; so though the rich are near, desire turns to the givers, even far away.
nuance: The sea is huge and useless to drink; the small well gives. Size of wealth does not draw anyone, only its being given. Mudaliar's commentary is missing for this quatrain, and Shanmuganar's appears under 261.

pope: In the world surrounded by the (all-)embracing sea, merit is quite an indifferent matter! Understanding ones are (poor); and even those of no understanding—who are like mere palm tree tufts and brinjals—live prosperously, clad in silks and rich garments.
reading: In this sea-girt world merit is a thing apart: while men of understanding are there, even those with no understanding, like the dice-piece and the brinjal, live clad in silk and fine cloth.
nuance: புண்ணியம் (merit) is set apart from understanding: prosperity follows merit, not sense. Mudaliar works out the two images: the dice-piece that returns to the board after being cut down (the shameless who come back to the assembly) and the brinjal that fruits hidden (those who hide their wealth). Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

pope: While pleasant folk and just abide (in poverty), you ponder why men unjust and ignorant have any joy. It is fruit of 'ancient deeds', thou whose long eyes are darts :—to thoughtful mind no other cause occurs.
reading: Long-eyed one, when the good and just remain poor, the only cause you will find on reflection for the unjust and unlearned having wealth is the fruit of old deeds.
nuance: The verse answers the scandal of undeserved wealth with former deeds, and so denies that present wealth says anything about present worth. Mudaliar specifies good deeds of a former birth. Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

pope: O golden dame, that sittest like a scentless leaf on a beauteous flower! Die, and fall in ashes to the ground: thou enterest homes of worthless men of perverse mind, forsaking good men pure as gold.
reading: Golden lady seated on the fine flower like its scentless outer petal, may you die and turn to ash on the earth: you leave the good, who are like gold, and go to the side of worthless men.
nuance: A curse on Lakshmi herself. Mudaliar explains the simile: as the outer petal lacks the flower's scent, the goddess who lives on the lotus has none of its softness.

pope: Has poverty, that bides with men of righteous souls, no shame? Does wealth to ungenerous men stick like glue?O thou of dart-like eye, with wonder see that thus, no just discernment made, these two abide !
reading: Does poverty feel no shame in staying with the good? Is the wealth of the useless a glue that holds fast? See with wonder, dart-eyed one, how these two stay just where they ought not.
nuance: Poverty and wealth are made into agents with manners: one shameless, the other sticky. The verse states the wonder without explaining it; 265 gives the explanation.

pope: Men who are not void of shame will travel forth on foot, and feed on scraps, —so pass their days ; the shameless ones make no journeys on foot, but feed on dainties at home, perspiring over the feast.
reading: Those who are not shameless walk long roads and live on mixed scraps, while the shameless never stir a foot and feast at home on fried dishes as rivers of ghee and milk flow over them.
nuance: Shame is what keeps the decent poor; its absence is what lets the others thrive. Mudaliar takes the scraps as begged food and the feasters as eating alone behind closed doors without giving; Shanmuganar names the feasters' fault as dishonesty and deceit.

pope: While the red paddy's golden germ is parched within the ear and dies, the cloud gleaming with lightnings pours forth its treasures on the sea. When silly men gain ample wealth, even so are their liberal gifts bestowed !
reading: While the golden red paddy withers in the ear, the lightning-lit cloud pours its rain into the sea; the giving of fools who come into great wealth is of the same kind.
nuance: The fault is not that fools never give but that they give where it is not needed. Mudaliar's 'also' (உம்மை) implies they otherwise do nothing good with wealth either.

pope: Men void of understanding, though they learn, learn not! Men of understanding, though unlearned, are as men learned! They are rich, though utter paupers, who never beg; the rich are paupers if they bestow nothing ! -------------
reading: Those without understanding remain unlearned though they study, and those with understanding are as the learned though they have not studied; those who never beg are rich though poor, and the rich are poor if they do not give.
nuance: Four reversals that make the inner quality, not the outward possession, decide the name. Mudaliar takes தூய்தாக as a pure mind, a condition on the poor who do not beg.

title: ஈயாமை
theme: Not giving (ஈயாமை): to cook and eat is to share; the miser who neither gives nor enjoys is mocked by his own hoard, loses it to strangers and heirs, and is worse off than the poor. Giving must be done now, in whatever measure one can, and wealth held without giving is a house of suffering.
structure_note: The chapter moves from the duty to share and to give now (271-272) to the miser's folly and loss (273-278), defines true liberality against the base man's forced yield (279), and ends with wealth itself as the dwelling of suffering (280).
source_issues: Quatrain 273: Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.
Quatrain 275: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of 276 and his commentary on it; 276's own Shanmuganar field is not aligned.
Quatrain 279: Pope's translation is not aligned, and Shanmuganar's field ends with the text of 280; Shanmuganar's commentary on 280 is missing.

pope: To eat your own meal, after sharing what you have cooked, to the extent of your ability, both with those who are friends and those who are not friends, is 'cooking and eating' (= is real house keeping). To the good-for-nothing human beings whose habit of life it is to shut themselves up and eat alone what they have cooked, the door of yonder world will be shut.
reading: To share what is cooked, as far as one has, with friends and with those who are not friends, and then eat, is what cooking and eating means; for the worthless who shut the door and eat inside, the door of the other world is shut.
nuance: The punishment mirrors the fault: a shut door for a shut door. Mudaliar takes 'friends' as kin and 'not friends' as guests; Pope has 'friends and foes', which widens the duty further than either commentator.

pope: Whatever the measure be, those who do even lesser acts of charity to the measure of their power shall attain to excellence. But those who, when they have obtained great wealth. say 'we will be wise (and give) by and by,' are lost in a sea of guilt.
reading: Those who do small acts of virtue, however little, within their means, rise; those who say they will think about it after they gain great wealth are lost in a sea of blame.
nuance: The verse reverses the usual excuse: it is the small giver who is great and the one waiting for great wealth who drowns. Mudaliar notes that 'are lost' is past tense for certainty.

pope: The senseless man who spends not time in enjoyment (of his wealth), and who gives nothing to pions devotees, but hoards and dies, —him his hoarded wealth derides; him all that is gracious in the world derides.
reading: The fool who neither enjoys his wealth nor gives anything to renunciants, but hoards it and dies, is laughed at by the very wealth he stored, and by the compassion in the world.
nuance: The wealth itself is made to mock him: it outlives him and was never used. The gift named is to renunciants (துறவோர்), a pointer to the Jain setting. Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

pope: The great wealth obtained by the man of straitened soul, who knows not how either to give or to enjoy, shall be enjoyed by a stranger, in due season—like lovely virgins remaining unmarried in the dwelling.
reading: The great wealth of the tight-hearted man who knows neither how to give nor how to enjoy will in due season be enjoyed by a stranger, like a lovely daughter of the house.
nuance: The daughter is raised in the house and goes to an outsider when she comes of age; the image makes the loss natural and certain, not a mishap.

pope: Though they have got the mighty sea with its dashing waves (to drink from), men wait for the stream slowly issuing from the little well, often dry, and drink there; so the exceeding poverty of the virtuous is preferable to the wealth of those who know not of the world to come.
reading: Though they live by the great sea with its dashing waves, people wait at a small, nearly dry well for its trickle and drink; so the deep poverty of the worthy is better than the wealth of those who know nothing of the next world.
nuance: The sea is plenty that cannot be used; the small well is little that can. Shanmuganar takes 'knowing the next world' as knowing and doing the good deeds that belong to it.

pope: As to the property which the wretched churl claims saying 'It is mine, it is mine ,' I too chime in with "It is mine, it is mine;' for if it is his, he himself spends it not, nor enjoys the benefit of it; and I, too, neither spend nor enjoy it!
reading: The wealth the fool keeps calling 'mine, mine', I too call 'mine, mine': if it is his, he neither gives it nor enjoys it, and neither do I.
nuance: A joke with a sting: ownership that produces no use is no different from not owning. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 275.

pope: The poor have escaped much from which rich men that dispense not suffer. They have escaped the reputation of having lost (their substance). They have escaped the toil of saving it. They have escaped (the labour of) digging (to hide it). They have escaped the ache of hands securing it from powerful plunderers. Many are the (sorrows) they have escaped.
reading: The poor have escaped much that troubles the rich who do not give: being called ruined, the toil of guarding, the digging to bury it, the aching hands that clutch it; many are their escapes.
nuance: The list is ironic consolation, not praise of poverty: the comparison is only with the miser. Pope reads the last escape as tying it up against powerful plunderers; Mudaliar as gripping it tight.

pope: While it was his he gave not; and his heirs, how it is theirs, give not. Before, while it was his, if he had given, they would not have reproved (him); and afterwards, if they had given, he would not have reproved them! Men's own avarice is the sole reason for the lack of charity.
reading: While it was his he did not give, and his heirs do not give once it is theirs; had he given first, they would not have stopped him, and when they give later, he cannot stop them.
nuance: The argument removes every excuse: nobody prevented either party from giving. Pope's added sentence states the moral, that only one's own avarice stops giving.

reading: Liberality is to yield gladly, as a cow does to its calf, the askers being the calf and the givers the cow; the base yield, like a cow milked by force, only when strong men press and torment them.
nuance: The same act, giving, is good or base by the way it comes out. Mudaliar records several readings of வாய் வைத்து: by many devices, by reviling, or with instruments. Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain.

pope: Gathering it together is trouble, and even so the guarding of resplendent wealth is severe trouble. If the guarded heap diminish, it is trouble. If it perish, it is trouble. Wealth is trouble's very dwelling-place! ---------------
reading: Gaining wealth is suffering, guarding it is bitter suffering, its dwindling is suffering and its loss is suffering: wealth is the very dwelling place of suffering.
nuance: The verse speaks of wealth itself, not only the miser's, though the chapter setting is not giving. Every stage, from earning to loss, is suffering, so no stage is safe. Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

title: இன்மை
theme: Poverty (இன்மை): the world honours a few coins over noble birth, kin and flatterers leave with wealth, and poverty strips away lineage, valour, learning, goodness and even sharpness of mind. For one who cannot help those who ask, the chapter says it is better to leave home and live as a guest or a beggar elsewhere.
structure_note: Observations of how the world treats the poor (281-285, 287) are interrupted by advice to the one who cannot give (286, 288) and close with a picture of fallen fortune (289) and a near repeat of 283 (290). Mudaliar notes the two repeats (288 with 286, 290 with 283) and explains them by the tradition that each quatrain had a different author.
source_issues: Quatrain 282: the last line reads புகற்கா஢ய with a garbled character, apparently புகற்கரிய.
Quatrain 285: the verse reads க்ழுஉங், apparently garbled; Mudaliar glosses கழூஉம்.
Quatrain 286: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of 287 and his commentary on it; 287's own Shanmuganar field is not aligned.
Quatrain 288: Pope's translation is not aligned.
Quatrain 290: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: Though he wraps a cloth dyed red around his loins, a dozen coins or so, will gain (the wretch) respect among many men! The man devoid of wealth, though born of noble race, is viler (in the world's estimation) than a lifeless corpse !
reading: Even one who lives with a dyed cloth wrapped round his waist gains standing among many if he has ten or eight coins; those who have nothing, though born into a fitting family, are lower than a corpse.
nuance: The ochre or patched cloth (Mudaliar gives both) marks someone of no standing; a handful of coins outweighs it, while noble birth without money counts for less than a dead body. The verse reports how the world judges, without endorsing it.

pope: Where water cannot enter! the more insinuating ghi glides in; and smoke as a subtler power to penetrate than even ghi. If you look into it, the man debased by poverty will enter haunts where smoke scarce finds a way.
reading: Ghee is said to be finer than water and everyone knows smoke is finer than ghee; but if you consider it, the man in the affliction of want gets in through openings even smoke can hardly pass.
nuance: A comic hyperbole of need pressing in anywhere for help. Mudaliar's first reading divides the phrase as இரப்பு இடும்பை, the affliction of begging, and gives நிரப்பு, poverty, as another; Shanmuganar and Pope take poverty.

pope: When on the high hill's crags the Kanthal blooms no more, the crimson-spotted beetle tribe seek not its boughs;—Lord of the hills wherefrom they scare parrots with stones! — the needy have no kin.
reading: Lord of the forest land where they scare parrots from the millet with stones: when the kanthal does not flower on the high rocky hill, the red-spotted bees do not go there; the poor have no kin.
nuance: Kin are bees and wealth the flower: they come for what is given, not for the person. The address to a hill chief borrows the frame of the akam poems.

pope: When wealth is there, obsequious myriads will assemble, like crows around the fallen corpse. When wealth, as the beetle wheels its flight, is gone, no one in all the world will ask, ‘Is it well with you?'
reading: While there is wealth, a thousand gather as servants, like crows at a carcass; when one wanders like a bee, no one in the world asks 'are you well?'
nuance: The crows at the carcass make the flatterers feeders on the rich man, not friends. Both commentators make the poor man the one wandering like a bee for food; Pope makes the wealth the thing that flies off like a beetle.

pope: Lord of the pleasant land of clustering hills whose crags are washed by sounding waterfalls !—Their race is nought, their manly prowess is nought, their rare learning is nought, when men are held in poverty's embrace.
reading: Lord of the good land of clustered hills where loud waterfalls wash the rocks: for those whom poverty has seized, the family they were born into, great manliness and their excellent learning all perish.
nuance: The three goods named are ones normally thought independent of wealth: birth, character and learning. Mudaliar lists the qualities of ஆண்மை as fullness, forbearance, discernment and firmness, or else as valour.

pope: Although he dwells within the village, and sees the poor draw nigh with hungry soul desiring aid, he yields them none : why then in the village does he vainly pass his days? It were better he went to be a guest himself !
reading: One who lives in his own village but can give nothing to those who come to him driven by hunger had better go away and be a guest somewhere than waste his life staying there.
nuance: Who is meant decides the tone. On Mudaliar's reading it is advice to a poor man, matching 288; on Shanmuganar's and Pope's it is scorn for a miser, and Shanmuganar lets 'guest' also mean a guest of the other world, that is, death.

pope: O thou whose teeth vie in sharpness with jasmine buds! — When sharp distress of poverty assails, men lose all their attributes of goodness at once, with the mind's acuteness gained from amplest stores of wisdom.
reading: Girl whose teeth outdo the sharp jasmine buds: those overtaken by the affliction called want lose at once not only their good nature but their fully risen sharpness of mind and everything else.
nuance: The verse plays on கூர்மை: the sharpness lost by the poor is held up against the sharpness of the girl's teeth. Mudaliar notes that நிரப்பு, literally fullness, is used here for its opposite. Shanmuganar's commentary appears under 286.

reading: Rather than live on in one's own village, straitened and blocked and struggling, unable to give to one who asks, it is better to go a long way and live the ruined life of holding out one's hand at row after row of houses.
nuance: Begging is ranked above the shame of refusing an asker at home. Mudaliar says it repeats 286 and cites Kural 478 for இட்டு (narrow). Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain.

pope: The hands once loaded with golden bracelets now cull the forest-herb and cook the meal; and then eat the mess unseasoned, from the palm-leaf for a dish! Thus sad at heart they live, when fortune is gone and ruin come.
reading: When their means are spent and gone, with the hands that once wore bracelets they pull down branches, pick greens, cook them, and eat the boiled leaves without salt from a folded palm-leaf, living on with broken spirit.
nuance: The bracelets on the hands that now strip branches carry the whole fall in one image. Mudaliar cites Kalittokai for குடை as a palm-leaf vessel.

pope: The humming spotted beetle tribes all bright in hue gather not on the branch that has ceased to blow. Lord of the good cool hilly land, of high renown, whence bounteous streams flow down unceasingly—the unprosperous have no kin! --------------
reading: Lord of the cool, good hill land whose waterfalls never fail: the bright, humming, spotted bees do not go to the branch that has flowered and finished; those who have lost their prosperity have no kin.
nuance: Mudaliar notes it shares the thought of 283. The difference is small: here the branch has flowered and finished, so the stress falls on prosperity once had and lost.

title: மானம்
theme: Honour (மானம்): those who have it burn at the arrogance and contempt of the rich, will not lay their need before the unworthy, keep away from patrons who demean them, and would rather die, or refuse heaven itself, than incur sin, blame or loss of honour. Honour is set in a scale of what people fear and is said to bring good in this world and the next.
structure_note: The chapter frames honour through the honourable poor man's relation to the rich (291-293, 296, 298-299), between general statements of its worth (294) and of choosing death over blame (295, 297), and ends with the tiger that will not eat what falls on its left (300). 291 and 298 are a pair, both comparing the honourable mind to fire.
source_issues: Quatrain 295: the verse reads சாயினும் where Mudaliar glosses சாவினும்.
Quatrain 296: Shanmuganar's field begins with the stray word துன்பவியல், a section heading.
Quatrain 300: Mudaliar glosses அழுங்க where the verse has மழுங்க, and Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: The mind of those possessed of honourable feeling will kindle into flame, like the fire that has caught the forest when the conflagration rages, whenever they behold the haughty acts of those who are destitute of virtuous habits, and to whom their wealth is their only strength.
reading: Whenever they see the arrogance of the worthless, whose only strength is their wealth, the minds of men of honour blaze like fire raging through a forest.
nuance: The fire is inward: the verse says the mind burns, not that they act on it. Mudaliar quotes a definition of மானம் as not falling from one's station and not living on when brought low by fate.

pope: Will (honourable men who are) 'masters of themselves' follow graceless men to tell of their sufferings, tbough fallen away to mere skeletons ? Do they not (rather) tell the pain they have felt to those enlightened souls that understand their sufferings before they speak ?
reading: Will those who own themselves follow the graceless to tell of their plight, even if they waste to bone? Will they not tell their pain to the clear-sighted, who grasp it before it is spoken?
nuance: Honour here does not forbid asking; it chooses whom to ask. The right patron reads the need before it is said, so the honourable never have to beg in words.

pope: As for ourselves we would introduce them (these friends) to our household : but as regards them, they are ashamed (of us), as though they said, as soon as they (the ladies) saw them (the friends,) it would be the destruction of their womanly reserve; and so they seat us at the backdoor and give us rice! Therefore let us dismiss all thought of rich men's friendship.
reading: We would bring our guests into our homes, but they, as if their wives' chastity would be lost if we so much as saw them, shame-faced, set rice before us at the back door; so forget the friendship of the rich.
nuance: Both commentators take the poor speaker as one who would let his wife serve guests, while the rich hide theirs and feed the poor at the back. Mudaliar notes another reading in which இல்லம் is simply the house and கற்பு is firmness.

pope: O thou whose locks diffuse the odour of pleasant musk! Behold, especially good is (it to cultivate) that which is esteemed by men of honourable mind; for in this world it is (obviously) good : and, since it leads to perseverance in the way of virtue, it will yield good things in yonder world also.
reading: Girl with hair fragrant with musk, see how good it is, the esteem of men of honour: it does good in this life and, never leaving the right way, yields good things in the next.
nuance: Honour is justified by its fruit in both worlds, which makes it a part of virtue rather than pride. Mudaliar glosses மதிப்பு as the principle men of honour hold, and notes another reading: being well regarded by others.

pope: The men 'fulfilled of excellence,' though death were the alternative, do not deeds that entail sin and guilt. Death is an affliction for one day, and for a little while. There is nothing that works irreparable ill like those (deeds).
reading: The worthy will not do what brings sin and blame, even if they must die: death is the pain of one day, one moment, and nothing does such lasting harm as those.
nuance: The argument is a calculation of duration: death's pain is brief, sin and blame's are not. Mudaliar separates them: sin follows one into later lives, blame stays in this world.

pope: Poor are the men that give not, even though deemed wealthiest of all that flourish on the teeming apple earth! They who even when they are poor seek not as suppliants wealthy men are 'Lords of the three mighty lands.'
reading: Among all who live in this rich, wide world, those who do not give are poor even if they are rich; and those who, even in poverty, do not go and beg from the rich are the great Muttaraiyar.
nuance: பெருமுத்தரையர் is a name of liberality: Mudaliar takes them as generous patrons of the author's time, also named in an earlier quatrain, and Shanmuganar as a royal line; Pope translates the name as 'lords of the three mighty lands'.

pope: Thou who hast long dart-like eyes with eye-brows extending far, like a bow! the lowest class of men dread burning hunger; the other (or middle class) dread what is unpleasant; all the chief of men fear words that impute crime.
reading: Girl of long dart-like eyes under wide bow-brows: the lowest all fear burning hunger, the middle fear hardship, and the highest fear only the blame in people's words.
nuance: A scale of persons by what they fear. Shanmuganar adds what follows from each fear: the lower will do anything, the highest refrain from wrong.

pope: When the very worthy and thoroughly learned see the rich men's glance of disparagement, as they say contemptuously, 'These are good people —persons in greatly reduced circumstances—poor folks,' does not their mind kindle into flame within them, like the fire by the breath of the bellows on the blacksmith's forge?
reading: When the rich look down on them and say with contempt, 'good people, very kind, now poor', the minds of the foremost worthy may burn within like fire blown in a smith's forge.
nuance: The insult is disguised as praise. Both commentators take அளியர் as kind or compassionate, and Shanmuganar makes the kindness the cause of the poverty; Pope takes it as pitiable, 'in greatly reduced circumstances'. Mudaliar glosses எற்றி where the verse has எள்ளி.

pope: It is no shame (disgrace) not to (be able to give to those who desire it of us. The shrinking on account of fear (felt) day by day is not shame (modesty). But to become reduced in other ways, and not to [dare to] tell what injuries those who love us not have inflicted on us is shame (disgrace, or self-respect).
reading: Not giving to those who come wanting is no shame, and shrinking each day from fear is no shame; the shame, when one is reduced by want, is to leave unspoken what one's superiors did to one.
nuance: What the superiors did is left unnamed, so the verse can mean either keeping silent about their slights or failing to acknowledge their help, and the sense of நாண் shifts with it. Mudaliar gives both readings; Pope takes it as not daring to tell their injuries.

pope: The jungle-haunting tiger that slays the wild cow, refuses to eat and passes by what has fallen (of itself) in its path (i. e. carrion); so the excellent, though the wide realms of heaven were within their reach, would not desire them, if to be obtained (only) by the loss of honour. --------------
reading: The forest tiger that has killed a great beast will starve to death rather than eat it if it falls on its left; so the excellent would not want even wide heaven placed in their hands if it came at the dulling of their honour.
nuance: Both commentators take கடமா as the elephant (Mudaliar also gives wild cow) and இடம் வீழ்ந்தது as falling on the left, citing a Purananuru poem on the tiger's custom; Pope reads a wild cow and carrion fallen in its path. Heaven itself, not just wealth, is refused.

title: இரவச்சம்
theme: The dread of begging (இரவச்சம்): a person of worth would rather go hungry and poor than ask, even of willing givers, because the mind melts at the thought of asking and a refusal kills. The only givers the chapter allows are those who welcome one in, and the last quatrain turns to the help owed to an old friend.
structure_note: 301, 303 and 304 say whom the worthy will not follow or approach. 302, 306 and 309 weigh hunger and poverty against begging and find begging worse. 305, 307 and 308 describe what begging feels like: shame, scorn, and death at a refusal. 310 closes on the giver's side, with the claim of old friendship.
source_issues: Quatrain 310: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 32.

pope: Will men themselves possessed of clear discerning knowledge follow after those who have yielded themselves up to mental bewilderment, and who (erroneously) say (of suppliants), ‘These poor folks depend entirely on us, evermore are they without resources in themselves ?'
reading: Would people of clear understanding follow after the self-deluded rich, who tell themselves that the poor live only through them and have no means of their own?
nuance: The fault named is the patron's self-importance, not his stinginess. Mudaliar glosses தம்மை மருண்ட as being dazed by one's own estimate of oneself.

pope: Is not a man's dying and birth again measured by the twinkling of an eye? Is it then a fault if a man rather choose to suffer hunger, doing no blameworthy actions, than to feed full, doing things that entail disgrace ?
reading: Since dying and being born again takes no longer than opening the eyes and blinking, is it wrong for a man to go hungry without doing anything blameworthy rather than eat his fill by doing what degrades him?
nuance: The argument rests on the shortness of a life: a full stomach bought with disgrace feeds a body that will be gone in a blink. Mudaliar gives three ways to take the eye image, one of them sleeping and waking, and cites Kural 339 for it.

pope: There will never be wanting those who, with their destitution as their support (making it their excuse), will venture upon mendicancy, and tread the way of humiliation; but will the noble-minded man enter (as a suppliant) the presence of any save of those who will embrace him and say, 'Enter my dwelling, eat of my food ?'
reading: Some, leaning on their poverty, will dare to beg and take the mean road, but the worthy go before no one except those who embrace them and say 'come in, eat'.
nuance: Mudaliar reads முகம் புகுதல் as putting up with a patron's frown, and Shanmuganar as showing one's own face to a patron. Either way, the only giver the worthy approach is one who receives them as a guest.

pope: Though fortune forsake him, and fate frown, the man of lofty soul, dwelling with steadfast mind on things above, disdains to stand with bending neck in the train of the foolish who hoard their wealth.
reading: Though fortune leaves him and the gods turn against him, the man of worth keeps his mind on his own high standing and never stands with bowed neck behind fools who hoard their wealth.
nuance: திரு and தெய்வம் are the two supports a person might count on, and the verse takes both away before asking for steadiness. The stance is independence from fortune, not defiance of it. Mudaliar takes உருத்த மனம் as a mind roused with energy.

pope: To live asking naught even from those dear as an eye, whose love is sure, and who never refuse, is happy life. Since the mind dissolves in shame at the very thought of beggary,— when men receive alms, what are the receivers' thoughts, I pray ?
reading: Real living is to live without asking even of those dear as one's eyes, whose love is firm and who hold nothing back; the heart melts at the mere thought of begging, so what must the asker feel at the moment of taking?
nuance: The last line moves from the giver to what the receiver feels while taking. Mudaliar reads கொள்வார் குறிப்பு as the taker's state of mind; Shanmuganar names it as shame.

pope: When a man himself, begs of himself, saying, ‘Let troubles come, let joys depart!' the sting of poverty is extracted; why then, for this purpose, should any one, his mind agitated with desire, and his eye wasted with weeping, beg of strangers ?
reading: When poverty can be ended by asking of oneself, 'let pain come, let pleasures go', why should anyone, with a mind racked by desire and eyes sunk, go begging of strangers?
nuance: Mudaliar divides தானிரப்ப two ways: தான் நிரப்ப, filling oneself with contentment, or தான் இரப்ப, begging of oneself. Pope takes the second and Shanmuganar the first. On either reading the cure for poverty is inward: consenting to hardship removes the want that drives begging.

pope: Lord of the land where gold is borne down by rushing waterfalls from every hilly slope! — Though in this world new (kinds of) men are continually born, that very man is never born that does not scorn mendicants.
reading: Though new people are born into this world every day, the man who does not scorn beggars has never been born, lord of the hill country where waterfalls carry gold down every slope.
nuance: Mudaliar gives two reasons for the overstatement: such a man reaches the good state and is not born again, or he simply cannot be found. The first plays on பிறக்கலான் ('is not born').

pope: Want wastes his outward frame; he lays aside wisdom, his inward being's good; and so resolving, begs of some stranger, saying, 'Give to me.’— If then the boon be refused, must he not that very instant die?
reading: With want wasting his body outside and his good sense put away inside, a man goes to another and says 'give to me'; if he is refused, will he not die on the spot?
nuance: Two losses come before the refusal: the body already worn down by want, and the understanding set aside so that asking is possible at all. Shanmuganar adds that the death would come from shame.

pope: Men form close intimacies with others and live as their dependants, and this is permissible ; but is it more painful quietly to go one's way (to the hermitage) than, lost to all sense of personal dignity, to say, 'Will ye not do aught for me?’
reading: It is proper to attach oneself to another and serve him with respect, but is the slow road of poverty more painful than losing one's dignity and saying 'won't you do something for me?'
nuance: Both commentators allow dependence on a patron, with deference, and forbid only the words of asking, so the line is drawn in speech. Mudaliar derives பைய from பை (suffering); Shanmuganar takes it as 'slowly'. Pope's 'to the hermitage' is his own addition.

pope: Relying on old friendship, in an affectionate manner, render such assistance as your intimacy Warrants. If he will not endure (the assistance), will it not be a fire heaped up and burning in his bosom? ----------------
reading: Where old acquaintance has grown into affection, one should do whatever help that intimacy calls for; if the claim of intimacy is not borne, it becomes a fire banked in the heart that burns without end.
nuance: Whose heart burns is not settled. Shanmuganar says it is the old friend who came to ask and was turned away. Pope reverses the roles: help is offered, and the needy friend who cannot bear to accept it burns. Mudaliar says only that the one asked fails to give the fitting help.

title: அவையறிதல்
theme: Knowing the assembly (அவையறிதல்): where learning should be spoken and before whom. The worthy keep silent before the ignorant and the quarrelsome, while those who memorise texts without understanding them expose themselves. A book's meaning is harder than its letter, and only those who can explain it, by the full method of commentary, count as scholars.
structure_note: 311 to 316 describe the bad assembly and the false scholar: the ignorant who spread error, the rote reciter who turns to abuse and violence, the itching debater, the brawler. 317 to 319 turn to books: the distance between text and meaning, the collector and the explainer, and what a commentary must do. 320 ends with good birth as the source of a restrained tongue.
source_issues: Quatrain 311: Pope's translation is not aligned.
Quatrain 316: the Tamil prints முடர் for மூடர். Shanmuganar's commentary opens with a stray பொதுவியல் and reads வாளர் இருப்பர், apparently for வாளா இருப்பர்.
Quatrain 317: the Tamil has a garbled character in அறிதற் கா஢ய, which Mudaliar's gloss (அருமையானவை) shows to be அரிய.
Quatrain 320: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 33 and the opening line of quatrain 321.

reading: Before people of dark understanding, who leave the way of an assembly of true knowledge, put forward some piece of ignorance, spread it everywhere and live by petty learning, let the wise leave their wisdom unspoken.
nuance: The advice is silence, not argument. Mudaliar records another reading of கைஞ்ஞானம் as 'skill of the hand', the habit of striking whoever objects, which would anticipate 312 and 315.

pope: Well-disciplined men come not near the heretic (=man of evil learning, the teacher of an evil system), who stores up (in his memory certain formulas, comp. 304), as though he understood their worth, and repeats them by rote (lit. as a tongue-lesson). The heretic, if worsted in the assembly, will abuse the family (of his opponents); or he will spring up and challenge them to fight.
reading: The disciplined keep away from the bad scholar who recites lessons by rote as if he knew their beauty; worsted in the assembly he will abuse their family, or else slap his shoulders and rise to fight.
nuance: Pope calls the தீப்புலவன் a heretic, the teacher of an evil system. Mudaliar's gloss is simply one without learning, and Shanmuganar's a false poet. The danger here is social: the loser turns to insult and violence.

pope: Many are the men that utter many things,—who long to raise up (in debate), from mere love of talking and an itching tongue; who do not themselves apprehend the power and might of learning; who know not the way to utter with penetrating force whatthey have learnt; and who know not what defeat means.
reading: Many people talk at length: they itch to rise and debate on the strength of a word, cannot judge the power of learning, do not know how to make what they learned reach the hearer, and do not know when they are beaten.
nuance: Mudaliar gives several ways to divide the opening words, one of them 'with words for goads', which Shanmuganar follows. The last failure, not knowing defeat, is what keeps the talk going.

pope: Without any learning of his own, the fool has obtained one formula from overhearing the lessons of a tutor (who was teaching others ), yet unabashed he enters the circle of the good, speaks it out, and makes exhibition of his mean understanding.
reading: With no learning of his own, a fool picks up a single sutra by overhearing a teacher's lesson, then walks unabashed into a gathering of the good, recites it, and shows how petty his understanding is.
nuance: Mudaliar specifies that the fool has only the bare text (மூல பாடம்) of the sutra, overheard from lessons given to other students.

pope: They who arise to utter words of wisdom, having associated themselves with the assembly of those who rage and burn and fume with anger, like beasts, for the mere sake of victory, not understanding the truth, shall see their own teeth like pumpkin seeds in their hands!
reading: Those who join people who rage and burn like beasts for the sake of victory and will not accept the truth, and who rise among them to show off their eloquence, will see their own teeth in their hands like gourd seeds.
nuance: Mudaliar names the figure: teeth in the hand say, without saying it, that they will be knocked out. The warning falls on the speaker who chooses that company, not on the brawlers.

pope: When foolish men chant their lesson, not knowing the fruit that lesson yields, but uttering words that gender wrath, the learned ones, whose fame dies not, will stand by ashamed, sorely pitying the mother that bare them.
reading: When fools who only recite the text and cannot make out its meaning say things that provoke anger, the worthy, whose renown does not decay, stand ashamed and grieve deeply for the mother who bore them.
nuance: The shame belongs to the listeners, not the fool. Mudaliar quotes the kind of lament the worthy might make, that she bore him for others to laugh at, and names the figure as imputed cause.

pope: Like the charms of those who sell their love for what they gain, the sacred texts are easy to those who rightly learn then; but like the minds of these whose forms are soft as tender shoots, the meaning is hard to all.
reading: Books are easy for anyone who learns them in due order, like the shoulders of women who take whatever they are paid, but their meaning is hard for anyone to grasp, like the minds of those same women with skin like tender mango shoots.
nuance: One simile does both halves of the work: access to the text is cheap and open, and understanding is closed. Pope's 'sacred texts' narrows நூல், which the commentators leave general.

pope: Although men gather together books in abundance, and, not understanding their contents, fill the whole house with them; the sages who merely take care of books are of one sort, and the sages who understand their contents, and make them clear to others, are of another sort.
reading: Some collect books in great numbers and fill the whole house with them without understanding what they say; the scholars who keep books are one kind, and those who understand them and make others understand are another.
nuance: Shanmuganar takes போற்றும் as keeping the books with worship (பூசை போட்டு) and calls the keepers false scholars. The verse itself says only that they are a different kind.

pope: Lord of the land of long chains of hills where the wild cattle assemble in herds! Is that a good commentary to a faultless composition, which consists of the words of those who do not sift it thoroughly, in the four divisions of summary, amplification, minute exposition, and supplementary information, and thus exhibit the full import?
reading: Lord of the long hills where herds of wild cattle gather, can the words of those who do not sift a faultless work through the four modes of summary, breadth, subtlety and remainder, and so show its full extent, be a good commentary on it?
nuance: A quatrain about commentary, on whose terms its commentators disagree. Mudaliar adds that others define the four modes differently again.

pope: Will those who are not of high family, however they may study learned works, be fit instruments to guard others from faults of speech? And men of good family who are well learned will not (seem to) be aware of the deficiencies of those who do not comprehend the works they talk of. -------------
reading: However many books they learn, can those not born of a good house be the means of guarding others' words? And the well-born wise take no notice of the petty understanding of those who do not grasp the books they talk of.
nuance: Pope offers a third reading of the first half: guarding others from faults of speech. The second half fits Mudaliar's reading best, since the well-born show the restraint the first half denies to the low-born by overlooking a fool's errors.

title: புல்லறிவாண்மை
theme: Petty understanding (புல்லறிவாண்மை): the small-minded scorn the teaching of virtue, see life slipping away and still do no good, nurse quarrels, hoard and put things off, until old age or death leaves them nothing. Folly is measured here by wasted time and wasted wealth.
structure_note: 321 and 322 are a pair of images for failing to taste good teaching: the ladle and the tanner's dog. 323 to 325 deal with conduct among others. 326 to 330 deal with wealth and years spent without virtue, ending with Death taking the people one loves.
source_issues: Quatrain 330: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 34.

pope: Men of sense receive as a reality the words from the mouth of the loving ones who graciously teach virtue. The (ignorant)wretch, himself unreal, speaks (of virtue) with contempt. Just so the ladle distinguishes not the flavour of the rice boiled in milk.
reading: The learned take as real worth the words of loving people who teach virtue out of compassion; the fool, himself of no worth, mocks them, as a ladle cannot taste the milk-rice it stirs.
nuance: The ladle is in the milk-rice all the time and tastes nothing: being near good teaching is not the same as taking it in. Mudaliar takes பொருளல்லா ஏழை as a fool of no account, and Shanmuganar as one who does not grasp the real meaning.

pope: When men of ungrudging soul declare the way of virtue, those who are not rightly disposed, although they give ear, hear not. Even so the currier's dog seizes on and devours leather, not appreciating the flavour of milk and rice.
reading: When those free of crookedness explain the way of virtue, those not rightly disposed do not hear it even when they lend an ear, just as the tanner's dog that chews leather cannot take the taste of milk-rice.
nuance: Mudaliar reads அவ்வியம் as crookedness of mind, or as envy standing for every bad trait. The image draws on a caste occupation: Mudaliar glosses குணுங்கர் as புலையர்.

pope: What matters it whether they live or die—the shameless stupid people who do no good, not even as much as a grain of millet, though they see by every species of example the way in which their life so sweet to them, passes away in the twinkling of an eye?
reading: What does it matter whether they die or live, those dull and shameless people who see in every way that their dear life may leave in the blink of an eye, and still do not a millet grain's worth of good?
nuance: Mudaliar lets நன்றி mean any good deed, or specifically help given to others.

pope: Since being's days are few, and life no safeguardowns, and guilt by many blamed is rife, mid many men, why, laughing not with all they see, should any sulk apart, and nurse a sullen hate ?
reading: The days left are few, life has no safeguard, and the blame that many spread is everywhere; why then should anyone, among so many, refuse to smile with those he meets and stand apart nursing a private enmity?
nuance: The case against sullen enmity rests on shortage of time rather than on virtue: with life brief and unsafe, hostility is a waste. Mudaliar lets ஏமம் mean pleasure as well as protection.

pope: A man has gone before the assembly that had gathered together, and contemning another has reviled him. Now if the reviled one remain silent, the reviler is to be wondered at if he survive; (for abuse is his very life, and the patience of the reviled one has closed his mouth.)
reading: If a man goes before a gathered assembly and reviles another, and the one reviled stays silent, it is a wonder if the reviler survives.
nuance: The verse doesn't say how the reviler is undone. Pope supplies a reason, that abuse is the reviler's life and silence stops his mouth. The commentators say only that he will not prosper.

pope: He who before old age comes, has not undertaken and zealously carried out works of virtue, will be pushed about in the house addressed in harsh language, and bidden to get on one side or to go out, by even the maid-servants.
reading: One who does not eagerly take up virtuous deeds and work at them before old age comes on will be pushed aside in his own house and told 'sit outside, go away' even by the maidservant.
nuance: The penalty is social, not karmic: humiliation in old age, inside one's own home.

pope: Men of scanty wisdom are those who do not themselves enjoy any sweets of life, bestow no benefactions on worthy persons, draw not nigh the good path that safeguards (the soul), but infatuated and absorbed in the acquisition of wealth, pass away their days of life in vain.
reading: People of petty understanding neither enjoy their wealth nor do good to the deserving nor join the good path that protects; dazed and sunk in their prosperity, they spend their days for nothing.
nuance: Mudaliar names the cause of the daze: not knowing that body and wealth do not last.

pope: In the very earliest time (in early youth) they take not food for the journey which they must make (into another world), tying tightly the wallet on their shoulders ; but tying tightly (their treasure bags), they say, 'In after days we will learn wisdom;' the gold these idiots will indict with their hands (as legacies, when they are speechless, and in the grasp of death) will be as sour vilam fruit.
reading: Fools who do not tie on tightly, early in life, the provisions for the road they must take, but tighten their grip on their wealth and say 'we will see to it later', will find that the gold they point to with their hands turns into a sour vilam fruit.
nuance: The commentators fill in a deathbed scene: the dying man, unable to speak, gestures for gold to give away, and his family takes the gesture to mean a sour vilam fruit. Mudaliar quotes a Civaka Cintamani verse telling this story. The quatrain gives only the gesture and the sour fruit.

pope: When poor, or when disease's deadly grasp they feel, to other world alone their minds are given ; but when wealth grows, no thought, small as a grain of mustard seed, give they to other world —these souls unwise!
reading: In poverty and in grave illness the small-minded think of the next world, but once they are able to act they give it not a mustard seed's worth of thought.
nuance: The irony is that concern for the next life arrives only when one is least able to act on it.

pope: Though they have gained a human frame, of virtue think they not! In vain they spent their days. Alas! and yet they see death eagerly hasting to snatch away those infinitely dear, like to their very souls! Why is this so? -------------
reading: Alas, though they have gained this human body they do not think of virtue and waste their days, even while they watch Death preparing to take those they love beyond measure, as dear as their own lives.
nuance: Shanmuganar calls the human body hard to obtain; the verse's இவ்வுடம்பு implies as much without saying it.

title: பேதைமை
theme: Folly (பேதைமை): the fool enjoys a world in which death is already at work, puts off virtue, relies on birth and status, clings to the rich and the unworthy, praises himself and quarrels for nothing. Most quatrains are comparisons that make his position look absurd.
structure_note: 331 and 332 are paired similes of misjudged time: the turtle in the heating pot and the bathers waiting for the sea to fall silent. 333 and 334 set status against usefulness. 335 to 340 show the fool among others: angry, ingratiating, clinging, rejecting, boastful.
source_issues: Quatrain 333: the Tamil reads குடிநம்முப் பைந்தும், apparently for குடிமூப் பைந்தும்; Mudaliar glosses குடிமை and மூப்பு, and all three readings count five things including age.

Quatrain 334: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of quatrain 335 with his commentary on it, and then the text of quatrain 336. Quatrains 335 and 336 have no Shanmuganar commentary aligned, and none on 336 appears anywhere. Mudaliar's gloss on 334 reads நளி for the verse's நனி.
Quatrain 338: Shanmuganar's field begins with the quatrain's last line before the commentary.
Quatrain 340: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 35.

pope: While the turtle's murderers have put it into the pot, and kindled fire beneath, it sports unconscious of its fate: such is their worth who joy entangled in life's not, while death, the mighty murderer, waits to seize them.
reading: As a turtle put in a pot by its killers, with the fire lit beneath, plays in the water without knowing its state, so are those who revel in this world's net while Death, the great killer, waits for the moment to seize them.
nuance: The water the turtle enjoys is what will kill it, just as the world's pleasures are the net. Mudaliar notes that மாண்பு ('worth') is used ironically.

pope: They went to bathe in the great sea, but cried 'we will wait till all its roar is hushed, then bathe!' Such is their worth who say, 'we will get rid of all our household toils and cares and then we will practise virtue and be wise.'
reading: Those who say they will see to virtue once the household's unfinished tasks are done are like people who went to bathe in the great sea and said they would bathe when its roar had died down.
nuance: Household duties, like the noise of the sea, never stop, so the simile turns postponement into permanent refusal.

pope: Though a man be of good caste, have performed deeds of ascetic virtue, acquired learning, is of good family and attained a ripe old age, so that in these five points he is faultless; yet his ignorance of what is thoroughly good, without stain, sanctioned by ancient precedent, and of good renown in the world's ways, will render all his advantages like thin, watery milk with boiled rice.
reading: Though one has all five, high caste, austerity, learning, standing and age, without lack, not knowing the good, stainless and anciently honoured உலகம் makes it all like milk-rice without ghee.
nuance: The commentators also divide on குடி: household prosperity for Mudaliar, good family for Shanmuganar. Pope's 'thin, watery milk' departs from the Tamil, which has rice without ghee.

pope: Stones are much better than low men ; since, though those (too) are utterly without apprehension of your words, yet they (stones) are of assistance to those that employ them, inasmuch as they at once stand (where they are fixed), remain (where they are put), lie (where they are laid), and remove (when they are moved).
reading: Stones are far better than base people: though they cannot understand words either, they serve whoever comes to them, at once, for standing, sitting, lying and walking on.
nuance: The comparison is not about intelligence, which both lack, but about use: the stone at least gives itself to others.

pope: If the fool, though nothing is to be gained (by such conduct), acting as though he had gained something, waxing wroth against those who disdain (or are unable) to contend with him, cannot say and utter forth in his wrath a string of evil words a grievous itching will gnaw his tongue.
reading: Though nothing is gained by it, the fool, as if he had gained something, grows angry even with those who don't deserve it, and if he cannot string harsh words together and say them, a fierce itch gnaws at his tongue.
nuance: The targets are read three ways: Mudaliar's ஏலாதார் are those for whom such anger is unfitting, Shanmuganar's (printed under 334) are superiors who are no match for the fool, and Pope's are those who will not or cannot contend with him.

pope: Lord of the sea-shore where the laurel with its bright foliage flowers! The poor (pretence of) intimacy enjoyed by those who follow after (wealthy but) utterly uncongenial men, and say 'we will bend them to our will,' is like loosing one's hand while digging into a rock.
reading: Those who follow people without good conduct, saying 'we will make them bow to us', have a poor kind of friendship, lord of the shore where the laurel with fine shoots flowers: it is like losing one's hand pinching a rock.
nuance: Mudaliar calls the bond a one-sided friendship and cites a Pazhamozhi line saying no one pinches a rock and keeps their hand. Pope supplies 'wealthy' for the people followed.

pope: If there be ghi in the pot, though they cannot get at it, the ants will swarm without ceasing around the outside ; and so the people of the world will cling to and not leave the possessors of wealth, though these give them nothing.
reading: If there is ghee inside a pot, ants keep circling its outside without leaving, though they cannot get at it; so people cling to the wealthy and won't leave them, though they give nothing.
nuance: The quatrain describes a habit of the world without blaming it in so many words; being placed in this chapter is what marks the habit as folly.

pope: No good each day they gain; nor deed of virtue do; nothing to needy men impart; nor know they joy of loved ones' sweet embrace ; devoid of fame they live: do such not loathe the days they live?
reading: They gain no good thing day by day, do no virtue, give nothing to the needy, never hold their beloved in their arms, and do not live with renown: will they not come to loathe the days they live?
nuance: The list mixes virtue, giving, married love and fame, so the fool fails at every aim of life, not only at renunciation. Mudaliar allows நல்லவை to be read as நல் அவை, a good assembly, and Shanmuganar takes that reading.

pope: Friendship with those who are destitute of exquisite goodness, and who, though you cultivate them with affectionate deference, (morosely) say we entertain affection for none,'—though it should yield as its fruit the earth, which the sea with its noisy chime of leaping billows girds around,—would be only affliction.
reading: When one person admires and seeks another who answers 'we don't want you', that friendship with those lacking discerning goodness is painful, even if it should yield the whole earth girdled by the roaring sea.
nuance: Mudaliar calls the bond a one-sided friendship, or a false one. The fool is the one who rejects the regard offered, but the warning is for the one who keeps offering it.

pope: The learning a man has acquired, his world - renowned excellence, and his nobility of birth, will gain for him respect when the bystanders celebrate them; but if he himself proclaim them, the young kinsmen crowding around will deride him as one afflicted with a mania not to be mitigated by any medicine. -----------
reading: Learning, wide gentleness and good birth win honour when others praise them; if a man praises them himself, his brothers-in-law multiply and mock him as a madman no medicine can cure.
nuance: Mudaliar explains மைத்துனர் (brothers-in-law) as mockers: the joking relationship stands for ridicule.

title: கீழ்மை
theme: Baseness (கீழ்மை): the base keep their nature whatever is done for them. Teaching, invitation, honour, wealth and care do not change them, and the chapter sets them beside the worthy, whom prosperity does not change either.
structure_note: Similes from animals and objects carry the argument: the hen (341), the dog (345), the jewelled sandal (347), the young bullocks (350). 343, 344, 346 and 349 set the worthy and the base side by side. 347 and 350 close on the same two lines.
source_issues: Quatrains 347 and 350 end with the same two lines (எய்திய செல்வத்த ராயினும் கீழ்களைச் செய்தொழிலாற் காணப் படும்). Mudaliar glosses them only under 347; Shanmuganar and Pope translate them under both. This may be the tradition's own repetition or a copying error.
Quatrain 345: Mudaliar's gloss reads யாதுகாத்துவரினும், apparently for பாதுகாத்துவரினும்.
Quatrain 348: Pope's translation is not aligned.

pope: The fowl, though each morning duly you scatter broken grain into its very mouth, will ceaselessly scratch in the refuse-heap; so, though you expound and show the base man works of learning, full of weighty wisdom, he will but the more resolutely go on in the way in which his mind finds delight.
reading: As a hen keeps scratching the rubbish heap though grain is poured into its mouth each morning, so the base man, however you lay open books full of weighty meaning for him, goes further along the way his mind likes.
nuance: மிகும் suggests excess, not just persistence: Mudaliar glosses it as going beyond bounds.

pope: If you say to the base man, ‘Let us without delay go to seek refuge with faultless sages possessors of mature wisdom,' he will probably get up and make off, exclaiming, 'Let us go and slumber,!’ or he will perhaps demur, and change the subject.
reading: Say to the base man 'let us go without delay to the faultless who hold firm learning', and he gets up and leaves saying 'let's sleep', or else refuses with some other excuse.
nuance: The comedy is in the excuses: sleep first, and failing that, anything else.

pope: Lord of the goodly land of swelling torrents! If thoroughly worthy men gain some added dignity, their nature knows no deviation, but they go on in the same even path of virtue ; and although the base obtain promotion, his conduct too changes not, (promotion betters him not.)
reading: Even if they gain great prosperity, the worthy keep one even course without falling from their nature; when the base gain it, the verse says only that they are 'able in one course', lord of the good land of shining waterfalls.
nuance: Pope agrees with Shanmuganar that the base man's conduct does not change. Mudaliar takes பெருநடை as wealth and records that others read it as great distinction.

pope: Lord of the goodly land of glistening torrents ! The excellent will deem any favour done them, though small as a grain of millet, to be large as a palm tree. You may constantly confer favours huge as a palm tree, but they are not benefits, when conferred on those who are not grateful.
reading: If they have enjoyed a good done to them, though it is only the size of a millet grain, the worthy think of it as a palm tree; but goods the size of a palm, done again and again, are no good at all to those who do not know a good, lord of the land of bright waterfalls.
nuance: Mudaliar cites Kural 104 and Parimelazhagar's remark that millet and palm are conventional measures of small and great.
