pope: The dog, though you tend it with care, feeding it from a golden vessel, will watch, eye fixed for others' leavings ; even so, although you receive the base as if they were possessed of greatness, the deeds they do will be otherwise (= their real character will be seen by their conduct).
reading: A dog, though reared on food from a golden bowl, watches unblinking for others' leftovers; so even if you treat the base as great, the deeds they do will be different.
nuance: The golden bowl is the honour shown: it changes the setting, not the appetite.

pope: Though they obtain imperial wealth, the excellent never utter a vaunting word ; but if at any time the base see some small fraction added to his scanty store, he will deem himself great as Indra.
reading: Even with an emperor's wealth the excellent never speak a boastful word, but if a base man gains a காணி on top of a முந்திரி, he thinks himself Indra.
nuance: The two words are tiny fractions. Shanmuganar gives முந்திரி as 1/320 and காணி as 1/80; Mudaliar gives காணி as 1/64 and முந்திரி as a quarter of that, and allows the words to be read in the other order.

pope: Though made of faultless yellow gold, enwrought with choicest pearls, the slipper serves but for one's foot; though the base be deemed prosperous through the wealth they have gained, their baseness will be seen by their actions.
reading: Though a sandal is made of flawless gold set with fine gems, it is still for the foot; so the base, though they have come into wealth, are known by the deeds they do.
nuance: The sandal's material is the wealth and its place is the nature: costly making does not move it from the foot.

reading: The base are quick to speak harshly, have no kindly regard, rejoice in others' troubles, fly into rage again and again, go where they please and scorn everyone, lord of the good land of mighty hills.
nuance: A plain list with no image, which Mudaliar classes as straightforward description (தன்மை நவிற்சி).

pope: Lord of the resounding sea's cool shore, where the Neythal breathes honied fragrance round! The worthy, if men for many days stand waiting in their train will say 'these are old acquaintance,' and will make the place pleasant to them; the base in such circumstances feel no affection, but simply despise them.
reading: If people stand by them for many days, the worthy grow kind to them, thinking 'these are old friends'; the base feel no warmth and simply scorn them, lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea where the neydal breathes honey.
nuance: Mudaliar takes standing by someone as being subordinate and obedient to them, so the test is how each kind treats long-serving dependants.

pope: Hear, O Sir! The little bullock-calves will not learn to bear the yoke and draw the chariot, though you give them cut grass, clip them, and constantly rub them down; so, though they have gained wealth, the base will be seen (to be so) by the deeds they do. -----------------
reading: Hear, sir: small bullocks will never learn to wear the yoke and draw the cart however long you feed them cut grass, and the base, though they have come into wealth, are known by the deeds they do.
nuance: Care cannot supply a capacity that is not there; the bullocks are well fed and still small.

title: கயமை
theme: The base (கயமை): their nature is not changed by age, learning or wealth. They give only under force, remember insults and forget kindnesses, speak ill of others to their faces, and hold their wealth without softening.
structure_note: Almost every quatrain sets the base against the worthy and carries the point with an image from nature or work: the hollow எருவை (351), the frog in the pond (352), the chisel (355), the boar's tusks (358), the lotus leaf (359) and the dry netti reed (360). 359 names no base person, and the link to the chapter is Mudaliar's.
source_issues: 351: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text of 352 and his commentary on it, and 352 has no Shanmuganar commentary aligned.
353: the Tamil reads கா஢தால், a garbled character; Mudaliar's gloss அரிது gives அரிதால்.
356: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text and his commentary for 357 and 358 and the text of 359; 357 and 358 have no Shanmuganar commentary aligned, and none exists for 359.
360: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.

pope: The thoroughly wise, though young in years, will guard themselves in stern self-repression. The low unwise as age comes on become mature in evil works, and are like reeds wind-shaken, hollow still!
reading: The fully wise restrain and guard themselves even when young in years, while the petty-minded grow more practised in wrongdoing the older they get and, like the எருவை, never lose their hollowness.
nuance: Age is set aside as a cause: wisdom doesn't wait for years, and years don't cure folly. Mudaliar gives two senses for both எருவை and போத்து: a reed that never fills its hollow, or a kite that never sheds its faults. Shanmuganar takes the kite and the faults, and Pope the hollow reed.

pope: Though frogs flourish long in a rich large lake, they never rid themselves of their slime; so it is hard for those void of fine perception, even when they have learned pure and excellent text-books, to acquire the gift of clear understanding.
reading: Frogs that live in a rich, large pond never rid themselves of their slime; in the same way, those without fine discernment rarely gain the power to examine what they read, even after studying flawless, excellent books.
nuance: What is missing is not learning but நுணுக்கம், a subtlety that study doesn't supply. The pond's abundance matches the excellence of the books: neither reaches what is already in the creature. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 351.

pope: Lord of the goodly land of mountain chains ! It is hard to stand before a man, and publish even his praise. How then can mean men's tongues depreciate a man's good qualities and proclaim his faults while standing before him?.
reading: Lord of the good land of clustered hills: it is hard even to speak of a man's virtues when he isn't present, so what are the tongues of petty people made of, that they stand at his side and proclaim his faults until his virtues are spoiled?
nuance: Both commentators read கண் இன்று as 'not before his eyes', and Mudaliar rejects splitting it as கண் நின்று. The contrast is then between a decent reluctance to praise someone even behind his back and the brazenness of faulting him beside him. Pope takes the other split and has the praise spoken to the man's face.

pope: Chaste women trick not out their charms of womanhood, as is as the wont of the wanton. Like fountains ever fresh those others make display of every charm, and vaunt their beauty as they pass.
reading: Household women do not know how to dress up their womanliness the way their maids do it for them; the other kind, like a fresh flood, put their charms on show themselves, think highly of themselves, and then pass on.
nuance: In a chapter on the base the verse works as a figure, and Mudaliar names it பிறிது மொழிதல்: the wise don't praise themselves, and fools vaunt themselves to extract wealth. The verse itself speaks only of the two kinds of women.

pope: The base are like the chisel, that, though it is over the bud (to be sculptured), moves not without some one to strike it. On those who are courteous these confer no boon whatever. They will do everything for those who use violent means.
reading: The base are like a chisel that won't cut in, even set on a tender shoot, unless someone strikes it: they do nothing at all for the kind, and anything at all for those who treat them harshly.
nuance: A tender shoot is the softest thing a chisel could meet, so the image says the base yield to nothing gentle. Mudaliar lets அளிநீரார் mean either the compassionate or those whose state calls for pity.

pope: The hill-man thinks upon the beauty of his hills; the farmer thinks upon his fields that have yielded him rich crops; the good think on the boons bestowed by worthy men; the base man's thoughts are fixed on abuse he has received.
reading: The hill-dweller thinks of the wealth of his hills and the farmer of the field that yielded; the worthy think of a good someone did them, while the base dwell on the time someone abused them.
nuance: The first two figures set up the rule that each mind returns to what it values; the last two say what the worthy and the base value. Mudaliar notes the verse calls the base man கயம், a neuter noun, to show how low he is.

pope: The good attach themselves to those that have done them one act of kindness, and forgive a hundred wrongs that arise. The base receive seven hundred benefits, but one wrong will turn them all to evil.
reading: The worthy bear a hundred faults, coming one after another, from someone who once did them a kindness; for the base, if one thing goes wrong after seven hundred kindnesses, all seven hundred turn into harm.
nuance: Mudaliar takes the hundred and the seven hundred as standing for 'many' and 'very many'. The asymmetry is the point: for one kind of person a single kindness outweighs a hundred wrongs, and for the other a single wrong cancels seven hundred kindnesses.

pope: Worthless persons even in high estate do not the deeds that men of noble birth perform even in their poverty. Okeen-eyed maid! Men may enring and arm the boar's tusks, but it will not even so become a warlike elephant.
reading: What those of good family do even when weakened by want, the utterly foolish don't do even at the height of their fortune; bright-eyed one, fit a boar's tusks with diamond rings and it still won't become an angry war elephant.
nuance: The verse doesn't name the deeds. Pope supplies liberality, and Mudaliar says only 'good deeds'. The base are called முழுமக்கள், which Mudaliar glosses as fools, so the lack here is of sense as well as of birth.

pope: ‘To-day, at once, a little hence, we shall gain our end!’ So many speak and think, and joyously tell it out among their friends ; but soon their eager minds are changed; and they have perished like a lotus leaf.
reading: Many people thought 'today we'll have it, right now, or in a little while', rejoiced as they said so to others, and then, their hopes overturned, perished like lotus leaves.
nuance: The verse doesn't say what they expected, and names no base person. Mudaliar supplies both: they waited to become rich without doing good, and withered like the lotus leaf that flourishes and dies where it stands. Shanmuganar's commentary for this quatrain is missing.

pope: Though born in the water, and its hue appear green, the Netti's pith knows no moisture; so in the world are men of amplest wealth whose hearts are hard as stones upon the rocky mountain fell. -------------
reading: Though it is born in water and is green, the netti reed has no moisture in its pith; in the same way the world holds men who stay hard as great rock slabs even while living in full, great wealth.
nuance: The image is exact: the plant lives in water and holds none, as these men live among plenty and give none. Mudaliar's gloss on the rock is that it never softens (இளகுதல்).

title: பன்னெறி
theme: Various ways (பன்னெறி): a closing miscellany of the Book of Wealth. It weighs the wife as what makes a house a home or a ruin, ranks the lives a person may lead with austerity first, and observes that sons inherit their fathers' minds, that the world turns upside down, and that the unfeeling are better dead.
structure_note: The quatrains fall into loose groups: the wife and household life (361-364), two ranked lists of lives, best, middle and worst (365, 366), and single observations (367-369). 370, on the courtesans' love, is almost a twin of 371 and leads into the Book of Love.
source_issues: 361: the Tamil reads கா஢யதோர், a garbled character for அரியதோர்.
362: Mudaliar glosses வழுக்கு where the verse reads வழக்கு, and reads the condition as பெறார் ஆயின் where the verse has பெறுவ ராயின்.
364: the Tamil reads இனித஧ருஉம், a garbled character; Mudaliar's gloss gives இனிது இரூஉம்.
366, 367: Pope's translation is not aligned.
370: Shanmuganar's field ends with the headings of the Book of Love and chapter 38 and the text of 371 with his commentary, which is repeated under 371.

pope: The mansion meets the clouds. A stately band of warders keep watch around. Gems glisten therein like lamps. What then? Where the owner has not a wife of dainty excellence: the house within is a waste, hard to explore.
reading: What use is a mansion where the clouds play, under fine guard, with jewels shining like lamps, if its owner has no admirable wife? That house is a wilderness too grim to look at.
nuance: Pope's 'hard to explore' reads காண்டற்கு அரிய as a trackless waste; Mudaliar reads it as a forest too harsh even to look at. Shanmuganar takes இழைவிளக்கு as a wick lamp that never goes out, where Mudaliar has jewels shining like lamps.

pope: Though compassed round with a faultless guard of swords, ifonce they gain freedom, in little time they are stained with every fault; and long is the time those soft-voiced once spurn every law of right
reading: Even when women are kept under a faultless guard of swords, the time in which soft-spoken women commit no fault is short and the time in which they don't keep to good conduct is long; the verse's condition on this is disputed.
nuance: This is one of the collection's harshest lines on women, and its scope depends on the condition in the second line. Mudaliar cites Kural 57 with it, though 57 praises women's own guard rather than doubting it.

pope: Death is the wife that stands and dares her spouse to strike! Disease is she who enters not the kitchen betimes! Demon domestic is she who cooks and gives no alms! These three are swords to slay their lords !
reading: The wife who stands up to her husband saying 'strike me' is Death; the one who doesn't go into the kitchen at dawn is an incurable disease; the one who doesn't serve the food she has cooked is a demon in the house; these three are weapons that kill the man who took them.
nuance: Pope's 'gives no alms' makes the third fault a failure of charity. Both commentators make it a failure to serve the husband, and Mudaliar adds that she eats the food herself.

pope: He hears (that marriage is another name for) dread, and yet he dreads it not! He hears the fearful funeral drum, but it gives him no sense ! Again to take a wife and to dwell bewildered amidst domestic enjoyments is a fault that merits stoning; sosay (the wise).
reading: He hears marriage called a dread and doesn't give it up; he hears the funeral drum beat loud enough to split heads and still doesn't see; to take a wife again and live lost in pleasure, they say, is the fault of stoning oneself.
nuance: Shanmuganar places the drum at the first wife's funeral, which makes this a verse about remarriage. Mudaliar points back to quatrain 56, where கடி names marriage as something to be dreaded. On either reading the verse goes further than a warning about remarrying: it treats household life itself as what the wise tell one to give up.

pope: The best thing is a life spent in penitential practices. The middle course is to live with dear ones around. The worst of all is, with the thought that we have not enough, through desire of wealth subserviently to follow those who understand us not.
reading: The best way to live is to strive in austerity; the middle way is to dwell with those one loves; the lowest is to follow, out of desire for wealth, people who don't recognise one's worth, even thinking it won't come.
nuance: இனியார் is general, 'the dear ones', and both commentators narrow it to wives. Mudaliar reads புணராது என்று எண்ணி as 'even while thinking it won't be gained', which makes the lowest life futile as well as servile; Pope's 'not enough' reads it as discontent.

reading: The best pass their time in learning, the middle in enjoying good things, and the lowest lie sleepless with resentment, saying 'we haven't eaten well, we haven't got enough'.
nuance: கல்லா here means 'having learned', not 'not learning'. Mudaliar specifies books of spiritual knowledge and goods gained by right means; the verse says only learning and good things. The lowest are marked by craving rather than by poverty.

reading: Lord of the rich-fielded town where the paddy fills the fields: since the sprout from red paddy grows again into that same red paddy, a son's understanding is his father's.
nuance: The verse states inheritance as a law, the way a seed breeds true. It doesn't say whether the son learns from his father or is born like him. Mudaliar's parallel, 'the son tells the father's worth', reads the son as the sign of his lineage.

pope: The wealthy men of great possessions and the perfect have perished, while wantons' sons and base men multiply. The lowest takes chief place, and, like the umbrella's handle, this world is upside down!
reading: The wealthy of long standing and the worthy decline, while concubines' sons and base men flourish; what belongs at the feet comes to the head, and like an umbrella's handle the world stands upside down.
nuance: Shanmuganar explains the umbrella: its handle points down when the umbrella is open and up when it is folded, so the same world can flip between orders. The complaint mixes moral and social rank, putting the worthy beside old wealth and the base beside concubines' sons.

pope: Lord of the good land of mighty hills whence streams descend sweeping along pearls! Better men should jump down a precipice than live with a mind not disposed to assuage the pain of the dear ones who tell them of their heart's pain.
reading: Lord of the good land of mighty hills, whose falls sweep down gems: those whose hearts don't ease the pain their dear ones tell them of would do better to leap from a cliff than to live.
nuance: The verse doesn't require them to remove the pain, only to be moved by it; a heart unmoved disqualifies a life. Mudaliar takes இனியார் as friends.

pope: ‘The mountain freshed, and the love of those adorned With pendant jewels rare examined calmly prove To differ nought: that fails when rains that feed it fail; And love of these fails too, when income fails !’ ------------
reading: Fresh floodwater and the friendship of women with fine earrings, examined calmly, are no different: the flood ends when the rain ends, and their love ends when the income ends.
nuance: Mudaliar records a second reading of விதுப்பு அற, 'without desire', which would make the examiner a man no longer infatuated.

title: பொது மகளிர்
theme: Courtesans (பொது மகளிர்): their love lasts as long as a man's money and turns hostile when it ends. The chapter blames the men who trust them as much as the women, calling them beasts, dupes and people whose bodies are full of sin.
structure_note: Two quatrains are the dupe's own speech: the death-pact abandoned at the cliff's edge (372) and the address to his own heart (376). The rest alternate between the women's mercenary love (371, 373, 374, 379) and the men who are fooled by it (375, 377, 378, 380).
source_issues: 374: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text of 375 and his commentary on it, and 375 has no Shanmuganar commentary aligned.
380: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 39.

pope: The lamp's light and harlot's love examined well are seen to differ not a whit; the lamp's light goes out when the feeding oil is consumed ! and the harlot's love is spent when the lavish hand has spent its wealth.
reading: The lamp's light and the friendship of harlots, examined steadily, are no different: the light ends when the oil runs out, and their love ends when the hand is empty.
nuance: Mudaliar takes கை, the hand, as the money held in it.

pope: She (of enticing beauty), adorned with choice jewels, said forsooth, 'I will leap with you down the steep precipice;' but on the very brow of the precipice, because I had no money, she, weeping and pointing to her aching feet, withdrew and left me alone!
reading: The woman with fine jewels said she would leap with us from the high peak; but at the peak, since we had no gold, she showed a pain in her feet, wept, and wouldn't come on.
nuance: The speaker is the dupe himself, and the promise he recalls is a lovers' death pact. Mudaliar takes the foot pain as a lie and the tears as feigned; the verse says only that she showed the pain and wept.

pope: Though he be Mal, the fiery-eyed, whom in the heaven's fair homes immortals worship, if in hand he bring no gift the women tender as the buds men cull, will straight dismiss him, bowing low with folded hands.
reading: Even if he were the red-eyed Mal whom the gods of the wide sky worship, women tender as plucked shoots would join their hands in worship and send away a man with nothing in his hand to give.
nuance: The joke lies in the gesture: hands joined as if in worship are the hands that dismiss him. Mudaliar takes மால் as Tirumal, with Indra as an alternative; Shanmuganar has Indra.

pope: To the damsels of loveless hearts, whose eyes are as beauteous as blue water-lilies, those who have no wealth are as poison! Even those who have turned the (oil) press, in sight of all men, if they have wealth, are as sugar to them.
reading: To women with loveless hearts and lovely blue-lily eyes, men without money are poison; but even a man seen by all driving an oil press is sugar to them if he has earned wealth.
nuance: Mudaliar glosses the oil press as a low trade. The verse says money erases even that rank in their eyes.

pope: The silly ones, who are as beasts, seek the embraces of women who are like the eel, which shows one head to the snake, and another head to the fish, in the sweet clear lake : (are of a double and deceitful nature).
reading: Like the eel that shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish in the clear, sweet pond, women of double conduct are embraced by the dull-witted, who are like beasts.
nuance: Mudaliar explains the eel's trick as matching each man's nature and showing him love. The verse turns part of the blame on the men, who are the beasts. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 374.

pope: ‘We will never part, like the precious stone strung on its thread, or the Andril,' said the damsel with golden bracelets: she has now become the horn of a fighting ram (she angrily repels me). Dear heart! dost linger still, or wilt thou go?
reading: The woman of golden bangles who said 'we'll never part from you', like a gem strung on its thread and the anril birds that never separate, has turned away like a fighting ram's horn; my good heart, will you stay, or will you go?
nuance: The speaker turns from her to his own heart, which is still with her. Both commentators take the last line as 'will you stay with her or come with me?', so the heart is a separate party the man has to win back.

pope: Those who fondly reckon upon the devoted love of the worthless wanton, that, like the wild ox, licks the hand and despoils men of their wealth, and then, like the buffalo, bounds away, shall suffer the deserved ridicule of many.
reading: Those who are fooled into thinking theirs the love of a worthless woman who licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from their hands, and then lies down like a balking ox, will be laughed at by many.
nuance: Mudaliar cites a belief that the wild cow's lick pleases at first and kills later. குப்புறூஉம் is either lying face down, as Mudaliar takes it first and Shanmuganar takes it, or bounding away, as in Pope.

pope: Those whose avowed purpose it is to walk in the way of rectitude seek not the embrace of the fascinating, fawn-eyed damsels, who walk in a way of their own' who are pleasant when gratified with gifts, and when they are filled( =when no more gifts are to be expected) are like the horn of the fighting ram.
reading: Those who mean to reach the right path won't embrace the large breasts of doe-eyed women who go their own way, women who seem kind while a man is infatuated and turn harsh as a ram's horn 'once they are full'; who is full is disputed.
nuance: Mudaliar glosses செந்நெறி as the path to liberation, which makes avoiding these women a renunciant's discipline; Shanmuganar has only 'the good way'.

pope: Let those accept (wantons' false love), who take them as their own believing the words uttered to inspire belief, by the bright-browed ones, who keep concealed within the cruelty that lurks in their heart. Those whose bodies are their sole wealth belong to none, (i. e. they have no souls to give!).
reading: Some do take bright-browed women as their own, trusting words spoken to be believed by women who hide their harmful intent; but such women belong to no one except their own bodies.
nuance: Pope adds 'they have no souls to give'. Mudaliar's gloss is narrower: their attachment reaches only as far as their own bodies.

pope: Though the dupes clearly discern and know the guileful intentions entertained by the bright browed ones, even where their minds are (apparently) set upon some persons, they whose bodies are full of sin do not recognise it! ---------
reading: The scheming of bright-browed women whose minds are with another man is clearly known, and still those whose bodies are full of sin don't grasp it; who it is that knows is disputed.

title: கற்புடை மகளிர்
theme: The chaste wife (கற்புடை மகளிர்): her worth is measured by self-guarding, hospitality in poverty, modesty that never wears off, and timely sulking. In the last four quatrains she speaks herself, as a wife wronged by a husband who goes to courtesans.
structure_note: 381-386 describe the good wife, and 385 is already in her voice. 387-390 are her complaints about her straying husband, two of them addressed to the minstrel who carries his messages (388, 390); Mudaliar says 387 shows the wife's own purity, which is why such speeches stand in this chapter.
source_issues: 383: Pope's text runs on into his translation of 384 ('The wife: placens uxor ...'), and 384 has no Pope translation aligned.
385: the Tamil reads பெருள்நசையால், apparently a misprint for பொருள்நசையால்.
386: Shanmuganar's field opens with the stray heading இன்ப வியல்.
390: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 40.

pope: Though women live famed as Ayirani for rarest gift of chastity, absence of men that stand enamoured of their charms is a help in way of good to those of fragrant brow who guard themselves.
reading: Even among women as famous as Indrani for a chastity hard to attain, the fragrant-browed woman who keeps the quality that leaves no man following her in desire is the good companion.
nuance: Pope reads it differently: the absence of admirers is a help to women who guard themselves, as though even the chaste benefit from not being tempted. Both commentators make the absence her own doing. Indrani is the standard of the comparison, so the claim is strong: even such women are measured by this.

pope: her duties with kindness of speech. When in the straitened time they cook and eat with but one pot of water on the hearth,— if relatives arrive enough to drain the sea, the soft-voiced dame, the glory of her home, well fulfils each seemly duty.
reading: Even in hard times, when the household cooks with a single pot of water, and even if kin arrive enough to drink the sea dry, the soft-spoken woman who keeps her duties as her settled way is the glory of the home.
nuance: The two hyperboles push in opposite directions, one pot against a sea, and her duty holds between them. Shanmuganar names the duty as hospitality.

pope: On every side the narrow dwelling lies open, on every part the rain drips down; yet, if the dame has noble gifts, praised by townsfolk for her modest worth, such a housewife's blest abode is indeed a home! The wife : 'placens uxor.' She is sweet to the eye, and adorned in the way that a lover loves; she enforces awe: her virtue shames the village folk; she is submissive; but in fitting place is stern, yet sweetly relents :—such a soft-voiced dame is a wife.
reading: Though the house is open on all four sides, tiny, and dripping with rain from the roof everywhere, where the excellent wife lives, capable in the highest virtues and praised by the town she lives in, that alone is a home.
nuance: Mudaliar draws the consequence the verse leaves unsaid, that other houses are forests, which completes the pair with 361.

reading: She is a wife who is lovely to the eye, adorns herself as her husband loves, holds him in awe, has the modesty that is shy before the town, and, in awe of him, knows when to sulk and relents sweetly: the soft-spoken woman.
nuance: Mudaliar gives two senses of ஊர்நாண் இயல்பினாள்: one who is shy before the townsfolk, or one whose conduct puts the townsfolk to shame. The translation attached to 383 in Pope's text takes the second. Sulking is counted among a good wife's virtues, provided it is well timed and quickly ended.

pope: ‘Whenever our spouse takes us in his embrace, we feel a timid shame as if we saw him then for the first time and they (wantons) daily, through desire of gain, submit to the embraces of many! How can this be?'
reading: However often our husband rises from our shoulders, we feel as shy as if we were seeing him for the first time; how, then, do those who embrace many men's chests for gain do it every day?
nuance: The wife speaks with wonder rather than scorn: she can't imagine the life she sets against her own.

pope: As the scroll that he reads, whose inmost heart well understands it, is goodly wealth with him who is graced by a generous spirit. As a keen weapon in the hand of a clear-souled hero, is the loveliness that a modest woman owns.
reading: Like the learning of one with understanding in his heart, like bright wealth in the hands of a generous man, like a sharp sword in the hand of a clear-minded hero, is the beauty a modest woman has.
nuance: The verse gives three similes and no explanation. Mudaliar supplies one: learning and a giver's wealth serve everyone, but a hero's sword destroys whoever stands against it, so a modest woman's beauty serves her husband alone and ruins any other who desires it. Shanmuganar pairs the first two similes as both useful and calls the sword only notable.

pope: 'The lord of the town has bought, it seems, black gram and red gram, a tuni and a pathakku, as if they were all the same! He, whose chest is broad as a mountain, having associated with the beautiful browed ones , — inferior to me! — unpurified, seeks my society too!'
reading: The lord of the town has bought, it seems, black gram and red gram, a tuni and a pathakku, all as one; the mountain-chested man who embraced bright-browed women unlike me comes, without bathing, to embrace me too.
nuance: The grain proverb is the wife's charge of indiscrimination: he treats the courtesans and his wife as one measure. Mudaliar says the verse shows the wife's own purity.

pope: ‘O minstrel, utter not cruel words, or if thou utter them, softly draw back thy step, and go to utter them to those who are like the lute's right side; for we, to the lord of the town, are as its left.'
reading: Minstrel, don't speak cruel words; if you must, step softly aside and go: to the lord of the town we are like the drum's left face, so tell it to those who are like its right face.
nuance: The right face of the துடி is struck and the left isn't, as Mudaliar explains: the wife calls herself the side that is no longer played. The minstrel is the husband's go-between.

pope: 'I am she, forsooth, that felt a pang when a fly alighted on the lord of the town, surrounded by cool rice-fields over which the waters gleam, where they pluck the rich grass! And I am she who have lived to look upon his breast adorned with cool sandal-wood paste, which has been warmly embraced by others.
reading: I am the one who grieved if a fly so much as flew over the lord of the cool town where water gleams once the reeds are pulled; and I am the one who has sat looking at his chest, its cool sandal paste smeared by breasts that struck it till sparks flew.
nuance: The repeated 'I am the one' sets two times side by side without comment, and the grief lies in the gap between them.

pope: 'Minstrel , utter not a gross falsehood, saying that he who wears a garland of opening buds will favour us!’ ‘To the lord of the town we are as the (tasteless) tip of the sugar-cane ; therefore, tell (such a tale) to them who are like its middle (sweet, juicy) joints.'
reading: Minstrel, don't tell the great lie that the man with the garland of opening buds will be kind to us; to the lord of the town we are like the end joints of the sugar-cane, so tell it to those who are like the middle joints.
nuance: Mudaliar gives the situation: the husband, back from a courtesan and refused, sends the minstrel to soothe her, and she mocks the messenger.

title: காமநுதலியல்
theme: The nature of love (காமநுதலியல்): love needs both union and the sulking that interrupts it, and its pain is separation, felt most at evening and in the rains. The chapter ends with a girl's flight with her lover, seen by her mother and herself, and a woman's grief at a lover gone to seek wealth.
structure_note: Nearly every quatrain is dramatised speech in the manner of akam poetry, and Mudaliar names the speaker and situation for most: the woman, her friend, the returning man, the lover praising her eyes, and the mother. 391 states a principle; 392-394 and 397 are separation at evening or in the rain; 396, 398 and 399 concern the elopement; 400 is separation for wealth.
source_issues: 394: Pope's translation is not aligned, and the Tamil reads சிதரா஢க்கண், a garbled character for சிதரரிக்கண் (Mudaliar: சிதர் அரி).
398: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text of 399 and his commentary on it, and 399 has no Shanmuganar commentary aligned.
399: the Tamil reads ஦வ்ருஉம், a garbled form of வெரூஉம் as Mudaliar glosses it; the printed verse has தீம்பாவை where Mudaliar and Shanmuganar's copy read பூம்பாவை.
400: Shanmuganar's field ends with his colophon and a closing verse in praise of the Naladiyar.

pope: 'Lord of the cool shore of the deep bay, where the gleaming ocean's restless billows beat! 'If there be no fond embrace, a sickly hue will spread itself (over her face); and, if there be no lovers' quarrels, love will lack its zest. ‘To embrace and disagree is the one way (of love).'
reading: Lord of the cool shore with long backwaters where the bright sea's restless waves beat: without embrace, pallor spreads; without sulking and pining, love has no salt; embracing and then sulking is one way.
nuance: Mudaliar takes உப்பு as sweetness and compares the Sanskrit theorists, who call separation the sweeter mode. The verse sets pallor and saltlessness as twin dangers: love needs both union and its interruption.

pope: ‘To those who were wont to strain in close embrace their own beloved whose broad breast was girt with garlands, when the rains patter down, it is as though one beat the funeral drum through all the regions where the muttering of the thunder is heard from out the clouds; since they are deprived of their loved one's society.'
reading: For women without the companion whose garlanded chest they would embrace till it swelled, the clouds thundering in every direction as the rain comes down sound like the beat of a funeral drum.
nuance: The verse doesn't say why the rain hurts. Mudaliar does: the man promised to come back by the rainy season, so the rains arriving without him are the sign of a broken word.

pope: At wildering eventide, when workmen all put by their tools, she culled choice flowers, and wove a gay garland ; — then let it fall from her hands, and wailed, 'What can this wreath avail to me who weep alone?’
reading: In the bewildering evening, when craftsmen have put away their tools, she was choosing flowers and weaving a garland; she threw down the garland in her hand and wept: 'What use is this garland to those without a companion?'
nuance: The verse ends on இம்மாலை, which can mean 'this garland' or 'this evening'. The commentators take it as the garland, but the double sense may be intended. Mudaliar has the friend report the scene to the man.

reading: Watching the setting sun, flicking away again and again with soft fingers the tears in her red-streaked eyes, sobbing, does she, alas, count the days on her soft fingers and reckon up my faults, lying on the bed with her arm for a pillow?
nuance: Mudaliar has the man speak this to his charioteer on the way home, imagining her grief, and cites Kural 1261. 'Our faults' turns her counting of days into a reckoning of his wrongs.

pope: ‘The little kingfisher seeing the eyes of my beloved (as she was disporting in the tank) and taking them for carp, followed her; but though it followed, and poised itself aloft, it darted not down, recognising her gleaming brow bent above them as a bow!
reading: Taking my beloved's eyes for carp, the little kingfisher followed her; but though it followed and rose eager to strike, it didn't dive, recognising her bright brow as a drawn bow.
nuance: Mudaliar calls it மயக்கவணி, the figure of mistaken identity, and has the man say it in wonder to his friend. Pope adds that the man is showing his own timid reverence.

pope: 'When I applied the (softest) cotton soaked in the red dye to the foot of her whose waist is lovely, and whose mouth breathes the fragrance of the red water-lily, did she not cry "gently, gently," and shrinking draw it back? And oh! has it endured the stony, desert path? '
reading: Feet that drew back in fear, crying 'gently, gently', even when red dye was applied with soft cotton: have they, alas, borne the stony desert path, the feet of my girl with lily-scented lips and lovely waist?
nuance: Mudaliar identifies the speaker as the girl's mother, who has learned that her daughter has gone with her lover through the wilderness. The verse sets the softest touch the mother knows against the hardest ground she can imagine.

pope: When those who con the palm leaf scrolls had ceased, in eve's din twilight hour, she thought of her absent spouse! and weeping plucked the flowers from out her wreath, and brushed the odorous sandal from her lovely breast!
reading: In the dim red evening, when the palm-leaf accountants fall silent, she thought of the parting of the man who married her, tore off her garland, and wept, rubbing away the sandal paste that adorned her lovely breasts.
nuance: Mudaliar records two settings: the friend describing her grief in his absence, or the friend telling the man she won't consent to his going. The second makes the parting still to come. He also reports a view that the silenced voices are schoolchildren reciting, which Shanmuganar adopts.

pope: 'Thou hast said, O maiden with burnished brace - lets ! have you strength to walk on the morrow after your beloved? When one (a warrior) has obtained a splendid horse, that very instant he has learned how to ride it! (his enthusiasm teaches him).
reading: You ask, friend of the bright bangles, whether I can walk tomorrow behind my young bull of a man through the forest that is hard to cross; a man who gets a great horse learns to ride it that very moment.
nuance: The answer is a proverb: the ability comes with the thing. Mudaliar spells out the hint, that following one's husband is not hard. Pope's 'his enthusiasm teaches him' is his own explanation.

pope: ‘My breast, my necklace of pearls, and my whole body she embraced ! I knew not what it portended. It was the sign, it seems, made by my lovely one that she was about to set out on the path where the herds of antelopes flee in fright from the tiger.'
reading: I didn't understand the sign at all when she embraced me so that my nipples, my pearls and my whole body were pressed; it seems the sign my sweet doll made meant she was about to take the path where herds of deer flee from the tiger.
nuance: Mudaliar has the mother speak after her daughter's flight. The embrace was a farewell that only the leaving gave meaning to.

pope: The triple-eyed (Civan), the crow, the hooded snake; the mother that bare me: what have these done amiss ? Maiden whose bosom bears the Gongu buds, all gold! The way my lover went for wealth is my pain.’
reading: The three-eyed one, the crow, the hooded snake, the mother who bore me: what wrong did they do? Friend with breasts like golden kongu buds, it is the road my lover took for wealth.
nuance: The verse names four suspects and acquits them without saying why. Both commentators supply the myths: Siva burned Kama and let him live again, the crow raised the koel's chick, the snake swallowed the moon and released it, and the mother let her live, so each lies behind one torment of separation. On that reading she refuses the easy targets and blames the one real cause, the journey for wealth. The verse closes the Naladiyar.
